title: A host-cell-based MRSA infection model identifies antibacterial activity not detected by conventional broth screening.
authors: Lee H; Lee Y; Lee H; Jeon Y; Shum D; Jang S
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Conventional broth screens may not capture host-associated conditions that influence antibiotic activity. This is relevant to Staphylococcus aureus, which can persist within or in association with host cells and contribute to recurrent infection.

OBJECTIVES: To establish a medium-throughput H460-S. aureus infection model for identifying compound activity in a host-cell infection context.

METHODS: GFP-expressing MRSA USA300 JE2 was used to infect NCI-H460 human lung carcinoma cells. After gentamicin treatment, compounds were added, and infection-associated bacterial burden was assessed by GFP fluorescence; propidium iodide (PI) was used as an initial membrane-compromise readout to define a PI-based non-cytotoxicity criterion. Representative hits underwent independent cytotoxicity testing in uninfected H460 cells using PI and resazurin. GFP responses were validated by viable cfu enumeration, and selected compounds were tested in RAW264.7 macrophages. The assay was applied to 2320 compounds.

RESULTS: The assay was screening-compatible (mean GFP Z' factor 0.7), and reference antibiotics showed compound-specific shifts relative to broth testing. Of 2320 compounds, 1468 met the predefined PI-based non-cytotoxicity criterion; 163 also showed mean GFP inhibition ≥80% across two screening replicates and underwent dose-response testing. Of these, 105 were active in both assay formats, whereas 58 showed activity in the host-cell assay but no detectable direct antibacterial activity against the bacteria in broth up to 100 μM. GFP fluorescence generally tracked viable bacterial burden, although the relationship varied among compounds.

CONCLUSIONS: The H460 infection assay complements direct antibacterial testing in broth by identifying compound activity that emerges in a host-cell infection context.

title: Effects of afabicin desphosphono (Debio 1452) on gut microbiota and subsequent risk of simulated Clostridium difficile infection in an in vitro human gut model.
authors: Normington C; Mitra S; Clark E; Berry A; Bentley K; Chogugudza C; Ewin D; Spittal W; Bromley J; Kaur K; Chaves RL; Cameron DR; Moura IB; Wilcox MH; Chilton CH
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Afabicin is a novel inhibitor of bacterial fatty-acid synthesis currently in clinical development for the treatment of staphylococcal bone and joint infections and acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections. This narrow-spectrum agent has been shown to spare murine and human gut microbiota. Afabicin (Debio 1450) is administered as a prodrug that is converted to the active moiety, Debio 1452. A validated in vitro human gut model was used to assess the impact of two Debio 1452 dosing regimens on gut microbiota composition, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) gene abundance and risk of simulated Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI).

METHODS: Four gut models were inoculated with pooled human faeces and challenged with 107 cfu C. difficile spores. Models were then exposed to either low-dose Debio 1452 (17.8 mg/L twice daily), high-dose Debio 1452 (35.7 mg/L twice daily), levofloxacin (140.55 mg/L once daily) or a dimethyl sulfoxide control, each for 14 days, followed by a 4-week observation period. C. difficile populations, cytotoxin levels and microbiota profiles (culture and sequencing) were monitored throughout.

RESULTS: Neither Debio 1452 regimen caused substantial disruption to gut microbiota or triggered simulated CDI, closely resembling the non-antimicrobial control. By contrast, levofloxacin induced marked microbiota perturbation, followed by C. difficile germination, proliferation and toxin production. Levofloxacin exposure also increased the abundance of several AMR gene classes, including macrolide, tetracycline and beta-lactam resistance determinants: an effect not observed with Debio 1452.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that Debio 1452 exerts minimal impact on the gut microbiota and may carry a lower risk of CDI compared with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

title: MaldiSuite: a Python ecosystem for MALDI-TOF spectral processing and analysis in antimicrobial resistance research.
authors: Rocchi E; Sala C; Castellani G
abstract:
MOTIVATION: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat requiring faster diagnostics than the 24-48 h needed for phenotypic antibiotic-susceptibility testing. Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry is widely used in clinical microbiology for species identification but does not directly capture AMR phenotypes. Machine learning on MALDI-TOF spectra offers a promising solution, yet existing software remains fragmented across legacy R preprocessing tools and ad hoc Python scripts, lacking standardized workflows, shared application programming interfaces (APIs), and safeguards against train-test leakage.

RESULTS: We present MaldiSuite, a unified Python ecosystem built on a shared data model and a scikit-learn-compatible API. It integrates three packages: MaldiAMRKit (Bruker-native and open-format input/output, standardized composable preprocessing, spectral warping, and temporal drift monitoring); MaldiBatchKit (multi-site batch correction, including MALDI-specific methods, with batch-mixing diagnostics); and MaldiDeepKit (four deep-learning classifiers: multilayer perceptron, one-dimensional convolutional neural network, residual network, and Vision Transformer). All components compose within sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline with leak-safe fit/transform semantics. On the public multi-site Database of Resistance Information on Antimicrobials and MALDI-TOF Mass Spectra (DRIAMS), MaldiSuite achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of up to 0.92 on the DRIAMS-A Staphylococcus aureus/oxacillin task, and a leakage experiment quantifies the optimistic bias that its leak-safe cross-validation removes.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: MaldiSuite is available on PyPI under the MIT licence (pip install maldisuite). Source code: https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiSuite, https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiAMRKit, https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiBatchKit, https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiDeepKit. The package versions described here and the analysis code of this paper (https://github.com/EttoreRocchi/MaldiSuite-paper), with the pinned environments, are archived at 10.5281/zenodo.24199316.

DOCUMENTATION: https://ettorerocchi.github.io/MaldiSuite/.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Evaluation of biofilm-related phenotypic and genotypic characteristics in clinical Acinetobacter baumannii isolates from Gorgan, northern Iran.
authors: Tanhaei M; Elahi G; Izanloo A; Ghomi MK; Ghaemi EA; Salamat F; Ardebili A
abstract: Biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance are key virulence characteristics of Acinetobacter baumannii that contribute to its persistence in hospital environments and the development of nosocomial infections. This study investigated antimicrobial susceptibility, biofilm formation potential, and the distribution of biofilm-associated genes in clinical isolates of A. baumannii. Endotracheal aspirate (ETA) specimens were obtained from intensive care unit (ICU) and subjected to microbiological culture for identification of A. baumannii. Isolates underwent testing for antimicrobial susceptibility, biofilm formation capacity, twitching motility, and the presence of the biofilm-associated genes. A total of 108 A. baumannii isolates were identified. All isolates exhibited multidrug resistance (MDR), and 98.1% were extensively drug-resistant (XDR). Eighty-seven (80.6%) isolates produced biofilm, including 27.8% strong-biofilm producers, 28.7% moderate-biofilm producers, and 24% weak-biofilm producers. No significant correlation was found between biofilm formation and resistance profiles or MDR/XDR phenotypes. The frequency of twitching motility phenotype was 34.2%. The most prevalent biofilm-related gene was bap (100%), followed by csuE (96.3%), bfmS (90.7%), bfmR (72.2%), ompA (52.7%), pilA (18.5%), and epsA (16.6%). All isolates carried more than three genes simultaneously. A significant relationship was not found between biofilm formation ability and the persence of biofilm-associated genes among A. baumannii isolates. The study demonstrated the high prevalence of MDR and XDR A. baumannii isolates capable of biofilm formation and highlighted the ongoing challenge of treating infections in intensive care settings. The lack of association between biofilm formation, gene presence, and resistance patterns suggests that additional factors influence the pathogenicity and antibiotic tolerance of A. baumannii.

title: Fosfomycin-containing combination therapies in carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales infections: limitations of fosfomycin MIC-based interpretation for clinical outcomes.
authors: Törüyenler Coşkunpınar M; Doğangönül Doyğun LE; Tekbaş Z; Öcal D; Çınar G
abstract: Therapeutic options for carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) infections remain limited, and the clinical interpretation of fosfomycin (FOF) minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) is uncertain. We retrospectively evaluated 126 adults with CPE infections treated with intravenous FOF-containing combination therapy for ≥72 h between January 2022 and December 2024. FOF MICs were determined by agar dilution. Klebsiella pneumoniae accounted for 96.8% of isolates. Clinical response was achieved in 63.5% of patients, and 30-day mortality was 35%. Higher FOF MICs (OR 1.004; 95% CI 1.000-1.007) and SOFA scores (OR 1.15; 95% CI 1.03-1.29) were independently associated with clinical non-response. However, FOF MIC showed limited discriminatory ability (AUC = 0.60) and was not associated with mortality, whereas SOFA score remained independently associated with mortality. Rather than identifying a clear binary threshold, our findings suggest a continuous association between increasing FOF MIC and clinical non-response, supporting its interpretation as a complementary microbiological parameter alongside disease severity.

title: Blood-based rapid molecular diagnostics for sepsis: current advances, clinical applications, and future perspectives.
authors: Shanmugam K; Chinna Kumar ND; Sakthivel V; R S; Ganesan PS; D S; Balasubramanian R
abstract: Sepsis remains a leading global cause of morbidity and mortality, necessitating rapid pathogen identification and targeted antimicrobial therapy. While conventional blood cultures are the diagnostic reference standard for bloodstream infection (BSI), they are limited by slow turnaround times, low sensitivity following antibiotic exposure, and delayed antimicrobial resistance (AMR) detection. This review examines rapid molecular diagnostics for sepsis and BSI, including PCR, multiplex syndromic panels, next-generation sequencing (NGS), metagenomic NGS (mNGS), isothermal amplification, rapid phenotypic testing, and point-of-care tools, and separates assays performed directly on whole blood from those performed on positive blood cultures. Multiplex PCR panels performed on positive blood cultures rapidly identify common pathogens and resistance genes and shorten time to appropriate therapy, although a consistent, statistically significant mortality reduction has not been demonstrated. Direct-from-blood assays and mNGS can detect nucleic acids of rare, fastidious, or non-cultured organisms, but a positive result does not by itself establish viable bacteremia or the cause of organ dysfunction. Isothermal techniques offer portable options for decentralized settings, although most data remain analytical. Despite these advantages, implementation challenges include target restrictions, genotype-phenotype discordances, contamination risks, high costs, and infrastructure demands. Ultimately, rapid molecular methods should complement, rather than replace, conventional cultures and phenotypic susceptibility testing to optimize antimicrobial stewardship and patient outcomes.

title: Which rapid susceptibility testing methods for new antibiotics in clinical practice? a narrative review.
authors: Jaureguy F; Dortet L; Zahar JR; Jeannot K; Dinh A
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria are among the leading contributors to antimicrobial resistance-associated morbidity and mortality worldwide, underscoring the need for prompt and effective antimicrobial therapy. Novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) combinations and cefiderocol have expanded therapeutic options against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii. However, conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) methods remain slow, resistance to these newer agents is emerging, and delayed results may prolong empirical broad-spectrum or inappropriate therapy.

OBJECTIVES: To summarize available rapid AST methods for novel anti-Gram-negative antibiotics, with a focus on analytical performances, practical limitations and laboratory implementation.

SOURCES: Narrative review of the literature on molecular and phenotypic rapid AST methods, including rapid disc diffusion method, AST platforms, and colorimetric assays applied to novel BL/BLI combinations and cefiderocol. Relevant literature was identified through non-systematic searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase conducted between January 2022 and May 2026.

CONTENT: Molecular assays allow rapid detection of resistance genes but remain complementary to phenotypic AST methods, owing to incomplete coverage of resistance mechanisms and imperfect genotype-phenotype correlation. Rapid disc diffusion and automated AST methods shorten time to results (TTR) and enable earlier phenotypic categorization, while innovative AST platforms can provide accurate minimum inhibitory concentrations. Rapid, low-cost colorimetric assays, not yet commercialised, can detect resistant isolates regardless of the underlying mechanism. However, only a few novel BL/BLI combinations are covered by these methods, and their performances depend strongly on the resistance mechanism. Cefiderocol testing is particularly challenging, as reliable susceptibility determination requires iron-depleted conditions, which limits rapid testing. Clinical outcome data remain scarce.

IMPLICATIONS: Rapid AST methods for novel antibiotics is advancing and can reduce TTR, but gaps persist in performances, antibiotic coverage and evidence of clinical impact. Integration into optimized laboratory workflows and antimicrobial stewardship programmes is essential to translate faster results into improved prescribing and patient outcomes.

title: Genomic epidemiology, population structure and lineage-associated genomic variation in KPC-producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
authors: Zhou T; Li N; Li J; Chen M; Li Y
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Metagenomics; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: KPC-producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa (KPC-PA) has emerged as an important multidrug-resistant pathogen, yet its population structure and lineage-associated genomic variation remain incompletely understood. We investigated the genomic epidemiology of an international collection of KPC-PA genomes to characterize population structure, evolutionary patterns, and lineage-associated genomic features.

METHODS: A complete genome of a clinical ST463 isolate (PA328) was generated using hybrid sequencing and analyzed together with 655 publicly available KPC-PA genomes. Comparative genomic, phylogenomic, pangenome, recombination, and Bayesian temporal analyses were performed to investigate population structure and identify genomic features associated with major lineages.

RESULTS: Among 656 KPC-PA genomes, blaKPC-2 (99.5%) and ST463 (43.6%) were predominant. Population genomic analysis resolved eight major phylogenetic lineages with distinct sequence-type compositions and geographic distributions, including ST463 in China, ST282 in the United States, and ST654 in Chile. Assembly-based screening identified candidate frameshift calls in genes annotated as being involved in metabolism, iron acquisition, transport, and virulence-associated functions, providing potential targets for further investigation using read-level confirmation. Descriptive analyses revealed lineage-associated patterns of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements co-occurrence. Within ST463, an operationally defined high-recombination region (HRR) contained genes annotated as being related to secretion systems, biofilm formation, metabolism, and mobile genetic elements. Bayesian analysis estimated the time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the sampled Chinese ST463 population at approximately 2005. Partial similarity between plasmid sequences and the HRR suggested potential evolutionary connections, although their specific relationship requires further investigation.

CONCLUSIONS: This study characterizes the population structure and lineage-associated genomic variation of KPC-PA within a large international genome collection. The findings provide a descriptive genomic resource for understanding KPC-PA evolution and surveillance, and highlight candidate genomic features that warrant further structure-aware analyses and experimental investigation.

title: Terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton indotineae and SQLE mutations in human and animal dermatophytosis: a One Health perspective.
authors: Taha M; Abdallah SA; Zaki MSA; Alqahtani AJ; Shaker A; Tartor YH
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dermatophytosis is an increasing public health and veterinary concern amid the emergence of terbinafine-resistant dermatophytes and recurrent treatment failures. This study characterized dermatophyte isolates from human and animal cases, assessed their antifungal susceptibility, and investigated terbinafine resistance-associated mutations in the squalene epoxidase (SQLE) gene.

METHODS: Twenty-two Trichophyton mentagrophytes complex isolates were recovered from skin scrapings of patients with recurrent tinea corporis and tinea cruris, and 39 isolates were obtained from animals with clinical signs of ringworm. Isolates were identified by sequencing the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region, and antifungal susceptibility was determined by broth microdilution method. The SQLE gene was sequenced to detect resistance-associated substitutions.

RESULTS: All human isolates were identified as Trichophyton indotineae; animal isolates comprised T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum, Microsporum canis, and one feline-derived T. rubrum isolate. Fluconazole resistance occurred among both human and animal isolates, but terbinafine resistance was largely confined to human-derived T. indotineae, while most animal isolates, particularly T. verrucosum and M. canis, remained susceptible. SQLE sequencing identified several resistance-associated substitutions: Phe397Leu, the most frequent mutation in T. indotineae, was consistently linked to elevated terbinafine MICs (0.5-16 μg/mL), and Gln408Leu was associated with an MIC of 8 μg/mL and pronounced growth on terbinafine-containing medium. Resistance-associated substitutions were also detected in animal isolates, including Leu393Ser (T. rubrum) and Ile415Ser (T. mentagrophytes), both recovered from cats. Three isolates carried two concurrent substitutions, Phe397Leu and Ala448Thr. ITS-based phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the studied human clinical isolates clustered with genetically related isolates from multiple countries, with no evident geographic segregation, suggesting widespread dissemination of closely related T. indotineae genotypes.

CONCLUSION: Terbinafine-resistant T. indotineae predominates among human dermatophyte isolates, driven largely by SQLE mutations, especially Phe397Leu. The presence of resistance-associated SQLE mutations in animal-derived dermatophytes indicates spillover of human-adapted resistant lineages into companion animals, underscoring the need for integrated antifungal susceptibility testing and One Health-based surveillance.

title: Delafloxacin activity against fluoroquinolone-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa: in vitro activity and mutant prevention concentration.
authors: Cintora-Mairal C; de la Rosa JMO; Cisneros JM; Lepe JA; Rodríguez-Villodres Á
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pseudomonas aeruginosa frequently develops resistance to fluoroquinolones limiting the usefulness of these agents for the treatment of healthcare-associated infections. This study evaluated the in vitro activity of delafloxacin in comparison with the older-generation fluoroquinolones against clinical P. aeruginosa isolates, and explored its potential to suppress the selection of resistant subpopulations.

METHODS: One hundred clinical isolates were tested against ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and delafloxacin by broth microdilution method. Susceptibility was interpreted according to EUCAST criteria for ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin and FDA criteria for delafloxacin. Mutant prevention concentrations (MPCs) were determined for the three fluoroquinolones in 12 selected isolates using a high-inoculum agar-based method.

RESULTS: Resistance was observed in 29% of isolates for both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, compared with 25% for delafloxacin. Among isolates resistant to both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, 32.0% were susceptible or intermediate to delafloxacin. The median MPC/MIC ratio was 4 (IQR, 4-8) for delafloxacin, compared with 8 (IQR, 7-16) for ciprofloxacin and 16 (IQR, 7-64) for levofloxacin.

DISCUSSION: Overall, delafloxacin retained in vitro activity against a subset of fluoroquinolone-resistant P. aeruginosa isolates and showed a favorable mutant prevention profile in the isolates tested, with a lower median MPC/MIC ratio than ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin. These findings provide preliminary evidence supporting further investigation of delafloxacin against fluoroquinolone-resistant P. aeruginosa.

title: Phenotypic Methicillin Resistance, mecA Carriage, Virulence Gene Profiles, and Antimicrobial Susceptibility of Clinical Staphylococcus aureus Isolates in Sana'a, Yemen.
authors: Al Hatami SM; Al-Mansoub MA; Al-Jaufy AY; Alshami HZ; Alafif AA; Alkassar WY; Al-Haifi AY; Al-Worafi Y; Al-Shami AS
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) remains a major clinical concern because antimicrobial resistance may coexist with virulence determinants that increase disease severity.

OBJECTIVE: To characterize methicillin resistance, mecA carriage, selected virulence-associated genes (pvl, hla, and tst), and antimicrobial susceptibility among clinical S. aureus isolates from Sana'a, Yemen.

METHODS: A laboratory-based cross-sectional study was conducted from September 2023 to July 2024. A total of 305 S. aureus isolates from wound, pus, and blood specimens were identified using conventional and automated microbiological methods. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by disk diffusion and minimum inhibitory concentration methods according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute criteria. Conventional PCR detected mecA, pvl, hla, and tst. Associations were assessed using categorical statistical tests, with p < 0.05 considered significant.

RESULTS: Of 305 isolates, 250 (82.0%) were phenotypically classified as MRSA and 55 (18.0%) as methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA). mecA, pvl, hla, and tst were detected in 72.5%, 31.1%, 13.1%, and 1.3% of isolates, respectively. mecA was more prevalent in MRSA than MSSA (84.0% vs 20.0%, p < 0.001), whereas pvl (26.0% vs 54.5%, p < 0.001) and hla (10.8% vs 23.6%, p = 0.011) were more frequent in MSSA. tst occurred only in MRSA (1.6%). Resistance was highest to amoxicillin-clavulanate (100%), oxacillin (97.6%), and penicillin (96.4%), but rare to vancomycin (0.4%), rifampicin (0.4%), and linezolid (0.8%). mecA carriage was significantly associated with clindamycin, tetracycline, and erythromycin resistance.

CONCLUSION: Clinical S. aureus isolates from Sana'a showed high phenotypic methicillin resistance, extensive β-lactam resistance, and heterogeneous virulence-gene carriage. Higher pvl and hla prevalence among MSSA indicates that important virulence determinants are not confined to MRSA. Phenotypic-genotypic discordance supports combining standardized susceptibility testing with molecular surveillance and strengthening antimicrobial stewardship, infection control, and genomic surveillance in Yemen.

title: FusionGDB 3.0: integrating breakpoints, generating personalized sequences, and inferring tumorigenic scenarios for human fusion genes.
authors: Kim P; Yang Z; Kim J; Amjad W; Dang VT; Kumar H; Zhou X; Rousan DHA
abstract: FusionGDB has served diverse biological, health, and clinical research communities as a unique functional annotation knowledgebase of human fusion genes. In this study, we report an updated resource of human fusion gene annotation (FusionGDB 3.0), available at https://compbio.uth.edu/FusionGDB/. FusionGDB 3.0 includes substantial content updates: 156K up-to-date human fusion genes established by integrating 216K RNA-seq-based and 100K WGS-based breakpoint events, comprehensive open reading frame annotations, protein domain retention searches, and 1.13 million personalized fusion protein sequences reflecting individual nsSNVs from TCGA and CCLE, as well as N- and C-truncated protein sequences alongside canonical in-frame products. Furthermore, it incorporates 18K potential tumorigenic scenarios, supported by evidence from the literature, spanning drug-targetable gene group fusions, the epigenomic architecture around breakpoint junctions, and therapeutic prioritization scoring. FusionGDB 3.0 establishes a systematic framework for the functional annotation of coding structural variants. FusionGDB 3.0 serves as a pivotal reference knowledgebase for the genomics, oncology, and precision pharmacology communities, while also functioning as a foundational benchmark dataset for training and validating machine learning models, structural biology platforms, and AI-driven therapeutic discovery pipelines.

title: Microbial risks of raw camel milk: Salmonella identification and antimicrobial susceptibility profiling in the pastoral settings of Somali region, Ethiopia.
authors: Bitew Z; Asnake K; Gebrezihier BG; Yihunie FB; Molla G
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Camel milk is the primary means of ensuring food security in pastoral settings of the Somali Region, where usually consumed raw. This untreated camel milk is believed to be a major source of foodborne illnesses; yet, the microbial risks-especially Salmonella contamination of raw camel milk and its antibiograms-are poorly understood in the area. Thus, the study was conducted to identify Salmonella contamination in raw camel milk, determine its antibiograms, and assess community perceptions and public health risks of raw camel milk consumption in the study area.

METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted to assess community awareness in public health risks of raw camel milk and identify Salmonella contamination in the production chains: udders, buckets, and bulk milk of raw camel milk, and determine its antibiogram. A total of 384 raw camel milk samples were collected from buckets (n = 225), bulk milk (n = 49), and udders (n = 110) and bacteriologically analyzed by isolation and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Chi-square, Phi, and Cramer's V-value were employed to assess the factors and the strength of associations with Salmonella recovery rates, respectively.

RESULT: Out of 384 total samples analyzed, 165 Salmonella isolates were recovered, representing an overall recovery rate of 43.0%. These isolates comprised 56 typhoidal Salmonella species (representing 14.6% of total samples) and 109 non-typhoidal Salmonella species (representing 28.4% of total samples). A high recovery rate of Salmonella was observed in bucket milk (109; 48.4%), and bulk milk (20; 40.8%), and bacterial isolation rate were strongly associated (all, p < 0.05; Phi = 0.599 to 0.491) with poor milkers' hand hygiene (122; 84.1%), buckets and bulk milk not cleaned regularly (84; 76.4%, and 17; 70.8%) respectively, and unsmoked buckets (92; 68.7%). The invitro antibiogram confirmed that isolates were resistant to Erythromycin (100%), Ampicillin (87.5%), and Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (62.5%), while showing high susceptibility to Streptomycin and Amikacin (100%) and Ceftriaxone (66.7%). Nine (75%) isolates of non-typhoidal Salmonella species developed multidrug resistance (MDR), resistant to Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, Ampicillin, and Chloramphenicol. Notably, only the non-typhoidal Salmonella were resistant to Ceftriaxone (41.7%); conversely, the typhoidal Salmonella were highly susceptible (83.3%). Also, all typhoidal Salmonella isolates (100%) were completely resistant to Ampicillin.

CONCLUSION: A high prevalence of both typhoidal and non-typhoidal Salmonella species is identified in raw camel milk under poor hygienic practices of milking and public health awareness. The presence of multidrug-resistant Salmonella isolates may have a public health concern in causing food-borne illness and posing a drug resistance threat.

title: Phylogenomics and antimicrobial resistance genes of invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella in the Ashanti region of Ghana.
authors: Agyapong FO; Owusu M; Darko E; Owusu-Ansah M; Twumasi-Ankrah S; Boahen KG; Nkrumah G; Parčina M; Karačić S; Ritter M; Debrah LB; Debrah AY; Jeon HJ; Marks F; Owusu-Dabo E; Adu-Sarkodie Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) disease is a major public health threat in developing countries, yet molecular epidemiological data from Ghana remain limited. This study characterizes the phylogenomic profiles and antimicrobial resistance determinants of iNTS isolates recovered from human blood cultures in Ghana.

METHODS: Over an eight-year surveillance period (2016-2023), thirty-one (31) iNTS blood culture isolates-drawn from a total of 271 bacterial pathogens identified-underwent whole-genome sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq platform. The iNTS isolates' genomic data were analyzed for serovar distribution, MLST profiles, Antimicrobial resistant (AMR) genes and virulence markers including plasmids and Salmonella Pathogenicity Islands (SPIs). Clades of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium ST 313 and lineages of Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis ST11 were determined referencing regionally important circulating strains.

RESULTS: S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis together constituted 67.7% (21/31) of iNTS isolates circulating in Ghana, whereas the remaining serovars were largely confined to isolates obtained within the past three years of the study period. S. Typhimurium ST 313 strains were of the L2 and L3 lineages which are associated with invasive disease in sub-Sahara Africa while S. Enteritidis ST 11 isolates clustered with the Global Epidemic and Central East Africa clades which are linked to widespread transmission and sub-Sahara African regional adaptation. All iNTS isolates harboured several SPIs known for invasiveness while 77.4.0% (24/31) carried plasmids including IncFIB(S) and IncFII(S). Nearly half (48.8%, 15/31) of the isolates carried at least one AMR gene with about 30.0% (9/31) harboring multiple AMR genes conferring resistance to three or more antibiotic classes. The commonest AMR gene identified was the blaTEM-1 gene coding for beta lactamase enzyme while quinolone resistant gene (qnrS1) was the least common.

CONCLUSION: Circulating iNTS pathogens in Ghana are diversified including S. Typhimurium ST313 lineages and S. Enteritidis ST 11 clades regionally known for invasive disease. These strains carry remarkable markers of virulence highlighting the need for enhanced surveillance and institution of preventive policies. Our findings highlight the utility of whole-genome sequencing for tracking circulating iNTS lineages and strengthening public health surveillance in Ghana.

title: A global livestock virome catalog links viruses with resistome assembly.
authors: Jiang L; Li B; Lei L; Liu Z; Sun W; Ma L; Cha CJ; Johnson T; Yu J; Chen Z; Zhang Y; Wang G; Yao C; Fan X; Liu F; Yang W; Wang W; Zhang H; Tiedje J; Qian X
abstract: Livestock manure is a prominent One Health setting for antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet the contribution of viruses to resistome assembly remains unresolved. Here we compile the Livestock Manure Virus Database (LMVD), a global catalog of 1,330,372 viral operational taxonomic units reconstructed from 4,017 metagenomes. Livestock manure viral communities exhibit restricted biogeographic distributions, and antibiotic use and farming scale show the highest relative predictive importance for viral diversity. Viral genomes contained 78 antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) subtypes, representing 9.1% of resistome diversity in livestock manure, but virus-encoded ARGs were infrequent. Bacteriophages instead showed extensive predicted links to bacterial hosts, with nearly all antibiotic-resistant bacteria linked to viruses, predominantly temperate viruses, and enrichment in pathogenic antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Together, these findings place bounds on the contribution of viruses to direct ARG dissemination and indicate that lysogenic interactions with resistant hosts may shape AMR risk.

title: Rationalizing local antibiotic therapies for biofilm-associated ventricular assist device driveline infections: an in vitro simulation.
authors: Qu Y; McGiffin D; Kaye DM; Sun Y; Spencer N; Peleg AY
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Recurrent ventricular assist device (VAD) driveline infections due to microbial biofilm growths in the driveline tunnel may be managed by local antibiotic therapies. This study aims to use in vitro simulation to rationalize and optimize local antibiotic therapies for biofilm-associated deep driveline infections.

METHODS: Laboratory reference strains and clinical isolates of Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis obtained from patients with driveline infections, together with seven conventional antibiotics, were selected for this study. Antibiotic susceptibility tests were performed for bacteria grown as microplate-based biofilms using endpoints relevant to clinical driveline infection management outcomes. Bacterial lethality and metabolic activity were investigated for each antibiotic across different concentrations to mechanistically understand their anti-biofilm efficacy. Localized antibiotics delivered via commercially available carriers were evaluated against staphylococcal biofilms established on driveline cutouts within simulated tissue tunnels, mimicking the conditions encountered in deep driveline infections.

RESULTS: Gentamicin and vancomycin combination at high concentrations outperformed single antibiotics or other combinations in eradicating microplate-based staphylococcal biofilms, achieving a complete killing in 3/5 strains. High concentrations of gentamicin demonstrated potent bacterial lethality that was less dependent on cell metabolic activity, whereas cell wall-targeting antibiotics killed only metabolically active cells. STIMULAN beads embedded with gentamicin and vancomycin showed ideal pharmacodynamics in the driveline tunnel and effectively kill driveline-based staphylococcal biofilms; vancomycin powder or TYRX incorporating rifampicin and minocycline only demonstrated limited anti-staphylococcal biofilm efficacy.

CONCLUSIONS: Local administration of high concentrations of gentamicin, ideally in combination with vancomycin, may serve as a potential curative strategy for staphylococcal driveline infections.

title: Caffeic acid phenethyl ester targets elongation factor Tu and displays in vitro and in vivo anti-gonococcal activity.
authors: Sun X; Zhang J; Yang F; Yan J; Song S; Yuan D; Qin Y; Lin X; Duttwyler S; Rao Y; Xu F; van der Veen S
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Ceftriaxone is the only remaining empirical antimicrobial therapy for Neisseria gonorrhoeae; however, global dissemination of the ceftriaxone-resistant FC428 clone jeopardizes the efficacy of ceftriaxone treatment. This study aimed to characterize the anti-gonococcal activity of caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) and identify its antimicrobial target.

METHODS: In vitro antimicrobial activity of CAPE was analysed by MIC testing and bactericidal activity analysis in time-kill assays. In vivo antimicrobial activity was evaluated in a mouse vaginal tract infection model. The target of CAPE was determined by pull-down assays and validated by isothermal titration calorimetry and enzyme activity assays. Specific target sites were identified by molecular docking analysis and validated by interaction studies with mutant proteins.

RESULTS: CAPE displayed a MIC of 16-32 µM against a collection of multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae strains, including isolates associated with the FC428 clone. Furthermore, CAPE displayed potent bactericidal activity and enhanced gonococcal clearance from a mouse infection model at a dose of 30 mg/kg. Pull-down assays identified elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) as the molecular target of CAPE, with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 3.34 μM. CAPE effectively accumulated intracellularly in N. gonorrhoeae and inhibited protein synthesis. Finally, CAPE displayed synergistic antimicrobial activity with ceftriaxone against strains associated with the FC428 clone.

CONCLUSIONS: CAPE exerts in vitro and in vivo antimicrobial activity against N. gonorrhoeae through inhibition of EF-Tu. CAPE displays synergistic activity with ceftriaxone, making it an interesting compound for further evaluation of a CAPE plus ceftriaxone dual anti-gonococcal therapy.

title: In vitro evaluation of the activity of pairwise combinations of zoliflodacin, gepotidacin and ciprofloxacin against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
authors: Bowcutt B; Mukherjee A; Palace SG; Grad YH
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Two new antibiotics, zoliflodacin and gepotidacin, were recently approved for the treatment of urogenital gonorrhoea. While combination therapy could, in principle, delay the emergence and spread of resistance, doing so depends on the absence of antagonism between the co-administered drugs. Furthermore, even in the absence of combination therapy, overlapping use of these new antibiotics with one another or with fluoroquinolones will likely occur in clinical contexts due to co-treatment for other infections or successive treatment for gonorrhoea if a second antibiotic is taken before the first has been cleared. We investigated the in vitro interactions of pairwise combinations of zoliflodacin, gepotidacin and ciprofloxacin with a panel of clinical isolates and an isogenic panel with relevant resistance mutations.

METHODS: An isogenic panel with gyrA and gyrB resistance mutations and a panel of clinical isolates representing a diversity of strain backgrounds were tested with agar dilution checkerboard assays of zoliflodacin, gepotidacin and ciprofloxacin.

RESULTS: We observed no evidence of antagonism for all pairwise combinations of zoliflodacin, gepotidacin and ciprofloxacin, including in strains with elevated ciprofloxacin MICs.

CONCLUSIONS: The lack of in vitro antagonism among these antibiotics across a range of epidemiologically important genetic backgrounds and clinically relevant resistance mutations indicates that combination use or overlapping use may not diminish efficacy, although additional experimental models are needed to establish the clinical usefulness of combination therapy.

title: Alternative oral therapies join the game against OXA-48 producers: in vitro evidence for cefixime ± amoxicillin/clavulanate in paediatric febrile UTI and mecillinam in lower UTI.
authors: Gits-Muselli M; Dawoud H; Benhadid-Brahmi Y; Monjault A; Zenon J; Cointe A; Bonacorsi S; Birgy A
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: OXA-48-like carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales are an increasing cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs), limiting oral treatment options. Cefixime activity against OXA-48-like enzymes remains poorly documented, whereas pivmecillinam has shown promising activity in surveillance studies. We assessed the in vitro activity of cefixime, cefixime combined with amoxicillin/clavulanate, mecillinam and mecillinam plus amoxicillin/clavulanate against paediatric OXA-48-like-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, with or without ESBL co-production.

METHODS: We tested 111 non-duplicate paediatric isolates collected in France: 76 E. coli and 35 K. pneumoniae. Isolates were classified as OXA-48-like only, OXA-48-like/ESBL or OXA-48-like with other additional resistance mechanisms. MICs were determined by Etest and mecillinam susceptibility was also assessed by disc diffusion method.

RESULTS: Cefixime was highly active against OXA-48-like-only isolates, with MIC90 values of 0.5 mg/L for E. coli and 0.094 mg/L for K. pneumoniae. Activity decreased markedly in ESBL co-producers (MIC90: 64-256 mg/L), but amoxicillin/clavulanate partially restored activity (MIC90: 2 mg/L for E. coli and 8 mg/L for K. pneumoniae). Mecillinam remained active across groups, with >95% susceptibility among OXA-48-like-only isolates and MIC90 values ≤0.5 mg/L, although susceptibility decreased in isolates with additional resistance mechanisms. Co-resistance to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and ciprofloxacin was frequent.

CONCLUSIONS: Given frequent co-resistance to standard oral agents and the limited availability of alternatives, cefixime (with or without amoxicillin/clavulanate) and pivmecillinam may represent an oral option for paediatric UTIs caused by OXA-48-like ± ESBL-producing E. coli or K. pneumoniae. Clinical studies will help clarify the potential role of these oral treatment options in paediatric UTIs.

title: Artificial intelligence-assisted interpretation of antimicrobial susceptibility testing in clinical microbiology: a scoping review.
authors: Hikmat R; Mardhiyah A; Syaefudin D; Tumanggor RD; Sukardin S; Mailani F
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to accelerate and standardize antimicrobial susceptibility testing in clinical microbiology.

PURPOSE: This scoping review mapped artificial intelligence applications for predicting and interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility, including data modalities, diagnostic performance, validation, and implementation gaps.

METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Embase were searched through 17 August 2026. English-language original studies published from 2017 to 2026 were included. Two independent reviewers conducted study selection, data charting, and synthesis, with third-reviewer adjudication when needed.

RESULTS: Nineteen studies were included. Applications involved whole-genome sequencing, transcriptomic and metagenomic data, mass spectrometry, microscopy, and disk-diffusion images. Genomic approaches predominated, while image-based systems showed promise for laboratory automation. Performance was generally high but varied across organisms, antimicrobials, and validation settings.

CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence shows strong potential for antimicrobial susceptibility assessment, but multicenter validation and workflow integration remain essential.

title: Five-year species-resolved antimicrobial susceptibility surveillance of nontuberculous mycobacteria at Beijing Chest Hospital, China, 2021-2025.
authors: Gong Z; Zhao J; Shi Y; Su D; Yang B; Lin W; Miao T; Ma S; Wang G
journal: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) surveillance often relies on species frequency and categorical susceptibility results, which may overlook changes in species composition and underlying MIC distributions. We examined temporal changes in species composition, host associations, species-resolved MIC phenotypes, temporal MIC shifts, and the relationship between clinical breakpoints and epidemiological MIC boundaries.

METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed routine NTM identification, clinical, and antimicrobial susceptibility data from Beijing Chest Hospital during 2021-2025. Analyses used the first single-NTM isolate recorded for each patient during the study period (n = 790). Species trends, host associations, and temporal MIC changes were assessed using logistic, multivariable, and cumulative-link models, with rank-based sensitivity analyses for temporal MIC trends. CLSI breakpoints were compared with published ECOFFs/TECOFFs where available.

RESULTS: Mycobacterium intracellulare was predominant (51.8%), followed by MABC (23.3%), M. avium (8.5%), and M. kansasii (7.3%). M. intracellulare increased from 42.4% in 2021 to 59.7% in 2025 (adjusted OR/year 1.20, 95% CI 1.09-1.33). MABC was associated with bronchiectasis and inpatient source, while M. kansasii was associated with male sex. Within M. intracellulare, moxifloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole MIC distributions shifted upward, whereas amikacin and tobramycin shifted downward; tobramycin also shifted downward in M. avium, while clarithromycin showed no clear directional shift. Clinical breakpoints and epidemiological cutoffs aligned for clarithromycin but were more widely separated for amikacin and linezolid.

CONCLUSIONS: NTM species composition and MIC distributions changed over time in a species- and drug-specific manner. Distribution-aware MIC surveillance may complement conventional S/I/R reporting and improve interpretation of evolving NTM phenotypes.

title: Long-Term Antimicrobial Non-Susceptibility Trends Among Community-Onset Enterobacterales Urinary Isolates in Southern Saudi Arabia, 2013-2023.
authors: Alharbi NA; Shabi Y; Binkhamis K; AlQarni FNM; Asiri KMA; Shehri ADA; Albarqi AZ; Saeed ZS; Alshehri AZ; Al Sadah MAM; Al Sadah AAM; Alshehri AAA; Alwaleedi HSA; Alharbi LS
abstract:
PURPOSE: Community-onset urinary tract infections are a major driver of antimicrobial use and resistance, yet long-term regional data on resistance trajectories among Enterobacterales in southern Saudi Arabia are limited. This retrospective repeated cross-sectional study assessed antimicrobial non-susceptibility trends.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: Urine cultures from ambulatory patients aged ≥12 years meeting the study definition of community onset collected between 2013 and 2023 were analyzed. Non-duplicate Enterobacterales isolates were included, and historical susceptibility categories were analyzed as recorded, without reinterpretation using later Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute breakpoints. Temporal trends were evaluated using segmented log-linear regression, reporting annual and average annual percentage changes.

RESULTS: A total of 4,825 isolates from 3,611 patients were analyzed. Extended-spectrum cephalosporin resistance (ESC-R), defined as non-susceptibility to at least one evaluated extended-spectrum cephalosporin, accounted for 37.3% of evaluable isolates (1,796/4,816). Overall fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility was 50.4%, with a significant increase after the 2020 breakpoint; prevalence among ESC-R isolates was 77.1%. Nitrofurantoin non-susceptibility increased steadily over time, particularly among Klebsiella pneumoniae, whereas trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole non-susceptibility declined overall. Concurrent non-susceptibility to all three evaluated oral options was present in 192/4,099 evaluable isolates (4.7%), with no significant overall temporal trend. ESC-R prevalence showed no significant overall temporal trend, with a decline in Escherichia coli and no significant trend in K. pneumoniae. Fosfomycin non-susceptibility was 13.0% among selectively tested isolates; limited testing precluded trend analysis.

CONCLUSION: These single-center findings support local surveillance, culture-guided prescribing, and caution with empiric fluoroquinolone use. Selective testing limits fosfomycin interpretation; further evaluation and standardized testing for appropriate uncomplicated E. coli cystitis are warranted.

title: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges of Mycobacterium avium Complex Pulmonary Disease in Patients with Lung Cancer: A Retrospective Case Series.
authors: Gao R; Zhu M
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To describe the clinical characteristics, diagnostic challenges, and therapeutic management of Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease (MAC-PD) in patients with lung cancer, and to highlight the diagnostic limitations and treatment dilemmas encountered in this vulnerable population.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed four patients with lung cancer complicated by MAC-PD at a tertiary respiratory center in Beijing, China, between 2017 and 2025. Clinical data, cancer characteristics, underlying structural lung disease, anticancer treatments, radiological findings, microbiological results, anti-MAC regimens, and clinical outcomes were analyzed. Diagnostic methods included sputum culture, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) next-generation sequencing (NGS), and T-SPOT.TB. The 2020 ATS/ERS/ESCMID/IDSA diagnostic framework for NTM-PD was referenced for case evaluation.

RESULTS: All four patients were male, aged 66-73 years (mean 70.5 years), with underlying bronchiectasis or structural lung abnormalities. Two had lung adenocarcinoma and two had squamous cell carcinoma. MAC-PD was detected during early anticancer therapy (n=1), during combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy (n=1), or after lung cancer surgery (n=2). Chest CT showed centrilobular nodules, tree-in-bud opacities, bronchiectasis, cavitary lesions, destroyed lung, and bronchopleural fistula, overlapping with tumor progression or bacterial pneumonia. MAC was identified by BALF NGS in three patients and sputum culture in one. In Cases 1, 2, and 4, clinical diagnoses of suspected MAC-PD were supported by BALF NGS without confirmatory mycobacterial culture. Causative organisms included M. intracellulare (n=2) and Mycobacterium avium complex not further speciated (n=2). All patients received multidrug anti-MAC therapy. Regimens were modified in two patients due to adverse events or drug-drug interactions. Two patients with destroyed lung and bronchopleural fistula had poor outcomes despite prolonged therapy (30 months and 17 months, respectively). No patient underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

CONCLUSION: MAC-PD should be considered in lung cancer patients with bronchiectasis or structural lung disease when new centrilobular nodules, tree-in-bud opacities, cavitary lesions, or progressive lung destruction cannot be explained by tumor progression. Early bronchoscopy with both culture and NGS is essential; NGS should be regarded as an adjunct to, not a substitute for, culture-based diagnosis and susceptibility testing. Drug-drug interactions-particularly rifamycin-antifungal combinations-require proactive evaluation, and the combination of rifapentine with voriconazole should be avoided. Once destroyed lung develops, treatment options are limited and prognosis is poor, underscoring the importance of early detection.

title: A phenotypic state variable for antimicrobial resistance: MIC-distribution entropy exposes population heterogeneity and phenotypically quiet genomic reservoirs.
authors: Ulaganathan SB; Shreya C; Sivashanmugam K
abstract: Antimicrobial-resistance surveillance reports an isolate as susceptible, intermediate, or resistant, and a genome as a list of resistance genes; neither shows whether a population is uniformly wild-type or harbours a resistant minority. Both discard the shape of the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) distribution, which encodes within-population resistance heterogeneity. We treated the Miller-Madow-corrected Shannon entropy of that distribution as a phenotypic state variable and asked whether it carries information beyond the resistance genome. Entropy was computed on a fixed 19-bin MIC ladder for 1,612 species-drug distributions (European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing [EUCAST], 252 species) and 11,259 species-drug-year series (Antimicrobial Testing Leadership and Surveillance [ATLAS], 241 species, 2004-2024), paired with resistance-gene annotations (Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database) for 64 species (6,382 genomes). Entropy rose with the non-wild-type fraction defined by epidemiological cut-offs (Spearman ρ = 0.72), indexing coexisting subpopulations. Across 50 paired species, resistance-gene content explained less than 2% of the variance in phenotypic distributional complexity (ordinary least squares R 2 = 0.014, p = 0.406). This decoupling was the most reproducible feature, recovered under phylogenetic correction (Pagel-λ phylogenetic generalised least squares p = 0.891), a mechanism-matched comparison (pooled R 2 = 0.002), and a 145-specification multiverse, although only |r| ≥ 0.39 could be excluded. In 33,862 Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center genomes with MICs, catalogued genes explained a minority of isolate-level entropy (median 20.7%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 18.5-25.2%). Population MIC complexity is therefore not reconstructable from the genome, and the residual is descriptive but stable: 14% of species expressed more complexity than their gene content predicts, 16% less, and 70% remained aligned, including all six ESKAPE species (Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter). Entropy was reproducible across estimators (Spearman ρ ≥ 0.92) and discriminated later resistant-subpopulation emergence in walk-forward testing (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.695, 95% CI 0.629-0.756), similar to a momentum baseline (0.665), but did not forecast escalation in a hold-out split at the record's midpoint (AUC = 0.535, 95% CI 0.472-0.594). MIC-distribution entropy therefore resolves a phenotypic dimension of resistance, heterogeneity consistent with heteroresistance, and silent genomic reservoirs, that is invisible to breakpoint categories and gene counts.

title: Human Discovertebral Infection Caused by Camelimonas Species Bacteria, France, 2025.
authors: Chombart L; Blosse A; Desclaux A; Jehanne Q; Dauchy FA; Neau D; Beinat R; Dubreil S; Toirot A; Ménard A; Brousse X
abstract: We describe a case of human Camelimonas species infection, highlighting this bacterium as a potential emerging zoonotic pathogen with bone tropism. Diagnosis required repeated biopsies and genome sequencing. The isolate was susceptible to trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and doxycycline; clinical improvement followed prolonged therapy. Our findings support this bacterium's pathogenic role in humans.

title: Secretory expression of mature recombinant elafin in Pichia pastoris and assessment of its in vitro antibacterial and antifungal effects.
authors: Mokhtari S; Lohrasbi-Nejad A; Torkzadeh-Mahani M; Zolala J
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elafin is a small human host-defense peptide derived from trappin-2/pre-elafin, known for its antiprotease and anti-inflammatory functions. However, direct comparative evidence on the antimicrobial activity of mature recombinant elafin, particularly against fungal organisms, remains limited. This study aimed to produce secreted mature recombinant elafin in Pichia pastoris X-33 and comparatively assess its antimicrobial activity in vitro against Escherichia coli ATCC 25,922, Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 15,442, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29,737, and Candida albicans ATCC 10,231 using agar well diffusion, viable-count assays, broth microdilution, and minimum bactericidal/minimum fungicidal concentration (MBC/MFC) determination.

RESULTS: The elafin insert was cloned into pPICZαA, and positive P. pastoris transformants were confirmed by colony PCR. Elafin was secreted into the culture medium, and the 66 h post-induction supernatant was selected for purification based on SDS-PAGE detection of a low-molecular-weight band in the expected size range. Purification resulted in a low-molecular-weight His-tagged recombinant product with migration consistent with the expected size of the designed elafin construct. In agar well diffusion assays, recombinant elafin produced inhibition zones of 32, 28, 25, and 22 mm for E. coli, P. aeruginosa, C. albicans, and S. aureus, respectively. Viable-count assays showed concentration- and time-dependent but modest reductions in recoverable cells, with all reductions remaining below 1 log₁₀ and the greatest effect observed at 62 µg/mL after 6 h. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values were 31 µg/mL for E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and C. albicans, and 62 µg/mL for S. aureus. The MBC values were 62 µg/mL for E. coli and P. aeruginosa, 124 µg/mL for S. aureus, and the MFC for C. albicans was 62 µg/mL.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the secretory expression and purification of a low-molecular-weight His-tagged recombinant product consistent with the designed mature elafin construct in P. pastoris. The purified peptide exhibited measurable in vitro inhibitory activity under defined assay conditions, supporting further evaluation of recombinant elafin in broader microbial and physiological models.

title: Bioactive composition and in vitro bioactivity of postbiotics from mixed probiotic cultures: antimicrobial, antioxidant, and antidiabetic effects.
authors: Asefa Z; Belay A; Damto T; Addi A; Tadesse MG; Amare E; Gebremariam FW; Sherif IA; Woldemariam HW
abstract: Postbiotics, bioactive metabolites produced during probiotic fermentation, are increasingly recognized for their health-promoting properties and potential applications in functional foods and natural biopreservation. This study evaluated the bioactive composition and in vitro bioactivities of postbiotics derived from defined mixed cultures of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103), Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (DSM 9843), Bifidobacterium longum (35624), and Bifidobacterium breve (DSM 16604). Freeze-dried postbiotics were quantified gravimetrically, and their composition analyzed for exopolysaccharides (EPS), titratable acidity, B-vitamin content, fatty acid profiles, and amino acid composition using standard methods. In vitro bioactivities, including antioxidant capacity, antidiabetic potential via α-amylase and α-glucosidase inhibition, and antimicrobial activity were evaluated via minimum inhibitory concentration, minimum bactericidal concentration, and log reduction assays. The fermentation yielded 70.60-70.78 g/L freeze-dried postbiotics. Compositional analysis revealed EPS content of 652.99-654.17 µg/g, titratable acidity of 21.79-22.51 g/kg, total B-vitamin content of 387.37-390.67 mg/kg, total amino acids of 4366 ± 0.5 µg/kg, and over 32 distinct fatty acids. Antimicrobial testing showed complete inhibition of Bacillus cereus at 2.5 mg/mL, whereas higher concentrations were required for Salmonella enterica and Shigella sonnei. The postbiotics exhibited notable antioxidant activity (80.45% radical scavenging, IC₅₀ = 5.69 mg/mL) and apparent antidiabetic effects, inhibiting α-amylase by 84.39% (IC₅₀ = 8.29 mg/mL) and α-glucosidase by 72.51% (IC₅₀ = 12.42 mg/mL) under in vitro conditions. These results suggest the multifunctional bioactivity of postbiotics derived from mixed probiotic cultures, highlighting their potential as natural biopreservatives and functional food ingredients. However, in vivo validation is required to confirm these activities.

title: Chromosomal integration of a bcrRABD-carrying integrative and conjugative element increases bacitracin resistance in Clostridium perfringens following restrictions in antimicrobial use in Canadian broiler chickens.
authors: Deslauriers N; Lamarre K; Vincent A; Boulianne M
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In response to the threat of antimicrobial resistance, the Chicken Farmers of Canada banned the prophylactic use of Category II antimicrobials in 2018, thereby increasing the reliance on bacitracin to prevent necrotic enteritis in broiler chickens. This study hypothesised that the significant increase in bacitracin use, a Category III antibiotic, following the ban may have increased the prevalence of bacitracin-resistant Clostridium perfringens isolates.

METHODS: Using genomic analyses, we correlated phenotypic resistance to bacitracin of C. perfringens clinical isolates from the pre-ban (n = 77) and post-ban (n = 54) periods with the presence of different bacitracin resistance genes.

RESULTS: The prevalence of bacitracin-resistant C. perfringens isolates was significantly higher (p < 0.005) in the post-ban period (48.1%) than in the pre-ban period (23.4%). Genomic analyses revealed the presence of the bcrB and bcrC genes in all isolates, and the bcrA, bcrD and bcrR genes in resistant isolates only. The locus bcrRABD was detected in all resistant isolates and was found to be located on integrative and conjugative elements.

CONCLUSIONS: Our results illustrate that the increased use of bacitracin in Canadian broiler chickens has led to a greater prevalence of C. perfringens resistance to this antimicrobial agent.

title: Livestock-Associated Methicillin-Susceptible Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia, Denmark, 2007-2023.
authors: Raisen CL; Pedersen AB; Dalsgaard A; Mølbak K; Petersen A; Larsen AR; Larsen J
abstract: Livestock-associated Staphylococcus aureus caused 200 human bloodstream infections in Denmark during 2007-2023; two thirds were caused by methicillin-susceptible isolates. Risk for death was comparable to that associated with human S. aureus clones. Industrial pig population size correlated strongly with disease prevalence. Seventeen percent of isolates showed signs of human adaptation.

title: Preferred evolutionary routes of convergence in Klebsiella pneumoniae favor siderophore acquisition over hypervirulence.
authors: Sapre AP; Martin MJ; Luo TL; Carlino-MacDonald U; Davies CJ; Mills EG; Ong AC; Maybank R; Odeyale MJ; Kwak YI; Kovalchuk V; Kondratiuk V; Fomina N; Hutson A; GEIS overseas consortium; Metreveli M; Byarugaba DK; Osman TS; Musila LA; Rios P; Velasco JM; Ruamsapp N; Bennett JW; Mc Gann PT; Russo TA; Lebreton F
abstract: The rise of Klebsiella pneumoniae combining antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes poses a major health threat, but the evolutionary routes and phenotypic consequences of this convergence are poorly understood. Here, phylogenetics of 1468 isolates and population analysis of 7520 plasmids, from >50 countries through the last two decades, reveal that convergence follows preferred, constrained evolutionary paths. The dominant route involves multidrug-resistant classical K. pneumoniae acquiring conjugative IncFIB(Mar)/IncHI1B(Mar) plasmids carrying an incomplete set of virulence biomarkers. Across 25 independent convergence events, the acquisition of the aerobactin siderophore locus was the only universal feature. These convergent isolates exhibit enhanced siderophore production but consistently lack the hypervirulent phenotype in vivo. In contrast, genuine hypervirulent strains that gain resistance remain rare. We conclude that enhanced siderophore production, not hypervirulence, is the primary adaptive trait driving the success of globally emerging convergent lineages, representing a distinct evolutionary state optimized for transmission rather than systemic invasion.

title: Outbreak of NDM-1-Producing Acinetobacter baumannii CC2 in Southeastern Brazil: genomic epidemiology and environmental contamination.
authors: Camargo CH; Yamada AY; Borges H; Sacchi CT; Campos KR; Oliveira CR; Moraes LL; Inoue FM; Kiffer CRV; Monteiro J
abstract:
BACKGROUND: New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM)-producing Acinetobacter baumannii (Acb) represents a critical global threat due to rapid dissemination and limited therapeutic options. We describe a clonal outbreak of NDM-1 and OXA-23 co-producing Acb from clonal complex 2 (CC2) in a high-complexity hospital in Brazil.

METHODS: Acb isolates (155) recovered between 2021 and 2024 were identified by MALDI-TOF MS and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility according to BrCAST/EUCAST standards. Carbapenemase genes and clonal complexes were screened by multiplex PCR, while genetic relatedness was assessed by PFGE. All NDM producing isolates underwent Illumina whole-genome sequencing, and one was additionally sequenced using PacBio for hybrid assembly. Core-genome SNP phylogeny included publicly available Latin American genomes.

RESULTS: CC2 was the predominant clonal complex (58/155; 37.4%). Seventeen clinical isolates (11%) and all three environmental isolates carried blaNDM-1 and were susceptible only to polymyxin B among the antimicrobials tested. NDM-1-producing and non-producing CC2 isolates shared PFGE pattern A. Hybrid assembly identified ST2 (Pasteur)/ST218 (Oxford) and chromosomal blaNDM-1, co-located with armA and flanked by ISAba125. The genome also contained AbGRI1-1 and two chromosomal blaOXA-23 copies within Tn2006. Environmental isolates from hospital instruments showed pulsotypes identical to clinical isolates. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated clustering with Brazilian ST218 strains.

CONCLUSIONS: This study describes the first NDM-1/OXA-23-producing CC2 Acb outbreak in Southeastern Brazil. Clonal persistence, chromosomal blaNDM-1 integration, and the detection of clonally related isolates in the hospital environment underscore the importance of environmental surveillance and reinforce the need for integrated microbiological, genomic, and epidemiological approaches to monitor the dissemination of high-risk clones.

title: Beyond pathogen-intrinsic resistance: the host context in AMR evolution.
authors: Mazumdar R; Barišić I
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is traditionally viewed as a pathogen-intrinsic, genetically encoded trait. However, growing evidence indicates that antimicrobial susceptibility is dynamically shaped by the host context during an infection. Gradients in oxygen, nutrients, pH, immune effectors, spatial structure, and polymicrobial interactions generate a highly dynamic microenvironment that can profoundly influence microbial physiology and drug response. Within each of these gradient niches, pathogens can frequently occupy metabolic states that alter their kill kinetics, promote tolerance, and enable persistence even without intrinsic genetic elements. Experimental models of infection further demonstrate that antimicrobial efficacy depends not only on drug potency and microbial genotype, but also on host-imposed constraints. In this review, we highlight a systems-level framework in which AMR emerges from dynamic interactions between the pathogen, host microenvironment, and antimicrobial exposure. Such a framework takes into account tolerance, persistence, and resistance along a physiological continuum shaped by a dynamic host-pathogen-drug interaction. Therefore, recognizing AMR as an emergent property of a dynamic interplay between host-pathogen and drug exposure challenges reliance on standardized in vitro susceptibility testing and underscores the need for physiologically relevant infection models. By incorporating host context into experimental design and therapeutic strategy, this framework offers a more mechanistic understanding of antimicrobial susceptibility and resistance evolution, and suggests new avenues to be explored for therapeutic development and future research.

title: Among major extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli lineages, ST69 shows temporal virulence escalation through clinical convergence and independent chromosomal events.
authors: Mannan ABA; Hossain MA; Sultana M
abstract: Extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) is a leading cause of bloodstream and urinary tract infections worldwide. Whether major ExPEC lineages increase their virulence gene content over time and whether such changes translate into greater clinical relevance remains unclear. We profiled virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes across five major ExPEC STs (ST10, ST69, ST73, ST95 and ST131; 2016-2025) using VFDB, VirulenceFinder, CARD and ResFinder. Mann-Kendall trend analysis identified significant virulence increases in ST69 (VFDB τ=+0.867, P<0.001) and ST10 (VirulenceFinder τ=+0.956, P<0.001). ST69 showed no significant change in antimicrobial resistance gene burden, whereas ST10 showed significant resistance-gene decline in both ResFinder and CARD. Focused pangenome analysis of ST69 (2,272 genomes from 64 countries) revealed 4 accessory-genome clusters. Temporal decomposition showed that the ST69 virulence increase was driven primarily by increasing gene content within existing clusters rather than by expansion of higher-burden clusters. Cluster 3 contributed the largest within-cluster effect (+2.16 VFDB units; 48.3% of positive contributions), and its mean VFDB burden increased by 7.6 genes/genome between 2016 and 2025. The increase remained significant after adjustment for source niche and country (slope=+0.52 genes/year, P=0.004). Gene-level analysis showed increases in capsule-associated genes, P-fimbrial genes and the sat gene, which were also strongly enriched among clinically derived ST69 isolates. The group 2 capsule-associated repertoire increased in Cluster 3, including G2-unknown types (+22.2% points), K1 (+6.9% points) and K5 (+3.6% points), while the K54/K96 group 3 category declined by 38.1% points. Plasmid profiling and genomic plasticity analysis supported physically independent chromosomal events involving capsule and pap/sat loci. ST10 showed a contrasting mechanism: its virulence increase was driven primarily by expansion of a high-virulence cluster, while its resistance-gene decline was explained by regional sampling shifts rather than a biological trend. These findings demonstrate that ExPEC lineages can acquire greater clinical relevance through distinct evolutionary mechanisms, highlighting the need for lineage-specific surveillance that considers virulence alongside antimicrobial resistance and population structure.

title: Clonal Transmission and Within-Host Ceftazidime-Avibactam Resistance Microevolution of Hypervirulent ST11-KL64 Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae in an Intensive Care Unit.
authors: Tian X; Liu X; Wang C
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The emergence of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) poses a severe clinical threat in China. This study aimed to investigate the clonal transmission, virulence characteristics, and resistance evolution mechanisms of ST11 CRKP isolated from an intensive care unit (ICU).

METHODS: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the VITEK 2 Compact system and the disk diffusion method. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) combined with the Kleborate pipeline was utilized for molecular subtyping and virulence/resistance scoring. Core genome single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) matrix and raw read mapping analyses were employed to determine genetic distance and the relative copy number of bla KPC-2 among paired isolates. A Galleria mellonella infection model and the string test were conducted to evaluate virulence phenotypes.

RESULTS: All six isolates belonged to the ST11-KL64 lineage, exhibited high-level multidrug resistance, and co-harbored bla KPC-2, bla CTX-M-65, and bla SHV-129, alongside disruptive outer membrane porin mutations (OmpK35: p.Lys28fs; OmpK36: p.134_135insGlyAsp). All six isolates achieved a Kleborate virulence score of 4. Although all isolates were string-test-negative due to a premature truncation mutation in rmpA2 (~47% truncation), the G. mellonella larval model confirmed a hypervirulent phenotype. Core genome SNP analysis revealed a local clonal outbreak within the ICU. Notably, the ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA)-susceptible strain and its resistant evolved counterpart from the same patient differed by only a single whole-genome SNP, while maintaining consistently low bla KPC-2 relative copy numbers without gene amplification.

CONCLUSIONS: The prevailing ST11-KL64 CRKP in the ICU possesses dual characteristics of high resistance and hypervirulence. Genomic evidence confirms that rapid CZA resistance evolution was directly driven by within-host microevolution under therapeutic pressure rather than cross-replacement of distinct clones or plasmid amplification.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Genomic Characteristics of Helicobacter pylori in Peptic Ulcer Disease: A Five-Case Series.
authors: Fang Y; Wang K
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Peptic ulcer disease is a well-established clinical manifestation of Helicobacter pylori infection. Antimicrobial resistance can compromise eradication, particularly after prior treatment. We describe a small surveillance-based case series integrating clinical history, phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility, and genomic findings; the series was not designed to estimate population-level resistance patterns.

METHODS: Five patients with endoscopically documented gastric and/or duodenal ulcer and culture-confirmed H. pylori infection were identified during routine clinical microbiological surveillance from March 2023 to April 2024. Clinical data, Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC)-based antimicrobial susceptibility, selected variants in resistance-related loci, virulence-associated genes, genome assembly characteristics, and a core-genome alignment-based comparative overview were analyzed descriptively; no inferential statistical testing was performed.

RESULTS: The five patients were 25-51 years old and had endoscopically documented gastric and/or duodenal ulcers; concomitant gastritis or mucosal erosion was recorded separately. Four patients had documented prior eradication exposure, whereas treatment history was incomplete for one. All five isolates were resistant to clarithromycin and metronidazole and susceptible to levofloxacin, tetracycline, and rifampicin; two were also resistant to amoxicillin and met the study definition of multidrug resistance. All isolates carried 23S rRNA substitutions including the established clarithromycin resistance-associated A2147G substitution, whereas no gyrA resistance-associated substitution was detected. cytotoxin-associated gene A (cagA) was detected in all five isolates. Draft genome sizes ranged from 1.55 to 1.65 Mb, with GC contents of 38.54-38.82%. In the descriptive core-genome alignment-based tree, isolates 207, 318, and 221 formed a relatively close branch, whereas isolates 171 and 317 were more distinct. These genomic relationships were not interpreted as evidence of epidemiological clustering.

CONCLUSION: This descriptive five-case series illustrates heterogeneous case-level antimicrobial susceptibility and genomic profiles in ulcer-associated H. pylori infection. The observations are not population-level resistance estimates, but they support the clinical value of culture-based susceptibility testing and/or validated molecular resistance detection for individualized management, particularly after prior eradication treatment.

title: Epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Aeromonas from pediatric diarrhea in Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China: 2017-2024.
authors: Yue M; Liu D; Li X; Ding J; Hu X; Sun Y; Qi Z; Zhao X
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study characterized the epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance of Aeromonas isolates from pediatric patients between 2017 and 2024 to inform improved clinical management and infection control.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis of 439 Aeromonas isolates from 2017 to 2024 included antimicrobial susceptibility testing of 316 isolates by the Kirby-Bauer method and whole-genome sequencing of 217 isolates for species identification, MLST, and resistance gene profiling.

RESULTS: The prevalence of Aeromonas spp. in feces was 2.36% (439/18,627) between 2017 and 2024, with significant temporal variation and a pronounced summer peak, while no age or sex differences were observed. Among 316 isolates, resistance was highest to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (45.25%) and lowest to amikacin (0.32%). Resistance to third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins ranged from 5.06% (cefepime) to 9.49%. Carbapenem resistance was higher for imipenem (8.23%) than for meropenem (1.58%). Among the 217 sequenced isolates, Aeromonas caviae predominated (86.18%), followed by A. veronii (5.07%), and most isolates (81.57%) belong to the novel sequence type. Several relatively uncommon species, such as A. trota, A. taiwanensis and A. sanarellii were detected in this study and formed a distinct phylogenetic clade separate from the major species. Additionally, a single A. veronii isolate (strain Q212) was found to branch distantly from other A. veronii strains, raising the possibility of unique genetic features. A. caviae and A. veronii exhibited the broadest resistance profiles, with A. veronii showing higher resistance to several antimicrobials. A total of 779 antimicrobial resistance genes were identified. cphA (5.07%) and imiH (0.92%) were detected in A. veronii, A. dhakensis, and A. hydrophila, whereas blaNDM-14 was detected in one A. caviae isolate. mcr-3 (11.06%) was predominantly detected in A. caviae. Genes such as ampH, ampS, and blaOXA-427 also showed species-associated distribution patterns.

CONCLUSIONS: Aeromonas, with A. caviae predominating, shows substantial genetic diversity and clinically relevant antimicrobial resistance, with species-specific resistance genes. Furthermore, the detection of rare species should not be overlooked. These findings provide critical evidence for empirical therapy and resistance surveillance.

title: Melon fruit microbiomes resemble aerial-tissue communities in a Turpan oasis field.
authors: Zhou D; Sun X; Ni G; Hu G; Wang G; Zhang J
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fruit-associated communities encounter belowground and aerial habitats, yet their position within the whole-plant microbiome remains unclear in field-grown melon. We profiled bacterial 16S rRNA gene and fungal internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) amplicons from rhizosphere soil and surface-disinfected roots, stems, leaves and fruits. Four cultivars were sampled at fruit set and maturity in a randomised-block Turpan oasis field.

RESULTS: Compartment was the strongest correlate of bacterial and fungal community structure. After nine melon-derived fungal operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were removed, the primary fungal analysis retained 805 OTUs across 152 samples. Compartment explained 28.6-46.8% of bacterial variation and 31.5-34.2% of fungal variation across Bray-Curtis and Aitchison distances; stage and compartment-by-stage terms were also supported. Primary whole-plot tests detected modest cultivar-associated variation under both distances, although the fungal Bray-Curtis result did not persist in the complete 120-sample sensitivity analysis, with a Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P value (q) of 0.167. Significant dispersion tests qualified several community-level effects. Fruit communities were closer to stems and leaves than to rhizosphere soil or roots. All four kingdom-by-distance fruit microbiome continuity scores exceeded their restricted null expectations, with one-sided P = q = 1/10,001. The dual-method screen identified 197 bacterial and 44 fungal stage-associated OTU-compartment associations. Seventeen bacterial OTUs met the abundance-occupancy criteria, whereas no fungal OTU met both thresholds. Whole-community composition was not significantly associated with the first principal component of fruit chemistry (PC1).

CONCLUSIONS: In this single-season field survey, melon fruit communities more closely resembled those of aerial tissues than those of belowground compartments.
