This pattern was consistent across kingdoms and distance measures, but it does not identify a source or route of microbial movement. The recurrent bacterial candidates and the absence of fungal OTUs meeting both recurrence thresholds provide focused targets for culture-based, localisation and strain-tracking experiments.

title: De novo design of lipopeptides with antimicrobial potency enabled by a chain-as-prompt deep learning framework.
authors: Zhang F; Yu X; Wu Y; Li L
abstract: Antimicrobial lipopeptides (AMLPs) represent a promising solution to global antibiotic crisis, yet their precision design remains challenging due to the inability of current computational models to account for N-terminal fatty acid modification. Here we develop a deep learning-driven AMLP model for de novo design of AMLPs by integrating a chain-as-prompt mechanism with domain-adaptive transfer learning, effectively bridging the representation gap between peptide sequence and lipid-induced bioactivity. Using the AMLP model, 2657 evolutionarily selected RiPP-derived core peptide sequences from 96,911 bacterial genomes are inspiringly designed for virtual lipidation with seven N-terminal fatty acid chains (C6-C18) followed by predictive screening, generating 6197 candidate sequences. Notably, we find that both high KRH rate ( ≥ 0.3) and common fatty acid tails (C12 and C16) are also critical for further selection of candidate AMLPs, resulting in 289 sequences. Then, 46 are randomly synthesized, with 44 showing antimicrobial activities (a positive rate of 95.7%). The lead antibiotic LP630 exhibits broad-spectrum activities against typical Gram-positive, Gram-negative and mycobacterial strains by targeting multiple bacterial cell membrane components, and demonstrates potent therapeutic efficacy in murine wound infection models. Our study provides a streamlined and universal paradigm for deep learning-enabled high-throughput discovery of novel lipopeptide therapeutics.

title: Are systemic breakpoints appropriate for ocular infections?
authors: André C; Abad L

title: Molecular characterization of antimicrobial resistance and virulence determinants in clinical Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates: Associations between carbapenem resistance and virulence genes.
authors: Açıkgül FÇ; Aslantaş Ö; Yalcin M; Nacaroglu MB; Başaran SN; Karaynir A; Yılmaz B
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections and readily acquires resistance and virulence determinants. We characterized resistance and virulence-associated genes and factors associated with carbapenem resistance.

METHODS: Susceptibility of 265 non-duplicate clinical K. pneumoniae isolates was interpreted using EUCAST breakpoints. Carbapenemase, ESBL and sulfonamide resistance genes and nine virulence-associated markers were investigated by PCR in all isolates. Associations were assessed using Fisher's exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and multivariable logistic regression.

RESULTS: Overall, 112/265 isolates (42.3%; 95% CI: 36.5-48.3) were carbapenem resistant. Among these, blaOXA-48, blaNDM and blaKPC were detected in 65.2%, 50.9% and 8.9%, respectively, and blaOXA-48 + blaNDM was the most common profile (44.6%). blaCTX-M (44.5%) and sul1 (65.0%) predominated among ceftazidime- and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-resistant isolates, respectively. mrkD (91.7%) and entB (87.2%) were the most prevalent virulence genes. In pairwise analyses, blaOXA-48 and blaNDM were positively associated with iutA (OR = 7.67 and 6.05; q < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, iutA (aOR = 4.38, 95% CI: 2.31-8.31), magA (aOR = 2.09, 95% CI: 1.04-4.20) and male sex (aOR = 2.25, 95% CI: 1.25-4.06) were associated with increased odds of carbapenem resistance, and urine specimens with decreased odds (aOR = 0.15, 95% CI: 0.08-0.30). Carbapenem-resistant and iutA-positive isolates had higher multiple antibiotic resistance indices (p < 0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Carbapenem resistance was common, and blaOXA-48 and blaNDM were the most frequently detected carbapenemase genes. Associations of iutA and magA with carbapenem resistance may partly reflect clonal expansion or shared mobile elements and require genome- and plasmid-resolved confirmation.

title: Prophages at the interface of antibiotic tolerance, persistence and antibiotic resistance: Evidence, mechanisms and therapeutic limits.
authors: Khan F; Tabassum N; Javaid A; Kim TH; Kim YM
abstract: Prophages are widespread in bacterial genomes, and several experimental systems show that they change how bacteria survive antibiotics. Using the consensus definitions of Balaban and colleagues, this review sorts the primary evidence by the endpoint actually measured: resistance defined by the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), tolerance (killing kinetics), persistence (biphasic killing), resuscitation (single-cell regrowth), and stress or biofilm survival. These endpoints are not treated as interchangeable. Effects depend on strain, prophage, antibiotic, and endpoint. In Escherichia coli, deleting nine cryptic prophages leaves persister formation unchanged but accelerates resuscitation. In Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, ciprofloxacin-induced Gifsy-1 lysis lowers persister survival, and TisB raises persister numbers largely by limiting that induction. In methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, φSA169 increases survival at a single 24 h vancomycin time point without changing the MIC, which is a survival difference at one time point and does not demonstrate tolerance or persistence. Unverified prophages can confound persistence assays. Prophage genomes rarely encode resistance genes; a Pseudomonas aeruginosa clinical collection showed only infrequent prophage-resistance associations, and transduction can nonetheless move resistance determinants. Whether prophage-associated survival under antibiotic exposure promotes or restricts the evolution of resistance is an open hypothesis, supported by one species, one antibiotic, and a preprint, and a serial-passaging design to test it is outlined. Gut and probiotic prophages are abundant and inducible, but persistence data for them are lacking. Therapeutic approaches are separated into those acting on resident prophages, temperate phage-antibiotic synergy, and related but distinct strategies. Evidence that any prophage-directed intervention eliminates persisters in infection models is currently lacking. A minimum reporting checklist for future studies is provided.

title: Plasma and intra-abdominal drain fluid pharmacokinetics of linezolid in critically ill patients with complicated intra-abdominal infections: implications for pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics target attainment against Enterococcus spp.
authors: Benítez-Cano A; De Antonio-Cuscó M; Ramos I; Prim N; Adalia R; Juanes-Borrego AM; Sorlí L; Luque S
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Linezolid is widely used for severe intra-abdominal infections (IAIs) caused by Enterococcus spp.; however, data on its peritoneal penetration are limited. We aimed to characterize plasma and peritoneal fluid (PF) linezolid exposure and evaluate pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) target attainment.

METHODS: In this prospective observational study, critically ill adults with confirmed or suspected IAIs received intravenous linezolid (600 mg every 12 h). Paired plasma and PF samples were collected at steady state (before dosing and, 1, 3, 5, 8 and 12 h after infusion). Linezolid concentrations were quantified by validated high-performance liquid chromatography. Area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 12 h (AUC0-12h) was calculated by non-compartmental analysis and peritoneal penetration as the PF-to-plasma AUC0-12h ratio. PK/PD target attainment (AUC0-24h/MIC ≥80, ≥100 and ≥120) was evaluated assuming Enterococcus spp. MICs of 1 and 2 mg/L.

RESULTS: Thirteen patients were included. Median (IQR) linezolid AUC0-12h was 62.3 (39.2-81.2) mg·h/L in plasma and 54.3 (40.5-68.8) mg·h/L in PF, with a median penetration ratio of 0.9 (0.8-1.0). Plasma and PF exposures were strongly correlated despite marked interindividual variability. Assuming an MIC of 1 mg/L, 69.2% and 76.9% of patients achieved an AUC0-24h/MIC ≥80 in plasma and PF, respectively, decreasing to 30.8% and 15.4% at a MIC of 2 mg/L.

CONCLUSIONS: Linezolid achieved substantial peritoneal penetration with comparable cumulative plasma and PF exposure despite marked interindividual variability. Target attainment decreased markedly when a MIC of 2 mg/L was assumed.

title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale.
authors: Bağcı C; Talamás-Tanner A; Ziemert N
abstract: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eight-fold to >16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes, single-amplified genomes, and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms, and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.ziemertlab.com/.

title: MGnify analyses in 2027: enhancing the depth and breadth of analyses across metabarcoding, unassembled metagenomes, and assembled datasets.
authors: Richardson L; Atallah C; Baldi G; Beracochea M; Colina JS; Escobar-Zepeda A; Sanchez S; Gupta V; Gurbich TA; Kale V; Karatzas E; Mattock J; Ochkalova S; Olendraite I; Pesant S; Rajković A; Rogers AB; Rozday T; Sakharova E; Shehu M; Vasilopoulou C; von Wachsmann J; Dezordi FZ; Finn RD
abstract: Microbiome derived nucleic acid sequence analysis has become an increasingly important aspect of many scientific fields. MGnify (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics/) provides standardized, versioned analysis pipelines for the taxonomic and functional characterization of microbiome samples. The latest release of the MGnify pipelines (version 6) provides amplicon sequence variant analysis, expanded functional annotations including viral and mobilome for assembly analysis, and a streamlined minimal raw-reads analysis. We have improved the reusability of the pipelines through transition to Nextflow as a workflow language and have undertaken a substantial overhaul of our automation systems, using Prefect to orchestrate the pipeline execution. Finally, we have released a new version of our programmatic and bulk access services to better support large-scale computational access of data, as well as rationalizing our contig browser to improve in-browser performance. These improvements serve to support the use of MGnify pipelines and data products going forward, and improve the AI-readiness of our outputs.

title: PhageScope 2.0: a million-scale resource for integrated exploration of phage genomic, functional, and structural diversity.
authors: Wang Y; Yang S; Wang R; Wang X; Li S
abstract: Understanding phage diversity is essential for studying microbial ecosystems and developing phage-based applications. However, existing phage databases lack systematic integration of protein family and structural information. Here, we present PhageScope 2.0 (https://phagescope.deepomics.org), a database and analysis platform for exploring phage genomic, functional, and structural diversity. The update incorporates 12 environmental and metagenomic data sources, expanding the collection to 2 576 925 phage sequences, with 12 610 425 protein families and structures for 58 314 540 proteins. The platform supports family-based exploration of functional annotations and genomic neighbourhoods, structure visualization, structure search with Foldseek, and sequence-based structure-similarity prediction with TM-Vec. New and updated tools further support phage recovery from sequencing reads and cross-checking of host, lifestyle, and taxonomic predictions against existing annotations. Together, these updates enable integrated exploration of phage diversity and guide functional studies of poorly characterized proteins.

title: Coupling of stable isotope probing and metagenomics reveals the diversity of viruses infecting formatotrophs during anaerobic digestion process.
authors: Ngo VQH; Talleu C; Enault F; Midoux C; Mariadassou M; Bouchez T; Krupovic M; Bize A
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Viruses play a major role in regulating microbial community composition and activity, yet their diversity and host associations in anaerobic digestion (AD)-a complex biotechnological process converting organic waste into biogas-remain poorly characterized. Linking viral sequences to metabolically active hosts in such complex communities is particularly challenging. Here, we applied an integrative approach combining 13C-stable isotope probing (SIP) with shotgun sequencing of viromes and microbiomes to identify and characterize viruses infecting the active formatotrophic guilds in batch AD microcosms.

RESULTS: Microcosms fed with 13C-labeled formate as sole carbon source selectively enriched two primary formate-consuming guilds: hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Methanobacteriales, predominantly Methanobacterium subterraneum) and acetogenic bacteria (family Natronincolaceae, genus Andreesenella). From cross-assembly of six viromes on the one hand, and six 13C-SIP microbiome fractions on the other, we assembled a catalogue of 2,368 vOTUs, of which 261 were selected for detailed analysis. The striking enrichment of vOTUs associated with methanogenic archaeal hosts, specifically in the heavy (13C-enriched) SIP fractions, contrasted with their near-absence in total viromes-demonstrates that DNA-SIP successfully resolved viruses of active formatotrophs at the viral community level. Novel viruses were identified for both primary guilds, including archaeal viruses of Methanobacteriales (family Anaerodiviridae and a possible novel family) and two Andreesenella viruses carrying diversity-generating retroelements. A provirus predicted to infect Methanothrix-a strictly acetoclastic methanogen-further illustrates the capacity of SIP-viromics to capture viral associations across trophic levels. Analysis of auxiliary viral genes (AVGs) revealed numerous defense-associated genes (dcm, metK, queC) and genuine metabolic AVG candidates, such as cysH (assimilatory sulfate reduction) and, a contiguous cluster including uxe, galU and serB (surface polysaccharide biosynthesis), which may influence on host metabolism.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the power of SIP-viromics for resolving virus-host associations in complex anaerobic communities, linking viral diversity directly to metabolically active formatotrophic and methanogenic guilds. The identification of novel viral lineages infecting key AD microorganisms, combined with AVGs with potential consequences for carbon and sulfur cycling, provides a foundation for understanding the functional role of viruses in AD process performance. Video Abstract.

title: Global biosynthetic potential of the phylum Acidobacteriota.
authors: Hrab P; Zdouc MM; Terlouw BR; Loureiro C; Schorn MA; de Ridder D; Medema MH; Sipkema D
abstract: Bacteria from the phylum Acidobacteriota are widely distributed across diverse environments yet only a few representatives have been isolated and described. Although recent studies suggest substantial biosynthetic potential in Acidobacteriota across soil and marine environments, no comprehensive cross-biome analysis of their biosynthetic diversity has been conducted. To address this gap, we analysed 19,720 metagenome-assembled genomes from Acidobacteriota along with their environmental description to provide a systematic overview of their biosynthetic potential. Our analyses reveal that Acidobacteriota harbour several phylogenetic clades with high biosynthetic potential, including families such as Acantopleurobacteraceae, UBA5704 and UBA2199. Remarkably, our results suggest that the biosynthetic potential of Acidobacteriota is on par with other prolific phyla such as Pseudomonadota. While soil-dwelling Acidobacteriota on average encode higher numbers of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), marine host-associated species display a specialized metabolic repertoire that is enriched in BGCs putatively encoding the production of halogenated metabolites. This study highlights biosynthetically rich taxonomic hotspots to aid the discovery of novel natural products.

title: Whole-soil microbial inoculation accelerates post-fire soil recovery in a mixed conifer forest.
authors: Weiss EL; Banfield JF
abstract: High-severity wildfires of increasing size and frequency result in release of carbon dioxide and destroy timber resources, and reduce biodiversity, soil integrity, water quality, and recreational opportunities. Forest recovery strongly depends on the reestablishment of soil microbial communities, motivating research on how restoration of soil microbiomes in burned forests can be accelerated. Here, we used a high-intensity burn pile experiment to test the effectiveness of post-fire native soil amendment as a microbial coalescence experiment. This design enabled simultaneous and repeated sampling of unburned, burned, and inoculated burned soils while holding abiotic factors constant. All conditions were sampled at six time points across an annual hydrological cycle and analyzed using amplicon sequencing, genome-resolved metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and soil chemistry. Fire sharply reduced bacterial and fungal diversity in surface soils and nearly eliminated ectomycorrhizal fungi. Inoculation shifted bulk community composition toward the unburned reference state, without measurably accelerating subsequent convergence. Inoculation also accelerated recovery of functions associated with nutrient cycling, especially nitrogen transformations, and introduced a diverse assemblage of mycorrhizal fungi, including genera capable of forming essential symbioses with conifers, though this signal declined over the study period. However, the introduction of host plants and the establishment of functional plant-fungal symbioses, which may prolong persistence, were not tested. Despite introducing the full diversity of soil microbes, only a subset of organisms engrafted, likely due to selection linked to pyrogenic effects. We conclude that whole-soil inoculation can shorten the dispersal-limited phase of post-fire microbial recovery, a promising step towards restoration of the soil microbiome.

title: The ecological impact of Ulva prolifera green tide outbreaks: microbial connectivity and metabolic divergence.
authors: Liu X; Xiao J; Fan S; Miao X; Xue S; Ma X; Fu M; Du G; Zhang X; Wang Z; Zang Y
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Green tides in coastal areas have become an increasing eco-environmental concern around the world. However, the influence of massive green tides on microorganism dispersal has not yet been explored in detail. In this study, we used amplicon and metagenomic sequencing to first systematically examine the dynamics of the microbial community among continuous microhabitats in the Ulva prolifera bloom area. We found that the phycospheric microbiota exhibited increased α-diversity and complex network topologies. The tracking of bacterial sources indicated that phycospheric microorganisms originated from the algal-surface microhabitat and were widely shared with the surrounding seawater, indicating that U. prolifera blooms strengthen horizontal connectivity among microhabitats and thus facilitate the dispersal of phycospheric microorganisms into the surrounding seawater. With respect to microbial assemblages, the phycosphere was governed primarily by deterministic processes, indicating that environmental factors strongly influence the community structure of the phycosphere. Furthermore, genes involved in carbon degradation, nitrogen retention, and sulfate reduction were enriched in the algal surfaces and phycosphere, facilitating the transformation and accumulation of complex algae-derived organic matter into dissolved organic matter. Bacteroidia, Gammaproteobacteria, and Alphaproteobacteria were the key taxa contributing to organic matter transformation in the phycosphere and algal surfaces, likely reflecting their high substrate utilization strategies. In general, these findings highlight the microscale dynamics and ecological risks of microbial dispersal and demonstrate the combined effects of large-scale U. prolifera blooms on microbial structure and function, thus forming a precise assessment of the effects of macroalgal blooms on marine biogeochemical cycles.

IMPORTANCE: Ulva prolifera green tides are among the largest macroalgal blooms worldwide, yet how these events reshape microbial communities and their ecological functions remains poorly understood. This study reveals that green tide formation restructures microbial connectivity across algal-associated habitats and promotes distinct microbial metabolic strategies involved in organic matter transformation. These findings improve our understanding of how large-scale macroalgal blooms alter coastal microbial processes and provide new insights into the ecological consequences of expanding green tide events.

title: Genome-wide association study of the cecal microbiota revealing novel genetic insights into lipid deposition.
authors: Mu Q; Xiao Y; Liu D; Liu H; Zhang H; Zhou W; Zhang S; Liu S; Zhang Y; Tang H; Wang Z; Wu Q; Ding X; Zhang Y; Zhang Z; Zhao B; Gai K; Liu T; Yu S; Lu M; Guo Z; Tang Y; Tang J; Hou S; Zhou Z
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lipid deposition is a critical indicator of the economic and nutritional value of animal products. Among various regulatory factors, the cecal microbiota has been recognized as an important effect influencing lipid deposition capacity in tissues such as skin fat and breast muscle in ducks. Elucidating how the host regulates the abundance of the cecal microbiota is crucial for a deeper understanding of the mechanisms driving variation in lipid deposition.

RESULTS: To elucidate the associations between the cecal microbiota and host genetics, we perform metagenomic sequencing on cecal content samples obtained from two duck populations: a Pekin × Liancheng white duck gradient consanguinity segregating population and a Pekin × Call duck F2 population. The level lipid deposition in the host and the community structure of cecal microbiota exhibits gradual variation along with differences in genetic structure. Regression analyses reveal significant associations between 921 microbial species and two key lipid deposition traits, skin fat ratio and intramuscular fat content. Genome-wide association analysis identifies 18 candidate genes implicated in modulating microbial relative abundance. 15 of these genes are functionally enriched in membrane-related signal transduction processes. We pinpoint two microbial species-Acinetobacter baumannii and Akkermansia muciniphila-that are associated with host lipid deposition and genetically linked to two genes LIMS2 and ST3GAL1 respectively.

CONCLUSION: Our findings reveal the significant role of membrane signal transduction-related genes in regulating the relative abundance of cecal microbiota linked to lipid deposition, offering deeper insight into how the host genetically modulates the cecal microbiota and its potential impact on lipid metabolism.

title: Inter‑symbiont horizontal gene transfer and functional partitioning in globally sampled lichen metagenomes.
authors: Zhang Y; Hui J; Dal Grande F; Li Q; Chen P; Wang C; Taylor JW; Wei XL; Gao C
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a fundamental eco‑evolutionary process, yet its functional and symbiotic significance in lichens remains poorly understood. Here, using 197 high‑completeness eukaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes derived from 533 lichen-associated metagenomes sampled across six continents, we detect 1,882 putative HGT‑acquired genes among ~1.6 million predicted genes (~0.12%) across the major symbiotic partners, most of which were of bacterial origin. This dataset enables us to test two hypotheses: (H1) HGT-acquired genes exhibit partner-specific functional profiles consistent with functional differentiation between the major symbiotic partners, and (H2) inter‑symbiont HGT has occurred across the fungal-algal interface. Consistent with H1, putative HGT‑acquired genes in mycobionts show greater representation of functions related to cell wall/membrane/envelope biogenesis, transcription, and defense mechanisms, whereas putative HGT‑acquired genes in photobionts show greater representation of functions related to amino acid transport and metabolism, signal transduction, and translation. Consistent with H2, we detect 31 putative inter‑symbiont HGT-acquired genes (16 inferred from mycobionts to photobionts and 15 inferred from photobionts to mycobionts), including multiple photobiont genes inferred to encode RfeF transcription factors with putative mycobiont origin, suggesting a potential contribution of HGT to regulatory evolution. These findings are consistent with a potential role of HGT in functional specialization and potential gene flow across fungal-algal boundaries, offering insights into the eco‑evolutionary dynamics of symbiotic systems.

title: Temporal strain-resolved metagenomics associates IBD dysbiosis with gastrointestinal inflammation.
authors: Ansorge R; Romano S; Frioux C; Korcsmáros T; Yoou M; Juge N; Sidorczuk K; Hildebrand F
abstract: The gut microbiome in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is enriched in proinflammatory bacteria, yet defining a consistent dysbiotic signature is challenging, due to substantial variation between individuals and over time. We performed a high-resolution meta-analysis of 4,839 public metagenomes to disentangle the effects of IBD subtypes, inflammation, temporal, and individual variability. After accounting for temporal variation, we show that IBD-associated dysbiosis was characterized primarily by relative depletion of commensal bacteria rather than expansion of disease-associated taxa, together with increased microbiome variability both within and between individuals. Although 30% of species were IBD-associated, only 73% of these associations remained consistent across all timepoints. IBD-associated bacteria showed reduced persistence within hosts, increased strain loss and diminished strain engraftment. 8% of commensal species displayed strain-level associations with IBD that were independent of species-level changes, suggesting distinct ecological strategies for persistence. Finally, defining an inflammatory index, we demonstrated that inflammation explains much of the observed variation in microbial composition and abundance. Together, our findings indicate that inflammation associates and likely contributes to loss of commensals, thereby limiting microbiome recovery and resilience.

title: Classical and mediterranean-modified ketogenic diets distinctly shape the gut microbiota composition and function in scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment model.
authors: Ayten Ş; Koc F; Patangia D; Stanton C; Ross RP; Kayabaşı B; Dincer S; Saglam ASY; Bilici S
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is associated with impaired cerebral glucose metabolism, and ketogenic diets may influence cognitive impairment (CI) via the gut-brain axis. We investigated whether classical ketogenic (KD) and Mediterranean-modified ketogenic diet (MMKD) differentially affect gut microbiome composition and function, as well as cognitive performance, in a rat model of scopolamine-induced CI.

METHODS: Twenty-eight male Wistar rats were assigned to a cognitively normal control group (CN), a scopolamine-induced CI group (SCOP) on standard diet, and two scopolamine-treated groups receiving either a classical KD (KD; 84% fat, 16% protein) or a MMKD (60% fat, predominantly olive oil, 30% protein, 10% carbohydrate, resveratrol, and inulin-supplemented) for 9 weeks. Spatial and recognition memory were assessed using the Morris Water Maze and Novel Object Recognition Test. Caecal microbiome composition and function were profiled by shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) analysis was conducted from caecal contents of rats. Brain and hippocampal brain derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and phosphorylated cyclic AMP response element-binding (p-CREB) protein levels were evaluated by Western blotting.

RESULTS: MMKD significantly improved spatial memory relative to other groups. MMKD had higher alpha diversity in the gut microbiome compared to the KD group. KD showed the most distinct gut microbiome profile, marked by enrichment of Bacteroides and Parabacteroides species and reduced carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. MMKD was characterized by enrichment of lactic acid bacteria with elevated coenzyme A and pyrimidine biosynthesis. Moreover, MMKD was associated with higher SCFA levels compared to the KD group. No significant differences in brain or hippocampal BDNF or p-CREB protein levels were observed among groups.

CONCLUSION: These findings show that KD and MMKD produce distinct gut microbiome compositional and functional signatures, with MMKD associated with higher microbial diversity, SCFA levels, and spatial learning performance.

title: Fish-derived Loigolactobacillus coryniformis LJR-37 enhances growth performance and disease resistance in tench in association with altered gut microbial ecology and predicted metabolic potential.
authors: Lin J; Liu S; Tang D; Zhu G; He Y; Xu N; Wang K; Sha W; Yin B; Dong W
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The extensive use of antibiotics in aquaculture has intensified concerns regarding antimicrobial resistance and environmental sustainability, highlighting the need for effective probiotic alternatives. Therefore, this study aimed to isolate a fish-derived lactic acid bacterium from fish and evaluate its probiotic potential, growth-promoting effects, and protective effects against Aeromonas hydrophila (A. hydrophila) infection in tench.

METHODS: A fish-derived lactic acid bacterium, Loigolactobacillus coryniformis (L. coryniformis) LJR-37, was isolated from crucian carp and characterized using whole-genome sequencing and in vitro assays. Its in vivo effects were further investigated in tench (Tinca tinca) through a 28-day feeding trial, followed by an A. hydrophila challenge.

RESULTS: Genome analysis and phenotypic assays demonstrated that LJR-37 possessed favorable probiotic traits, including in vitro survival under acidic and bile-salt conditions, antagonistic activity against A. hydrophila, and biofilm-forming ability. Moreover, LJR-37 showed no hemolytic activity, and genome-wide screening against the VFDB and CARD databases detected no sequence with high similarity to known virulence or acquired antibiotic resistance genes. Dietary supplementation with LJR-37 improved growth performance, preserved intestinal morphology, and enhanced digestive enzyme activity. Metagenomic analysis further showed that LJR-37 supplementation was associated with higher relative abundances of Lactobacillus-related taxa and lower relative abundances of opportunistic pathogens, including Aeromonas and Acinetobacter, and an altered predicted functional profile, with higher relative representation of carbohydrate utilization and biosynthesis pathways and lower relative representation of degradative pathways. Following the A. hydrophila challenge, fish receiving LJR-37 exhibited higher survival, attenuated inflammatory responses, enhanced immune function, and alleviated intestinal tissue damage.

DISCUSSION: Collectively, these findings indicate that the fish-derived probiotic LJR-37 promoted growth and may improve resistance to A. hydrophila, with these effects accompanied by changes in gut microbial composition and predicted functional potential. This study provides evidence at the level of association supporting the application of fish-derived probiotics as sustainable alternatives to antibiotics in aquaculture disease prevention.

title: Comparative shotgun metagenomic analysis of the feline fecal microbiome in response to fresh, dry, and wet diets in a randomized crossover trial.
authors: Tanprasertsuk J; Tate DE; Tarr DS; Shmalberg J; Honaker RW
abstract: Fresh (mildly cooked) cat foods are an increasingly popular alternative to conventional extruded dry and retorted wet diets, differing in their processing and formulation. While the gut microbiota play an important role in feline health and physiological functions, characterization of the gut microbiome in cats fed fresh diets and direct comparisons with dry and wet diets have not yet been performed. In this 42-day, 3 × 3 Latin square crossover trial, 15 healthy adult cats received commercial, chicken-based, complete fresh, dry, and wet diets in one of three randomized diet sequences. Each diet was fed for 14 days, with fecal samples collected on days 12-14 for shotgun metagenomic sequencing, followed by taxonomic and functional annotation. Shannon and Simpson indices were lower with the dry diet than with the other two diets (p < 0.001 for fresh vs. dry, p < 0.01 for wet vs. dry for both indices), while Chao1 was higher for the wet diet than for the dry (p < 0.05) and fresh diets (p < 0.001). PERMANOVA using Bray-Curtis distances showed significant differences in species, pathway, and CAZy term compositions among diets (all p < 0.001). The five most abundant phyla with the fresh and wet diets were Bacteroidota, Bacillota_A, Actinomycetota, Pseudomonadota, and Bacillota, whereas Bacillota_C replaced Pseudomonadota when cats were fed the dry diet. Differential abundance analysis of taxonomic and functional data using MaAsLin2 identified diet-associated changes (FDR-adjusted p < 0.10). Collinsella, Bacteroides, and Blautia species were enriched and Prevotella species were depleted with the fresh compared with the dry diet, while Prevotella species were depleted with the fresh compared with the wet diet. The dry diet was associated with amino acid biosynthesis, bacterial cell envelope biosynthesis, and polysaccharide degradation; the fresh diet with amino acid degradation, lipid biosynthesis, and utilization of starch/glycogen, fructans, and host-associated glycans; and the wet diet shared functional similarities with the other two diets. The current study demonstrates differences in the feline fecal microbiome at the species level and in predicted functional profiles among fresh, dry, and wet diets, however health implications remain unclear before they can inform feeding recommendations.

title: Multi-omics analysis reveals the anti-hyperlipidemic mechanism of 1,8-cineole from Camphora longepaniculata essential oil via gut microbiota and lipid metabolism modulation.
authors: Nan G; Yang J; Chen H; Tahri W; Fan Z; Zhang J; Yuan J; Xie T; Jiang S; Wei Q; Yang S; Liu L; Wu Q
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-fat diet-induced hyperlipidemia exerts prominent impacts on human health and economic development. 1,8-cineole (CIN), the major component of Camphora longepaniculata essential oil, possesses bioactive properties. However, the lipid-lowering efficacy and molecular mechanisms of CIN remain insufficiently and systematically investigated.

METHODS: This study assessed the effects of CIN on physiological indices and serum biochemical parameters in high-fat diet-fed mice. Metagenomic sequencing, transcriptomics, and untargeted metabolomics were further adopted to analyze CIN-induced changes in gut microbiota composition, hepatic gene expression, and serum metabolite profiles.

RESULTS: The results showed that CIN significantly decreased serum TG and LDL-C while increasing the level of HDL-C. In addition, CIN treatment was associated with a reduced Bacillota/Bacteroidota ratio, a restoration of the HFD-induced Bacteroidota shift and a modulation of Bacteroides at the genus and species level, modulation of hepatic expression of Fasn, Hmgcs1, Cyp4a14, and Acot1, and remodeling of serum metabolites involved in glycerophospholipid and linoleic acid metabolism.

CONCLUSION: This study provides novel insights into the treatment of hyperlipidemia and validates the potential development of CIN as a functional food component.

title: High-throughput screening for central nervous system infection-associated pathogens using TaqMan array cards, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and targeted next-generation sequencing: a retrospective study.
authors: Jia X; Hu L; Wu M; Chen J; Tian D; Yi Z; Ling Y; Shen Y; Zhang X
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Central nervous system (CNS) infections feature diverse pathogens and ambiguous clinical manifestations, which complicate rapid and accurate etiological diagnosis. This study aimed to characterize the pathogen spectrum in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimens from patients with clinically suspected CNS infections and to evaluate the detection performance of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) for pathogen identification in CSF.

METHODS: This study employed three relatively independent workflows, namely TaqMan Array Cards (TAC) screening, Illumina-based unbiased mNGS, and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT)-based tNGS, for the identification of CNS pathogens.

RESULTS: In this retrospective study, 316 clinical CSF specimens were examined. The overall pathogen-positive rate of TAC-qPCR strategy was 24.68%, and polymicrobial positive samples accounted for 4.11% of all samples. We further compared the pathogen detection performance of mNGS and tNGS using 48 representative CSF samples (25 qPCR-positive, 23 qPCR-negative). The sensitivities of mNGS and tNGS for identifying CNS pathogens among qPCR-positive CSF samples were 68.57 and 65.71%, respectively, indicating comparable overall sensitivity; however, mNGS achieved higher specificity (82.35%) than tNGS (72.73%). Unbiased mNGS enables the identification of pathogens not covered by the qPCR panel; for instance, Human parvovirus B19 was detected by mNGS in several samples and further confirmed by qPCR. By contrast, benefiting from targeted amplification, tNGS yielded approximately 692-fold higher pathogen RPM and only 9.2% host reads (versus 89.0% in mNGS), as well as a substantially shortened sample-to-answer turnaround time (10 h versus 30 h). However, tNGS carried a risk of false positives caused by elevated signals from environmental contaminant bacteria. Our combined TAC-qPCR, Illumina-mNGS and Nanopore-tNGS testing identified a broad spectrum of CNS pathogens covering the major viral, fungal and bacterial etiological agents of central nervous system infections.

CONCLUSION: The TAC strategy enables high-throughput preliminary pathogen screening of large sample cohorts, while the unbiased mNGS workflow allows identification of rare or unexpected pathogens outside predefined panels, and tNGS achieves robust target enrichment and a greatly shortened testing turnaround time. Therefore, the optimal sequencing approach should be selected on a case-by-case basis according to clinical demands and suspected pathogens.

title: Fecal microbiota transplantation restores gut microbiota diversity and butyrogenic taxa more effectively than fidaxomicin in recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection.
authors: Ballestero L; Barbero-Herranz R; Morales C; Palacios E; Moreno-Blanco A; Cantón R; Del Río P; Basterra J; Avendaño-Ortiz J; Del Campo R
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI) is commonly treated with fidaxomicin or fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Although both achieve high clinical cure rates, their differential impact on gut microbiota composition and function remain uncharacterized.

METHODS: Twenty-seven patients from the phase III ICD-01 trial (EudraCT 2020-004591-17) were included, 12 of them received FMT and the remaining 15 received fidaxomicin. Stool samples were collected at baseline and 8 weeks post-treatment. Microbiota composition was assessed by shotgun metagenomics and functionality by short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) quantification. Metatranscriptomic sequencing was additionally performed in a subset of 7 patients (3 FMT and 4 fidaxomicin). Differential abundance, alpha/beta-diversity, resistome, and toxin-gene burden and expression were evaluated.

RESULTS: No clinical recurrence occurred at 8 weeks in either group, however alpha-diversity (species richness, Shannon and Simpson indexes) only increased significantly after FMT. Both treatments induced significant shifts in beta-diversity. FMT produced marked enrichment of butyrate-producing taxa, including Ruminococcus, Oscillospiraceae, Fusicatenibacter, Anaerostipes, Roseburia and Dorea. Fidaxomicin expanded Blautia while reducing Enterobacteriaceae, Veillonella and Parvimonas. C. difficile abundance did not change significantly, although their toxin genes (tcdA/tcdB) decreased after both interventions, as well as the total abundance of antibiotic-resistance genes. Among the significant changes in fecal SCFA concentrations, increases in acetate, isovalerate, and hexanoate were observed in both groups; butyrate and isovalerate increased most after FMT, whereas propionate, isobutyrate, and valerate only with fidaxomicin.

CONCLUSION: FMT drives substantially greater restoration of microbial diversity and a selective expansion of butyrogenic taxa than fidaxomicin.

title: Fungal lignocellulose-degradation potential is associated with bacterial metabolic dysbiosis in the human gut.
authors: Liu F; Liu MY; Zeng ZQ; Zhuang WY; Cao B; Zhao RL
abstract: Fungi encode diverse carbohydrate-processing functions, yet the genomic basis of their lignocellulose-degradation potential and its relevance to the human gut remain poorly understood. Here, we experimentally assessed cellulase-, xylanase-, and laccase-associated activities across 762 environmentally derived fungal isolates and sequenced 170 representative strains, retaining 160 genomes for genome-phenotype analyses. By integrating functional annotations with orthogroup presence-absence variation and machine-learning models, we identified lignocellulose-degradation-associated genomic features that improved phenotype prediction beyond conventional annotation alone. We then applied this framework to 2,116 publicly available fungal genomes and 704 cultivated gut fungal genomes from a previously published collection to construct a non-redundant catalogue of lignocellulose-degradation-associated genes (LDAGs), comprising canonical degradative enzymes, annotated phenotype-associated features, and candidate orthogroups. Across fungal lineages, xylanase-associated potential was broadly distributed, cellulase-associated potential showed an intermediate pattern, whereas laccase-associated oxidative potential was concentrated in a more restricted subset of taxa. Analysis of approximately 1,500 publicly available human gut metagenomes identified disease-associated differences in LDAG profiles in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ACVD), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and obesity. Under stringent read-remapping criteria, total LDAG abundance differences remained significant in ACVD and IBD but were attenuated in obesity, whereas compositional differences persisted across all three cohorts with modest effect sizes. These fungal genomic signatures covaried with bacterial taxa, including Escherichia coli, and pathways involved in central carbon and carbohydrate metabolism. Together, our findings establish a phenotype-informed genomic framework for resolving fungal lignocellulose-degradation potential and reveal its consistent association with disease-related bacterial and metabolic configurations in the human gut.

title: Microbiota-derived deoxycholic and lithocholic acids attenuate diabetic kidney disease through suppression of podocyte ferroptosis via TGR5-SLC7A11 interaction.
authors: Zheng GL; Yin AL; Lu XX; Liu HT; Yang MT; Zhu XX; Lin SB; Sun HJ; Lu QB
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is related to gut dysbiosis, yet the specific causative microbes remain unclear. This study integrated multi-omics, including 16S rRNA sequencing, metagenomics, and bile acid metabolomics on fecal samples from DKD patients and mice.

METHODS: Parabacteroides goldsteinii (P. goldsteinii) was orally administered to DKD mice, with assessment of podocyte injury, glomerular function, renal inflammation, and gut barrier integrity.

RESULTS: In this study, we found a significant depletion of the gut commensal P. goldsteinii in both murine models and patients with DKD. Oral administration of P. goldsteinii ameliorated podocyte injury, glomerular dysfunction, renal inflammation, and gut barrier disruption in diabetic mice. The protective effects were mediated by microbially derived bile acids, deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA), which activate Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5), with the combined treatment producing greater protective effects than either bile acid alone. Furthermore, inhibition of bile acid hydrolysis (BSH) activity blocked the production of DCA/LCA and eliminated the renal benefits of P. goldsteinii. Mechanistically, DCA and LCA inhibited ferroptosis by promoting the interaction between TGR5 and SLC7A11 in podocytes. This interaction may contribute to the preservation of SLC7A11 function and enhancement of cellular antioxidant capacity, thereby attenuating iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. Podocyte-specific knockdown of TGR5 abolished the renoprotection conferred by P. goldsteinii and DCA/LCA.

CONCLUSION: Collectively, our work identified a gut-kidney axis in which P. goldsteinii-derived bile acids regulated the TGR5-SLC7A11 macromolecular interaction to suppress podocyte ferroptosis, thereby attenuating DKD progression. These findings revealed a functional interaction between TGR5 and SLC7A11 and highlighted its regulation by microbial metabolites as a potential therapeutic mechanism for DKD.

title: Genomic characterization and immunoinformatics analysis of the Brucella melitensis vaccine strain BA0711.
authors: Zhang M; Cheng Y; Yin Z; Niu S; Li H; Jing H; Liao L; Yan Y; Huang Z; Du L; Gao H; Man C; Wang F; Chen Q; Chen S
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Metagenomics; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract:
BACKGROUND: B. melitensis BA0711 is a novel genetically engineered attenuated live vaccine strain constructed by the targeted deletion of the cold shock protein A (CspA) gene. While previous studies demonstrated its safety and protective efficacy in animals, its underlying comparative genomic characteristics, pathogenicity evolution, and theoretically predicted immunogenic potential from a genome-wide perspective remain to be systematically elucidated.

RESULTS: In this study, a high-quality complete genome of B. melitensis BA0711 was obtained using a hybrid next-generation sequencing and third-generation sequencing strategy. The genome comprised two closed circular chromosomes totaling 3,310,449 bp, with no plasmids or exogenously acquired antimicrobial resistance genes detected. Phylogenetic, multilocus sequence typing, and whole-genome similarity analyses determined B. melitensis BA0711 as the ST8 lineage and revealed its closest genetic relationship with B. melitensis M28 among the reference strains analyzed. Whole-genome collinearity and pangenome analyses further revealed a highly conserved genomic backbone and macro-syntenic organization. Horizontal gene transfer analysis identified 263 putative horizontally transferred genes, including a pathogenicity-associated genomic island, GI_6, containing multiple core lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and modification genes. Comparative profiling of core virulence factors confirmed the targeted absence of cspA and revealed lineage-associated amino-acid variation in several virulence-related proteins. Following host-homology screening, immunoinformatics analysis of 78 core virulence-associated proteins retained 5,212 non-host-homologous MHC-I strong-binding epitope records, 7,476 non-host-homologous MHC-II strong-binding epitope records, and 574 non-host-homologous linear B-cell epitope candidates. Cgs and BPE043 were prioritized as representative T-cell epitope-rich proteins. Sequential screening based on antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and HLA-binding breadth further identified four representative peptides: SSAAISSAF, LSMFVAPTF, SLNSLSVDIARAIDH, and RRFIRQLPLYKVPLE. AlphaFold 3 modeling and complementary HPEPDOCK analysis supported structurally plausible presentation of these peptides within the corresponding canonical HLA-binding grooves. The targeted deletion of cspA was additionally confirmed by PCR.

CONCLUSIONS: Our whole-genome comparative analysis elucidates the genomic architecture and evolutionary background of B. melitensis BA0711. The strain possesses a conserved ST8-associated genomic background and shows the closest genetic relationship with B. melitensis M28 among the analyzed reference strains. Systematic profiling of genome organization, putative horizontally transferred genes, and virulence-factor variation provides a molecular framework for understanding this vaccine strain. Moreover, immunoinformatics analysis prioritized Cgs and BPE043 as representative T-cell epitope-rich proteins and identified four peptide candidates with computationally plausible HLA-presentation modes. These in silico findings identify experimentally testable candidates for further investigation but require experimental validation of HLA binding and immunogenicity.

title: Population-level characterisation of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites.
authors: Louca P; Khan Mirzaei M; Kouraki A; Khamespanah E; Lin Y; Peng X; Pope R; Visconti A; Asnicar F; Kirk D; Costeira R; Segata N; Falchi M; Bell JT; Spector TD; Edwards LA; Deng L; Valdes AM; Menni C
abstract: Bacteriophages, viruses infecting bacteria, are abundant in the human gut, but their population-level structure and metabolic associations remain unclear Here we present a foundational characterisation of the gut phageome using deep shotgun metagenomic data in a large population-based cohort (n = 1,069: TwinsUK). We assembled 116,740 non-redundant vOTUs of which 52.9% were predicted to be temperate and 47.0% virulent. Individuals harboured an average of 3,370 vOTUs, mostly at low abundances, exhibiting structured population-level co-abundance patterns with bacterial species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Blautia wexlerae. Phageome diversity was mostly driven by environmental factors, with modest heritable components. We detected 4 significant vOTU diet associations. Additionally, 6,572 phages were associated with short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids, identifying extensive population-level associations between phage-associated genomic variation and microbial metabolites. Over 100 vOTUs encoded auxiliary metabolic genes, while a distinct subset of phages encoded virulence-associated genes, including vacuolating autotransporter toxin (vat) and LPS glucosyltransferases (gtrA, gtrB, gtr) implicated in O-antigen modification and immune invasion, and showed consistent co-abundance patterns with bacterial species previously associated with opportunistic or pathobiont features. These results identify structured population-level associations between phage-associated genomic elements, bacterial communities, and microbial metabolites, motivating future experimental and mechanistic studies.

title: Culture-independent identification and serotyping of Streptococcus pneumoniae by targeted metagenomics in pleural fluid samples.
authors: Smith SAM; Rockett RJ; Oftadeh S; Tam KK; Payne M; Golubchik T; Sintchenko V
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of empyema and pneumonia in children and monitoring of effectiveness of polyvalent pneumococcal vaccines has been essential for controlling invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) in children and elderly adults. Conventional serotyping of pneumococci has relied on Quellung reaction following laboratory culture; however, more recently whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has been implemented in many reference laboratories to enhance traditional typing. Pleural fluid samples from cases with empyema are often culture negative, limiting the utility of WGS and requiring PCR or 16S rRNA sequencing to detect S. pneumoniae. These molecular methods have limited sensitivity and capacity to characterize pneumococcus in clinical samples, especially in specimens with a low pathogen abundance. This study applied capture-based enrichment [(targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS)] to identify and characterize S. pneumoniae directly from pleural fluid samples. A total of 50 pleural fluid samples were subjected to tNGS with a custom probe panel, including 39 known positive fluids collected from IPD cases between 2018 and 2025 in New South Wales, Australia. tNGS results were benchmarked against molecular-based serotyping. Our tNGS achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity in detecting S. pneumoniae. Serotyping results were concordant with PCR, and 95% (37/39) of S. pneumoniae PCR-positive pleural fluid cases could be serotyped using tNGS. Standard molecular methods, however, could only determine serotype in 56% (22/39) of samples. This tNGS enabled 39% improvement in ability to directly identify and serotype IPD-associated serotypes of S. pneumoniae in difficult-to-culture pleural fluids, which can significantly enhance laboratory surveillance of IPD as well as our understanding of vaccine effectiveness.

title: Revised Consensus Clinical Trial Response Criteria by the Mycoses Study Group Education & Research Consortium and European Confederation of Medical Mycology.
authors: Hoenigl M; Thompson GR; Pappas PG; Cornely OA; Perfect JR; Gow NAR; Kontoyiannis DP; Lass-Flörl C; Maertens J; Slavin MA; Gangneux JP; Miceli MH; Munoz P; Alastruey-Izquierdo A; Bicanic T; Boulware DR; Vazquez JA; Arikan-Akdagli S; Jones CT; Ostrosky-Zeichner L
abstract: Invasive fungal diseases remain a significant cause of patient morbidity and mortality. Improvement in clinical outcomes have been the result of progress in risk stratification, diagnostics, adjunctive care, antifungal therapy, and/or prophylaxis. Yet significant challenges remain, requiring the development of novel treatment strategies. Outcome evaluation in most mycology clinical trials is currently based on consensus criteria published in 2008. However, advances in diagnosis and management of various mycoses and the ever-expanding population of patients at risk necessitate a revision and refinement of these criteria. Appropriate categorization of antifungal treatment response is crucial in assessing the effects of new therapeutic interventions. An international expert panel nominated by the European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM) and Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (MSGERC) was convened to update the current outcome evaluation criteria. The panel achieved consensus on updated guidelines for assessing treatment responses and defining study outcomes in clinical trials of aspergillosis and other mold diseases, invasive candidiasis, cryptococcosis, and dimorphic fungi in both adults and children. This summary manuscript provides details on the methods, outlines key changes in the criteria, and discusses the next steps and areas for future research.

title: Clinical Characteristics and Interpretive Challenges of CSF Varicella-Zoster Virus Detection by Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing: A Retrospective Case Series.
authors: Wei Y; Wang X; Yu W; Zhao C; Wang Z; Sun H; Xu L; Sun L; Wang P; Xu Y
abstract:
PURPOSE: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) may cause heterogeneous central nervous system (CNS) manifestations, often without a typical herpes zoster rash. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) enables broad pathogen detection in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), but VZV reads may be difficult to interpret when additional microorganisms are detected or confirmatory testing is incomplete. This study described the clinical characteristics and interpretive challenges of patients with suspected CNS infection in whom VZV was detected in CSF by mNGS.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: This retrospective descriptive case series included patients evaluated at The Second Qilu Hospital of Shandong University from January 2019 to December 2024. Among 278 patients with suspected CNS infection who underwent CSF mNGS, 23 met the prespecified operational inclusion criteria. Clinical, CSF, neuroimaging, microbiological, treatment, and short-term outcome data were reviewed. Detected microorganisms were interpreted through integrated clinical assessment rather than sequencing findings alone. No comparison group was included.

RESULTS: VZV reads meeting the inclusion criteria were detected in 23 of 278 patients (8.3%). The median age was 44 years, and 15 patients (65.2%) were male. Clinical syndromes spanned encephalitis, meningitis, meningoencephalitis, encephalomyelitis, and myelitis. A herpes zoster-associated rash was present in 10 patients (43.5%). All patients had CSF leukocytosis with lymphocytic predominance, and 21 (91.3%) had elevated CSF protein. VZV-specific polymerase chain reaction was not performed. Qualitative CSF anti-VZV IgM and IgG testing was performed in six patients, of whom two had positive IgM results. Additional microorganisms were co-detected in six patients, including Epstein-Barr virus, low-abundance herpes simplex virus type 1, and Listeria monocytogenes. The median Karnofsky Performance Status score at discharge was 90 (interquartile range, 90-100), with three patients (13.0%) scoring below 90.

CONCLUSION: VZV detection by CSF mNGS occurred across heterogeneous neurological presentations, sometimes alongside additional microorganisms. VZV reads alone cannot establish pathogen causality, and their clinical significance requires integrated assessment of the neurological syndrome, CSF findings, neuroimaging, conventional microbiological investigations, immune status, co-detected microorganisms, and clinical course. The findings are descriptive and do not establish the diagnostic accuracy of mNGS.

title: Genomic characterization of a novel Lactobacillus species from pangolin feces: phylogenomic placement and unique functional gene repertoire.
authors: Yu S; Hong P; Chou S; Liang TF; Lin KS; Lai CH; Wang CM
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Metagenomics; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The genus Lactobacillus represents a phylogenetically and ecologically diverse group of lactic acid bacteria intimately linked to host gastrointestinal homeostasis and widely regarded as prime probiotic candidates. Pangolin conservation is severely challenged by high mortality rates driven by digestive tract diseases, yet their native gut microbial ecology, particularly the functional roles of resident lactobacilli, remains largely unexplored.

RESULTS: In this study, a novel Lactobacillus strain, designated M44, was isolated from the feces of a wild Formosan pangolin, and its complete genome was resolved via whole-genome sequencing. Genome-wide taxonomic metrics (ANI, AAI, and dDDH) fell substantially below the established thresholds for known species. Phylogenomic reconstruction based on single-copy orthologs confirmed that strain M44 forms a distinct, novel evolutionary lineage clustering adjacent to L. psittaci, L. jensenii, and L. mulieris. Comparative genomic analysis revealed that while M44 shares a core of 936 orthogroups with these phylogenetically related peers, it maintains a unique repertoire of 207 strain-specific orthogroups. Multi-pipeline functional mining identified a robust gene cluster for exopolysaccharide biosynthesis, alongside an array of surface-anchored adhesins that support its strong mucosal colonization potential. From an antimicrobial defense perspective, genome mining identified no canonical bacteriocin gene clusters, while genes associated with organic acid and hydrogen peroxide biosynthesis were present. Metabolic pathway reconstruction identified genomic capacity for exogenous carbohydrate and peptide utilization, including catabolic pathways for trehalose and N-acetylglucosamine, as well as a comprehensive oligopeptide permease system and an extensive intracellular peptidase repertoire. Genomic safety screening confirmed the complete absence of acquired antimicrobial resistance genes and intact mobile genetic elements, reinforced by an active Type I-E CRISPR-Cas adaptive immune system.

CONCLUSION: These genomic insights establish strain M44 as a novel Lactobacillus species with a functional architecture encompassing broad exogenous carbohydrate and peptide utilization capacity, enhanced intestinal adherence capabilities, and organic acid-mediated antimicrobial defense. The demonstration of a favorable genomic safety profile, combined with prior in vitro phenotypic screening, positions Lactobacillus sp. M44 as a scientifically compelling subject for wildlife microbiome exploration and a candidate worthy of further investigation for potential application in captive pangolin management.

title: Grain-induced rumen fermentation shifts drive ecological enrichment of high-turnover tryptophanase variants for precision microbiome modulation.
authors: Wang J; Xu Z; Zhang T; Xiong N; Xie F; Liu P; Zhao H; Hu G; Mao S; Shen H
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Indole acts as a critical interkingdom signal, promoting gastrointestinal homeostasis at basal levels while driving cytotoxicity and inflammation when accumulated at supraphysiological concentrations. Current interventions relying on broad-spectrum antibiotics or non-specific inhibitors lack the precision to distinguish pathological overproduction from homeostatic signaling, often disrupting essential commensal networks. Resolving this therapeutic dilemma requires elucidating whether indole hyperproduction arises from proportional expansion of indole-producing bacteria or from ecological enrichment of intrinsically hyperactive tryptophanase (TnaA) variants. Here, using dairy cow rumen as a model ecosystem, we integrated evolutionary genomics, computational structure modeling, and biochemical validation to dissect the structural and kinetic properties of TnaA variants and to determine their contribution to diet-induced indole hyperproduction.

RESULTS: By integrating 462 TnaA orthologs from 21,471 reference genomes and 197 rumen metagenomes, we revealed a "conserved-fold, divergent-pocket" architecture: despite extensive sequence divergence (30-100% identity), TnaAs maintained a highly conserved global fold (TM-score 0.89-1.00) while exhibiting distinct active-site geometries and substrate affinities. Phylogenetic reconstruction and genome-scale metabolic modeling are consistent with this architecture reflecting dual, hierarchically operating selective pressures in the bovine rumen. At the macro-evolutionary scale, intense competition for colonization niches in the high-density rumen environment is associated with structural conservation of the TnaA scaffold compatible with a purifying-selection-like constraint across diverse lineages. At the micro-evolutionary scale, diet-induced rumen fermentation shifts were associated with differential enrichment of TnaA variants with distinct kinetic properties. Specifically, high-grain (HG) conditions were associated with enrichment of high-turnover variants consistent with indole-mediated competitive advantages, whereas low-grain (LG) conditions favored attenuated variants compatible with indole's role as a cooperative signaling molecule. Exploiting these structural distinctions, we identified luteolin as a variant-selective inhibitor that preferentially targets high-turnover TnaA variants (IC50 = 4.62 µM) through unobstructed active-site penetration, while sparing the sterically gated attenuated commensal forms (IC50 = 25.27 µM).

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal that grain-induced fermentation shifts are associated with the enrichment of TnaA variants with distinct kinetic properties within rumen microbial ecosystems, and that exploiting naturally evolved structural vulnerabilities enables precision targeting of dysbiotic metabolic functions while preserving homeostatic microbial networks. These results offer a conceptual framework for transitioning from ecosystem-disrupting antimicrobials to function-selective microbiome modulation. Video Abstract.

title: Metagenome and metabolome integration reveals microbial signatures of sheep milk flavor.
authors: Li D; Chen X; Chen Z; Guo S; Liu X; Xiang B; Su Y; Li J; Wang S; Wang G; Li F; Ahmad N; Zhang X; Yao J; Wu S; Zhang L; Song Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The flavor of ruminant milk largely determines consumer acceptance and dietary preferences for dairy products. Milk volatile organic compounds (VOCs) constitute and characterize the key sensory attributes of milk. However, the relationships between rumen microbial variation and inter-individual differences in these flavor compounds, as well as their potential functional links, remain insufficiently understood.

RESULTS: In 447 dairy sheep, milk volatilomics detected 306 VOCs, and 29 compounds with key contributions to sheep milk flavor were further identified, including (E)-2-octenal, diallyl sulfur compounds, and p-cymene. Notably, for 20 of these key flavor compounds, a larger proportion of phenotypic variance was explained by the rumen microbiome than by host genetic factors. Rumen metagenomic analysis revealed significant differences in microbial community structure between the high and low VOC-profile groups and identified 133 differential species, among which Paludibacteraceae bacterium, Hallella mizrahii, and Sodaliphilus pleomorphus emerged as key microbial signatures distinguishing the two flavor groups. At the functional level, flavor-associated differences were mainly observed in the metagenomic functional potential related to sulfur metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis. Reconstruction of 2,041 SGBs linked differentially abundant functional genes to their putative species-level carriers. In addition, the aldehyde flavor cluster was positively correlated with ruminal linoleic acid and negatively correlated with stearic acid. Compared with the low VOC-profile group, the high VOC-profile group exhibited significantly lower abundances of PUFA biohydrogenation related BBI and PAI type isomerases and reductases, together with a clear divergence in enzyme-type preference between groups. These results reveal a close relationship between rumen microbial PUFA biohydrogenation potential and variation in milk flavor-associated volatile compounds.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that variation in the rumen microbiome is closely associated with inter-individual variation in key sheep milk flavor compounds. By systematically characterizing the relationships between rumen microbial taxa, functional features, and sheep milk flavor compounds, this study provides new evidence for elucidating the potential mechanisms by which rumen microbes contribute to flavor formation in ruminant milk.

title: Gut bacteriophage diversity is inversely associated with organ dysfunction severity in critically ill patients: a two-cohort metagenomic study.
authors: Wang Y; Meng H; Hu D; Xie W; Qu Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The gut microbiota is profoundly disrupted during critical illness, yet the bacteriophage component has received almost no systematic study. Bacteriophages actively shape bacterial community composition through lytic and lysogenic interactions, but whether gut phage diversity tracks organ dysfunction severity in critically ill patients-and whether any such relationship is reproducible-is unknown.

METHODS: We analysed shotgun metagenomes from two independent ICU cohorts: a discovery cohort of 196 medical ICU patients (BioProject PRJNA1134172 Chicago Cohort, US) and an external exploratory replication cohort of 22 ARDS patients from a geographically distinct centre Qingdao cohort, China. A catalogue of 1,815 non-redundant viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs) was constructed using geNomad and CheckV and clustered at 95% average nucleotide identity over 85% alignment fraction. Phage alpha diversity was correlated with the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score by Spearman rank correlation, with partial correlation controlling for sequencing depth, comorbidity, sampling time and age. Bacterial hosts were predicted with iPHoP; phage-bacteria co-occurrence was assessed with FastSpar. To test whether the diversity-SOFA association was robust to catalogue choice, a cohort-specific de novo viral catalogue (644 vOTUs) was additionally constructed from the replication cohort.

RESULTS: Phage richness and Shannon diversity were each inversely correlated with SOFA score in the discovery cohort (richness: r = - 0.308, p = 1.1 × 10⁻5; Shannon: r = - 0.259, p = 2.5 × 10⁻4) and remained significant after full adjustment (richness partial r = - 0.255; Shannon partial r = - 0.224). The association was directionally consistent in the external exploratory replication cohort, where both alpha-diversity metrics showed significant inverse associations (richness: r = - 0.442, p = 0.040; Shannon: r = - 0.430, p = 0.046). Co-occurrence analysis identified thirteen high-confidence phage-bacteria pairs (r = 0.339-0.636) targeting Enterococcus faecium and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus; the quadrant of high phage detection with undetected host was entirely empty for both hosts, while the co-detection quadrant showed the highest illness severity. Individual vOTUs were largely cohort-specific: none of the thirteen focal pairs was detected in more than one replication-cohort sample, only 12.1% (78/644) of replication cohort de novo vOTUs matched the discovery catalogue, and median catalogue mapping rates were 3.06% versus 0.44% across cohorts. In contrast, community-level diversity estimates were robust to catalogue choice (per-sample richness r = 0.82, Shannon r = 0.77 between catalogues).

CONCLUSIONS: Gut bacteriophage diversity is cross-sectionally associated with organ dysfunction severity in critically ill patients, and this association was directionally consistent across two independent cohorts. These exploratory, association-based findings are hypothesis-generating and motivate confirmation in larger prospective cohorts with dedicated virome sequencing.

title: Mapping the Tibetan Plateau microbiome across ecosystems provides a resource for biodiscovery.
authors: Liu Y; Yu T; Ji M; Battin TJ; Dumont MG; Yang Y; Liu P; Zhuang X; Xing P; Wang J; Mao G; Deng Y; Hu A; Zhu Y; Jiao N
abstract: Microbial genetics can inspire innovations in biotechnology, but many microbial communities remain poorly understood. The genetic repertoire of high-mountain microbiomes remains largely untapped for biotechnology. Here we present the Tibetan Environmental Genome (TEG) catalogue, comprising 51,921 metagenome-assembled genomes from 1,698 environmental samples spanning 868 sites across 6 terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems of the Tibetan Plateau, Earth's highest and largest mountain region. The TEG spans 105 phyla encompassing 17,920 species, of which nearly 90% are previously uncharacterized. Importantly, TEG establishes a comprehensive repository for biodiscovery, revealing 44,719 biosynthetic gene clusters, 19,168 candidate antimicrobial peptides, 1,262 low-identity CRISPR-Cas systems and 1,077 candidate polyethylene terephthalate hydrolases. To validate these findings, 29 candidate antimicrobial peptides were synthesized and all exhibited inhibitory activity against at least 1 of 7 tested pathogens, with 5 showing broad-spectrum activity. This catalogue reveals a rich and previously inaccessible pool of enzymes, bioactive compounds and programmable molecular systems, establishing a foundational resource for discovery and application in biotechnology.

title: Suspected Schizophyllum commune Pulmonary Disease in an Apparently Immunocompetent Host: A Case Report and Literature Review.
authors: Liu J; Jiang W; Duan J; Zhang L; Yang X; Yang W
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Schizophyllum commune causes allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) and other respiratory disorders. Its detection in a respiratory specimen, however, does not establish whether it is responsible for the illness.

CASE PRESENTATION: An apparently immunocompetent 45-year-old man developed cough and wheezing two weeks after cleaning a moldy basement without respiratory protection. Symptoms persisted despite moxifloxacin, with marked blood eosinophilia and elevated total IgE. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) detected S. commune and Haemophilus influenzae. BALF fungal culture was not performed, and an endobronchial biopsy showed no fungal elements. Symptoms resolved during combined corticosteroid, antibacterial and antifungal treatment. The patient continued oral voriconazole after discharge but stopped it without medical advice during the fourth month. Cough and wheezing recurred approximately two weeks later, with an absolute eosinophil count of 17.83 × 109/L and no interval change on chest computed tomography (CT). Voriconazole was resumed together with a 10-week course of oral prednisone acetate, and symptoms resolved. The interval from starting voriconazole to final discontinuation was six months, including the interruption. The patient remained symptom-free during 12 months of follow-up after treatment ended. This interval reflects the individual clinical course and should not be interpreted as a recommended treatment duration.

CONCLUSION: This case illustrates the difficulty of interpreting BALF mNGS detection of S. commune in a patient with recurrent wheezing and eosinophilia. Neither ABPM nor invasive infection was established. Concurrent corticosteroid and antifungal treatment limited assessment of the contribution of each drug.

title: Seasonal dietary shifts drive gut microbiome and metabolome adaptation in wild Northern Pike (Esox lucius).
authors: Yang Y; Wu X; Feng H; Zheng Y; Wang Z; Wu R; Zhang J
abstract: The gut microbiome of fish faces challenges in maintaining stability during seasonal dietary shifts, which directly impacts host nutrition and fitness. In this study, environmental DNA metabarcoding, metagenomics, and metabolomics were employed to characterize seasonal differences in diet, gut microbiome composition, metabolites, and digestive enzyme activity of Esox lucius between spring and autumn. E. lucius exhibited broadly and opportunistically in spring but shifted to a markedly narrower in autumn. Microbiome composition exhibited marked seasonality, with spring dominated by Mycoplasma and Yersinia, whereas autumn were characterized by Aeromonas, Acinetobacter, environmental bacteria, and were accompanied by increased trypsin and lipase activities, which suggested a capacity for enhanced lipid and protein digestion for winter energy storage. Metabolomic analysis revealed enrichment of sphingolipid metabolites in autumn, which implicated in lipid metabolism and immune regulation. Furthermore, the autumn exhibited a greater diversity and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes. Our results demonstrated that seasonal dietary variation, digestive enzyme adaptation, microbiota reshaping, metabolite-mediated signaling collectively enabled E. lucius to regulate digestive physiology, as well as efficiently assimilating nutrients and maintaining energy balance in response to fluctuating resource availability in wild. Our study offers valuable insights into the ecological adaptation mechanisms of cold-water fish species.

title: Population genomics of the endangered Peruvian algarrobo (Neltuma pallida) reveals low genetic diversity and a recent bottleneck in a protected dry-forest population.
authors: La Torre Ramirez RD; Caycho E; Saucedo-Bazalar M; Saldaña CL; Bieker VC; Arbizu CI; Orjeda G
abstract: The Pomac Forest Historic Sanctuary (SHBP), a protected area on the northern coast of Peru, conserves biodiversity representative of Equatorial dry forests. SHBP is mainly composed of algarrobo (Neltuma pallida), a species adapted to the variable climate conditions and known for its multiple ecological functions and ecosystem services. Algarrobos face an unprecedented population decline despite their remarkable natural adaptation, worsened by their ongoing habitat degradation and overexploitation. In this study, we aim to characterize the genomic diversity of the protected forest in the SHBP to establish a baseline for future monitoring and research. Results show that the algarrobo population in the SHBP is unstructured, has low inbreeding indices, an average autosomal heterozygosity of 0.19%, and a per-site nucleotide diversity of 0.0023. Patterns of low genetic diversity are associated with a recent bottleneck decline starting around four generations ago. Potentially deleterious variants with varying effects, possibly playing a role in population adaptability were predicted. In conclusion, our results provide reference genetic indices for future monitoring of algarrobo in its native range and raises questions about the impact of recent habitat degradation on its genome.

title: Genomic characterization of virulence factors in hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates using long-read sequencing.
authors: Okalin SS; Oktem MA
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The virulence of Klebsiella pneumoniae is mediated by a diverse repertoire of genetic determinants involved in immune evasion, iron acquisition, colonization, and invasive disease. These virulence-associated traits have contributed to its recognition as an important cause of bloodstream and healthcare-associated infections. This study aimed to characterize the virulence genes, sequence types, capsule types, and O antigen types of Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates exhibiting hypermucoviscous phenotypes using whole-genome sequencing analysis.

METHODS: Five hypermucoviscous K. pneumoniae isolates recovered from blood cultures were subjected to whole-genome sequencing using the Oxford Nanopore MinION platform. Sequence types, Capsule types, and O-antigen types were identified using the CGE, BIGSdb, and Kaptive databases, respectively. Virulence genes were detected through VFDB and BacWGSTdb, while plasmid profiles were characterized using PLSDB and PlasmidFinder.

RESULTS: Among 244 K. pneumoniae bloodstream isolates screened, 10 were identified as hypermucoviscous by the string test. Of these, five representative isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing. The DEUKp9961_18 isolate was identified as ST1322, DEUKp1212_19 as ST268, DEUKp4822_20 as ST461, DEUKp6718_20 as ST14, and DEUKp5889_19 as ST29.
