These isolates carried the KL139, K20, K62, K2, and K54 capsule types, respectively, and all exhibited the O2a antigen type. All isolates carried genes encoding Type 3 fimbriae, Type I fimbriae, efflux pumps, aerobactin, enterobactin, salmochelin, yersiniabactin, and T6SS-associated virulence factors. Additionally, two isolates carried plasmid-encoded virulence determinants. Capsule regulation genes (rmpA/rmpA2) and aerobactin-associated genes (iucABCD and iutA) were located on the IncFIB(pNDM_Mar)-IncHI1(pNDM_MAR)-IncR plasmid of DEUKp6718_20, whereas these genes, together with the salmochelin-related genes (iroBCDN), were identified on the repB plasmid of DEUKp5889_19.

CONCLUSIONS: Although two isolates carried genomic determinants associated with hypervirulence, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a confirmed hypervirulent phenotype because no functional virulence assays were performed. Confirmation of hypervirulence requires evidence from invasive clinical disease together with functional and/or in vivo virulence studies.

title: Phenotypic-genomic discordance in a hypermucoviscous OXA-48-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream isolate: insights from whole-genome sequencing.
authors: Tuzemen NU; Saticioglu IB; Duman M; Onal U; Ak Aksoy S; Yusuf S; Iscimen R; Akalin H; Ozakin C; Ozer EA
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypermucoviscosity has historically been associated with hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae; however, this phenotype does not necessarily correlate with the presence of characteristic hypervirulence-associated genomic determinants. This study aimed to characterize the genomic features of a hypermucoviscous, multidrug-resistant (MDR), OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae bloodstream isolate from Türkiye and assess its phylogenetic context.

METHODS: Hypermucoviscosity was assessed using the string test. Whole-genome sequencing was performed using the Oxford Nanopore PromethION platform. Resistance genes, plasmid replicons, sequence type, capsule locus, and virulence-associated determinants were characterized using AMRFinderPlus, Abricate, Kleborate, and Kaptive. Publicly available OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae genomes from Türkiye with Kleborate virulence scores ≥1 were included for comparative phylogenetic analysis.

RESULTS: The isolate exhibited a pronounced positive string test indicative of hypermucoviscosity and resistance to all tested antimicrobial agents except amikacin and ceftazidime-avibactam. Whole-genome sequencing identified multiple resistance determinants, including blaOXA-48 on an IncL plasmid within a conserved IS1999-associated region consistent with a Tn1999-like structure. The isolate belonged to ST395 and carried the KL2 capsule locus. Kleborate identified a yersiniabactin-associated locus (ybt16, ICEKp12), with a virulence score of 1, but no complete aerobactin or salmochelin loci. Comparative phylogenetic analysis revealed genomic heterogeneity among the selected publicly available OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae isolates from Türkiye.

CONCLUSION: This study documents the coexistence of a positive string test and the absence of a typical hypervirulence-associated genomic profile in an MDR OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae bloodstream isolate. These findings highlight the limitations of using hypermucoviscosity alone to infer hypervirulence, while the molecular basis of the observed phenotype remains undetermined.

title: Distinct gut viral communities across life stages in dairy cattle.
authors: Cook R; Blanchard AM; Marsh C; Ponsero AJ; Reynolds J; Adriaenssens EM; Hudson C; Hobman JL; Stekel DJ; Jones MA; Millard AD
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ruminant gut microbial communities influence host health, productivity, and methane emissions, yet viral communities across life stages remain uncharacterized. Whilst bacteriophages shape microbial communities in many ecosystems, their role across dairy cattle life stages is unknown. We characterized DNA viral community composition, diversity, and ecology in cows belonging to four life stages: calf, heifer, dry adult, and lactating adult.

RESULTS: Using hybrid Illumina and Oxford Nanopore sequencing, we assembled 30,321 viral operational taxonomic units from fecal samples, including 1338 complete genomes (92% representing novel genera). Viral communities showed distinct life-stage stratification. Calves harbored low-diversity communities (Shannon index: 2.49 vs >6.58 in adults). They also showed a higher proportion of temperate phages (49% vs <24% in adults), though this difference was not statistically significant given the small calf sample (n = 3). Adult viromes showed 50-fold higher community evenness than calves. Viral and bacterial diversity were inversely correlated (Spearman's rho = -0.69), with viral diversity peaking during the drying-off period when bacterial diversity was lowest. Dry cows showed the highest viral loads (3.61% of microbial DNA vs 1.52% in lactating cows) and elevated virus-host ratios, coinciding with increased positive selection on viral genes. Twenty-six vOTUs targeting the methanogen Methanobrevibacter were detected in adults but not calves, paralleling a 757-fold higher relative abundance of Methanobrevibacter in adults. Additionally, we identified viruses carrying putative auxiliary metabolic genes involved in methane metabolism pathways.

CONCLUSIONS: The dairy cattle gut virome is extensive, almost entirely novel, and clearly stratified by life stage-characterised here across calves, heifers, dry adults, and lactating adults for the first time. Viral and bacterial diversity showed a significant inverse relationship that was most pronounced around drying-off, and viruses targeting the methanogen Methanobrevibacter were present in adults but absent from calves. Although cross-sectional, the data establish life stage as a key variable in the ruminant gut virome and identify methanogen-infecting phages as a candidate for reducing enteric methane emissions. Video Abstract.

title: Karmii: a Kraken-based approach for robust microbial isolate identification.
authors: Seppey M; Rincón C; Ngom-Bru C; Barretto C
abstract: Accurate microbial isolate identification and confirmation of culture purity are fundamental prerequisites for generating reproducible research outcomes and ensuring the long-term reliability of microbial collections. Genomic data provide an ideal means of achieving high-quality and robust results concerning isolate taxonomic identification and purity assessment, particularly when other analytical methods cannot identify an organism. However, analyses based on assembled sequences, whether through marker genes or ANI, may overlook contamination present only in unassembled reads or discarded contigs. Here, we present Karmii, a Kraken 2-based workflow designed to confirm species identification and purity of sequenced isolates from short- or long-read data. The specificity of the method is to query single-isolate reads in a two-step process, first against a generic database to generate a shortlist of candidate species and second towards the pre-selected single-species databases. Having reads classified against only one species would strongly support purity and robust identification. Results are summarized in an intuitive plot showing the proportion of classified reads across all tested species as classification stringency increases. Thresholds are used to guide decision-making. To obtain reliable results, the composition of the reference database is crucial and must maximize represented diversity while excluding inconsistent taxonomic annotations. We therefore also describe a procedure for building a resource-efficient, comprehensive and curated reference database to support the analysis. A Nextflow implementation of this workflow for prokaryotic isolate analysis is provided with this article.

title: High-resolution transcriptome analysis reveals a multilayered and dynamic transcriptional architecture in the archaeal virus SSV1.
authors: Magnus W; Boon M; Poppeliers J; Abshier J; Stedman K; Lavigne R; Peeters E
abstract: Members of Fuselloviridae infecting thermoacidophilic Sulfolobales are among the best-studied archaeal viruses, with the Saccharolobus spindle-shaped virus 1 (SSV1)-Saccharolobus solfataricus interaction serving as a model system. After infection, SSV1 establishes a chronic infection with new virions continuously budding from the infected cell. UV irradiation triggers virus replication, increased virion production, and a tightly orchestrated temporal transcription cycle. However, gene regulatory mechanisms post-UV induction remain elusive. In this study, we investigated the SSV1 transcriptomic landscape post-UV induction using high-resolution, long-read Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) cappable RNA sequencing. Through end-to-end sequencing of primary transcripts, we generated a comprehensive transcript map of SSV1, identifying 21 transcription start sites (TSSs), including 12 newly described sites, and 19 termination sites (TTSs), of which 9 are novel. This enabled refinement of transcription units and operon structures across the genome. Five new start sites of antisense transcription were discovered, including one antisense to the open reading frame of a putative viral toxin gene a291, which we hypothesize to be a cis-encoded regulatory RNA. In addition, spontaneous recombination between two direct repeats in the SSV1 structural genes vp1 and vp3 was confirmed. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation of cappable-seq for an archaeal virus and the first base-resolution analysis of the SSV1 transcriptome. It reveals a previously unappreciated level of transcriptional complexity, illustrating how high-resolution transcriptomics can deepen understanding of viral transcriptome architecture and regulatory networks.IMPORTANCEArchaeal viruses remain among the least understood viruses in the virosphere, despite their ecological and evolutionary significance. Saccharolobus spindle-shaped virus 1 (SSV1) is a key model for the study of virus-host interactions in archaea. Yet, its gene regulatory mechanisms have remained poorly resolved. Here, we provide the first base-pair resolution transcriptome of an archaeal virus, revealing a complex and multi-layered transcriptional architecture. We uncover alternative transcription start and termination sites, as well as antisense transcription, pointing to regulatory mechanisms beyond a simple temporal gene expression program. These findings suggest that archaeal viruses use sophisticated transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms similar to those in bacterial and eukaryotic viruses. By establishing a high-resolution map of the SSV1 transcriptome, this work advances our understanding of archaeal virus biology.

title: A Comprehensive Genomic Comparison Study on Streptococcus agalactiae Virulence and Antimicrobial Resistance Determinants.
authors: Xu Z; Hong J; Lin X; Soteyome T; Yin X; Yuan L; Wang C; Zou C; Premarathna M; Liu J; Ye Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Group B Streptococcus (GBS), primarily Streptococcus agalactiae, is a significant opportunistic pathogen responsible for neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and infections in immunocompromised individuals. The C5a peptidase, encoded by scpB, represents a key invasin potentially involved in GBS colonization of damaged epithelium. However, the distribution and genomic context of the bca-cfb-scpB-lmb virulence cluster across diverse GBS isolates remain incompletely characterized.

METHODS: In this study, a clinical GBS strain Guangzhou-SAG092 isolated from a patient with invasive infection in 2018 underwent complete genome sequencing using PacBio technology. We performed comparative genomic and SNA-based genome phylogenetic analyses of 85 complete GBS genomes, comprising 83 publicly available NCBI complete genomes plus Guangzhou-SAG036 and Guangzhou-SAG092. The dataset included isolates from 11 countries; host metadata were available for 77 isolates (41 human and 36 non-human), and 8 unknown-host isolates were excluded from host comparisons. Virulence factor distribution, especially the invasion-associated gene scpB, was analyzed. Statistical comparisons were performed to assess differences in virulence gene distribution between human and non-human isolates.

RESULTS: Strain Guangzhou-SAG092 was identified as sequence type ST-885, with a genome size of 2,265,243 bp containing 2,230 predicted genes. The genome harbors 19 identified virulence factor genes, including the bca-cfb-scpB-lmb cluster. The scpB gene was present in 84 of 85 Strains, with only strain YZ1605 lacking this gene. Significant differences were identified in the distribution of certain virulence genes between human and non-human isolates. All 85 Strains carried macrolide resistance genes, 40 carried tetracycline resistance genes, 8 carried aminoglycoside resistance genes, 2 carried phenolic resistance genes, and 3 carried glycopeptide resistance genes. Guangzhou-SAG092 carried aph(3')-IIIa, tetO, tetM, ermB, and cat but was phenotypically susceptible to all 10 tested antibiotics, indicating a genotype-phenotype discordance.

CONCLUSION: This genomic characterization provides a foundation for understanding the distribution of the bca-cfb-scpB-lmb virulence cluster in GBS. However, gene carriage alone does not establish pathogenicity or host adaptation, functional and expression studies are required to determine the biological significance of these associations.

title: Production of abundant defective viral genomes by an insect-specific alphavirus revealed by nanopore sequencing.
authors: Tan L; Guo Z; Gu G; Liu X; Zhang Y; Shao Y; Chen W; Kim DY; Li R
abstract: Defective viral genomes (DVGs) shape virus-host interactions and evolution, yet remain poorly characterized in insect-specific viruses. Using Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS), we profile full-length RNA species of Eilat virus (EILV), a mosquito-restricted alphavirus. We found that EILV produces abundant deletion-type DVGs far exceeding those seen in related arboviruses under identical conditions. These DVGs retain intact terminal sequences with conserved junction motifs. A modified DRS approach reveals widespread premature termination during EILV genomic RNA synthesis, linking DVG formation to reduced replicase processivity. Notably, a subset of DVGs is selectively replicated and packaged, accumulating over serial passages and interfering with parental virus replication. Our findings uncover an intrinsic, high DVG-generating capacity in EILV, linking low-processivity RNA synthesis with increased genomic plasticity. This suggests that elevated DVG production may be an adaptive mechanism, providing important insights into alphavirus evolution and replication fidelity in insect-specific RNA viruses.

title: Machine learning-driven prediction of antimicrobial resistance in Staphylococcus aureus using genomic and allelic signatures.
authors: Ghosh J; Kant R; Taneja J
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus is a growing clinical threat, and machine learning (ML) offers a scalable approach to identifying allele-level resistance determinants.

METHODS: Using a dataset of 300 clinical isolates, we trained and compared seven ML models - LSTM, CNN, Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Decision Tree, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) - to predict resistance across six clinically important antibiotics from allele, locus-tag, and EggNOG-annotation features. Training-set class imbalance was corrected with SMOTE and all seven models were retrained under one identical pipeline.

RESULTS: XGBoost achieved the strongest overall test-set performance (accuracy 95%, ROC AUC 0.9745, F1-score 0.9474), closely matched by Decision Tree (accuracy 95%, F1-score 0.9520). Both outperformed the deep-learning architectures (LSTM, CNN, MLP), which showed pronounced overfitting after class-imbalance correction. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified "cat__allele_Cluster_1015_Allele_8" as the most influential feature; this association is hypothesis-generating and reflects statistical importance within this dataset, not a confirmed causal or biological mechanism.

DISCUSSION: The genomic feature set was selected once, on the full isolate collection, by a prior SVM-RFE pipeline before the present train/test split, and no external, temporal, or multi-center validation dataset was used. Reported performance should therefore be read as an upper-bound, best-case estimate rather than a validated benchmark. These findings support ML, and ensemble methods such as XGBoost and Decision Tree in particular, as candidate components of future AMR surveillance and diagnostic pipelines, pending external and prospective validation.

title: Metabologenomic assessment of biosynthetic capabilities in the genus Salinibacterium: untapped bioactive chemistry produced by marine strain AL4.1 isolated in the Chilean Patagonia.
authors: Sánchez-Carvajal E; Serna-Cardona N; Claverías FP; Vargas N; Dacal-Barahona T; González V; González-Sanabria M; Parra J; Cámara B
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance represents one of the most critical global public health challenges. Increasing evidence suggests that rare actinomycetes can harbour novel biosynthetic diversity to produce antimicrobial compounds. This work explores the capabilities for the biosynthesis of antimicrobial natural products of Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1, in contrast with those of Salinibacterium sp. VpJ6, through a comparative metabologenomic approach. Comparative bioactivity tests using both Salinibacterium strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 revealed antimicrobial bioactivity of crude extracts from strain AL4.1 against Staphylococcus aureus. Liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry was performed on the tested samples, allowing for metabolite dereplication as well as identification of bioactivity-associated features. This revealed the presence of potential aromatic polyketides structurally related to known bioactive compounds such as phloretin, for which bacterial production had not been reported to date, as well as other potentially novel alkaloids and peptides. The genomes of both strains were sequenced and mined for their biosynthetic capabilities and further compared to those of other Salinibacterium strains with available genomic data. Phylogenomic studies suggested that both strains AL4.1 and VpJ6 could represent potentially new species. A mainly phylogeny-dependent distribution of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) was observed, emphasizing the presence of a widely distributed type III polyketide synthase BGC, which could be linked to the bioactive compounds. These results suggest that Salinibacterium sp. AL4.1 can produce novel bioactive natural products, and the genus Salinibacterium holds relevant and underexplored biosynthetic potential.

title: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid against extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Escherichia coli in an in vitro bladder infection model: impact on clinical breakpoints
authors: Anderson, C. R. B.; van Gorp, E.; Won, H.; Roberts, J. A.; Cottingham, H.; Breen, S. K. J.; Landersdorfer, C. B.; Meletiadis, J.; Peleg, A. Y.; Abbott, I.
abstract: Uropathogens with acquired ESBL-genes can limit effective oral treatment options. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid can be used as targeted therapy (500/125mg, 8-hourly). Despite favorable urinary pharmacokinetics (PK), there is little urine-specific data that quantifies the exposure required for bacterial clearance. A dynamic in vitro bladder model was employed, allowing for the simulated treatment of UTIs with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Sixteen Escherichia coli isolates (12 clinical ceftriaxone-resistant uropathogens, 4 laboratory isolates) were selected. Bacterial response to treatment, emergence of resistance, exposure-response targets and PK/PD indexes were explored. Following simulation of standard-dose oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (500/125mg, 8-hourly; Cmax 935mg/L; AUC0-24 14272mg/L), 14/16 isolates displayed no growth at the end of treatment, with elimination in seven isolates confirmed after a 24h antibiotic-free follow up. As exposure was reduced, greater survival and regrowth were observed. Only two isolates had significant post-exposure rises in MIC (32 to 128mg/L, 64 to 256mg/L). %T>MIC was the best predictor for end of treatment outcome (?log10cfu/mL: stasis 52.7%, 1log10 kill 61.8%, 2log10 kill 71.1%, R2=0.9062). Lower R2 values were found with EUCAST MIC measurements (fixed 2mg/L clavulanic acid) as compared to CLSI MIC measurements (2:1 amoxicillin to clavulanic acid). Monte Carlo simulations indicated that standard-dose 8-hourly would achieve all %T>MIC targets in >95% of virtual patients with MICs ?64 mg/L, regardless of MIC method (CLSI or EUCAST). Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid displays time-dependent killing against ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli. This data supports clinical breakpoints for uncomplicated UTI for isolates with MIC ? 64mg/L, assuming 500/125mg oral dosing 8-hourly.

title: High-resolution 3D genome mapping of late replicative senescence reveals hypomethylation-associated loop expansion, weakened cell identity, and locus-specific L1 derepression
authors: Kelsey, M. M. G.; Dalgarno, A.; Evans, S. A.; Nunez, T. A.; Rocha, A.; Clark, K.; Sedivy, J. M.; Neretti, N.
abstract: Cellular senescence contributes to aging and age-associated diseases through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which is fueled in part by derepression of retrotransposable elements. While senescence is driven by transcriptional and epigenetic changes, the contribution of higher-order genome organization remains incompletely defined, particularly at the resolution required to detect chromatin loops. Here we present ~3 kb-resolution Hi-C maps of late-stage replicatively senescent (RS), proliferating, and quiescent human lung fibroblasts, integrated with total RNA-seq and Nanopore long-read DNA sequencing. RS cells exhibit widespread compartment and subcompartment switching toward active states, consistent with a global loss of heterochromatin. We observe a striking expansion of chromatin loops in RS cells, with an approximately sixfold excess of senescence-specific loops over proliferation- or quiescence-specific loops. These senescence-specific loops are enriched in the B compartment relative to other loop classes, are accompanied by DNA hypomethylation at loop anchors, and are enriched for neuronal-lineage gene programs that are concordantly upregulated, suggesting a structural correlate of the loss of cell-type identity recently described in aging chromatin. Compartment and subcompartment reorganization, but not loop status, is associated with retrotransposon derepression. We identify L1HS_14q23.2_3, an intact L1HS element, as a locus where compartment switching, subcompartment activation, novel loop formation, and pronounced promoter demethylation appear to promote locus-specific derepression. Quiescent fibroblasts unexpectedly share inflammatory transcriptional features with RS cells, raising important considerations for experimental design in senescence research.

title: From species-wide genomics to cellular diversity: characterizing multidrug-resistant extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli ST744
authors: Nesporova, K.; Steemans, B.; Palkovicova, J.; Krutekova, K.; Meunier, A.; Valcek, A.; Dolejska, M.; Govers, S. K.
abstract: The species Escherichia coli represents a wide and heterogeneous range of strains. Here, we exploited this genomic diversity to examine the distribution of virulence-associated genes (VAGs) and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) within a collection of 131,610 E. coli genomes. Across lineages of extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), we identified a negative correlation between VAG and ARG content, with ST744 carrying the most resistance genes on average. Phylogenomic analysis of a global ST744 cohort revealed the existence of two main clades, and substantial variation in accessory gene content, resistance-region organization, and plasmid carriage. Subsequent phenotypic characterization revealed that the interpretability of genomic information depends on the trait being considered. Whereas antibiotic susceptibility measurements generally agreed with genomic predictions, limited correspondence was observed between the presence of specific metabolic and stress-associated genes and enhanced growth under such conditions. Image-based profiling also revealed extensive diversity in cell morphology, nucleoid organization and cell-cycle timing across strains, even among nearly clonal isolates. Together, our findings provide an in-depth characterization of E. coli ST744, within the broader diversity of E. coli and EXPEC, as well as a framework for examining how genomic differences relate to phenotypic diversity within other ExPEC lineages.

title: Different assembly and binning strategies recover contrasting genome catalogues and community profiles
authors: Eisenhofer, R.; Alberdi, A.; Aizpurua, O.
abstract: In genome-resolved metagenomics, different assembly and binning strategies can be employed to reconstruct microbial genomes and community profiles. We used metagenomic data from a longitudinal experiment, in which mice were exposed to a series of environmental stressors, to compare four approaches: single-coverage, multi-coverage, co-assembly, and multi-split. We evaluated their effectiveness in reconstructing microbial genomes, determining their relative abundances, and analysing functional profiles while accounting for computational efficiency. Our findings indicate significant differences in the quantity and quality of recovered genomes across strategies, which in turn influenced community profiles and research outcomes related to microbiota resilience to environmental pressures and functional differences between exposure to contrasting temperatures. We conclude that the choice of assembly and binning strategies is crucial and needs to be thoroughly assessed considering available resources, study design, and research aims, as the strategy employed for data processing can significantly affect the results and conclusions of metagenomic studies.

title: Cave ecosystems as drivers of viral diversity, endemism, andecological function at a global scale
authors: Barosa, B.; Firrincieli, A.; Gabrieli, L.; Turatto, A.; Lopo, E.; Ghezzi, D.; Garcia, L.; Costantini, P. E.; Danielli, A.; De Waele, J.; Sauro, F.; Selensky, M.; Osburn, M.; Cappelletti, M.
abstract: Caves are subterranean ecosystems that host diverse microbial communities involved in key biogeochemical processes. Yet, the diversity and ecological roles of viruses within these systems remain poorly understood. Here, we analyzed metagenomic data collected from 30 globally distributed cave systems, identifying 8,176 viral operational taxonomic units ([≥] 10kb size) that have little representation within a recent database of environmental viruses. In addition, cave-specific environmental fingerprints are shown to be a strong driver of viral distribution, reflected in a high degree of endemism both within and across cave systems. Viral-host associations suggest that viruses are primarily associated with Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota lineages, the most abundant groups across all samples and involved in diverse carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen metabolisms. The high proportion of lytic viruses targeting these groups suggests strong top-down viral control, with virus-mediated microbial turnover likely contributing to organic matter recycling. This is further supported by lytic viruses carrying the majority of auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs), with functions related to enhancing viral progeny production by increasing resource availability and reallocating cellular resources toward viral replication. In this study, we highlight how cave environments shape viral ecology and unveil a still yet unknown component of the subsurface virosphere.

title: Genomic tessellations
authors: Ekim, B.; Cheng, H.
abstract: Periodicity is ubiquitous in genomic data. Assembled sequences are dense with homopolymers, microsatellites, and large satellite arrays, which contribute to phenotype, variation, and disease. Third-generation sequencing technologies, such as Oxford Nanopore (ONT) and PacBio HiFi, has enabled longer and increasingly accurate reads, but have brought with them systematic error biases in repetitive regions, where insertions and deletions can distort array lengths and mimic or obscure biological variation. This periodicity is not benign: local repetitiveness makes sequence alignment ambiguous and genome assembly error-prone. In sequence analysis, these two manifestations of periodicity are simultaneously at play, each compounding the challenges of the other; a unified representation of repetitive and non-repetitive sequence is necessary to account for their combined effects consistently. We propose a paradigm under which (either repetitive and non-repetitive) DNA is split into its identity (its irreducible components) and its geometry (how its components are realized). A genomic tessellation {tau} is a canonical factorization of any sequence S of length n over the DNA alphabet into a sequence of tiles partitioning S, where each t in {tau}S is described as a quasi-periodic run of a canonical unit identity ut with geometry consisting of span st, phase {varphi}t, and a set of exceptions Xt. We show that, for a prescribed error bound k [≥] 1 and fixed maximum unit length P, S can be tessellated in O(n) time such that every tile has a unique identity whose periodic expansion differs from the tiled sequence by at most k edits, and that tiles sharing an identity are related by a bounded number of geometric adjustments. We introduce the tessellated Burrows-Wheeler transform (tBWT), which indexes {tau}S by concatenating, over all tiles in order, the identity ut of each tile. For a tessellated query q of m tiles, the tBWT counts the repeat-agnostic occurrences of q in O(m) time, and for sampling interval r locates its h occurrences in {tau}S in O(m + hr) time. We demonstrate that tessellations avoid the well-known speed-accuracy tradeoff and outperform state-of-the-art long-read mappers in repeat-dense regions in both speed and accuracy. On a 20x simulated set of both ONT and HiFi reads on the HG002 maternal X chromosome with synthetically-expanded repeat arrays, locating and chaining exact tile identity matches obtained from the tBWT is up to 57x and 83x faster, respectively, than the state-of-the-art mappers minimap2 and Winnowmap2, with comparable accuracy. Furthermore, by abstracting away differences in geometry, tessellations of a set of input sequences onto itself (an autotessellation) reveals homology otherwise obscured by array-length variation and local sequence divergence. A geometry-only polishing of an an ONT-only assembly of the HG002 maternal X chromosome with [~]50x PacBio HiFi reads improves assembly QV from 45.4 to 60.6 in under a minute using less than 10GB of memory. Tessellated-read evidence over the autotessellation of this assembly organizes 167 mitochondrial contigs totaling [~]4 Mbp into a single family with a [~]16.5kbp representative, which aligns to the HG002 Q100 mitochondrial genome with 100% identity. Genomic tessellations provide a canonical representation of repetitive and non-repetitive DNA and enable efficient sequence analyses while preserving homology.

title: Identifying the metacommunity scale reconciles deterministic and stochastic assembly in a natural mainland-island microbial system
authors: Cuadrado Corz, J.; Ramoneda, J.; Alcon, D.; Bell, T.; Pascual-Garcia, A.
abstract: Disentangling the deterministic and stochastic processes that shape microbial communities remains a central challenge in microbial ecology. The framework proposed by Vellend---selection, drift, dispersal and speciation---offers a natural conceptual scaffold, but testing these processes in natural communities is technically demanding, and analyses are often narrowed to a single process, which can lead to seemingly contradictory conclusions. Here we illustrate the promise and the pitfalls of a comprehensive application of this framework by re-analysing a temporally resolved dataset of microbial communities inhabiting water-filled tree-holes at the base of a single beech tree, a natural mainland--island system for which both neutral assembly and strong selection have been reported. We show that these views are compatible once unsupervised compositional clustering is used to identify the scale at which assembly processes should be tested. Treating each compositional cluster as a set of local communities that receive immigrants from a distinct metacommunity, we applied neutral, phylogenetic and null-model tests of selection and dispersal, metagenomic prediction and association inference. Selection operated chiefly as environmental filtering at the metacommunity level, associated with tree-hole size and shape, whereas local communities were statistically indistinguishable from stochastic assembly. Variable selection and dispersal limitation acted between metacommunities, whereas homogenizing dispersal prevailed within them. Association networks recapitulated metacommunity structure, indicating that co-occurrence largely reflects shared environment rather than interactions. In summary, performing some analyses while excluding others leads to misleading conclusions: comprehensive analyses and identifying the intrinsic scale in which selection may operate are needed to move beyond the deterministic--stochastic dichotomy.

title: Detection, Persistence, and Antimicrobial Resistance Profiles of Escherichia coli and Shiga Toxin-Producing E. coli in Nut Orchards with Integrated Grazing Animals
authors: Rothwell, J. G.; Cheong, S.; Schlesener, C.; Miramontes, C.; Shaw, C.; Pereira, R. V. V.; Weimer, B. C.; Pires, A.
abstract: Integrating grazing animals into nut orchards can introduce foodborne pathogens including Salmonella enterica and Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) into crop production environments. This study investigated pathogen transfer and persistence in the soil following livestock grazing (sheep/chicken) in two organic almond orchards and one walnut orchard in California. Soil and fecal samples were collected periodically for 120 days after grazing. Enrichment, selective culture and PCR were used for STEC and Salmonella enterica detection. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was assessed using microdilution assays, and whole genome sequencing (WGS) was used to characterize AMR genes, virulence genes and population structure. All 284 soil and 79 fecal samples collected tested negative for Salmonella enterica and E. coli O157. Presumptive STEC was detected by colony PCR in 3.2% (n = 9/284, 95% CI 1.7-5.9%) of the soil samples, and 34.2% (n = 27/79, 95% CI 24.7-45.2%) of fecal samples. Shiga toxin genes were confirmed by WGS in 15 of 31 sequenced isolates. Predominant subtypes were stx1c and stx2b, and O176:H4 and O174:H2 were the most common serotypes. Phenotypic AMR was detected in 33.3% (n = 12/36) of isolates, with multidrug resistance in 8.3% (n = 3/36). A soil and a sheep fecal isolate differed by one core-genome single nucleotide polymorphism and shared a closed multidrug-resistance plasmid of identical gene content, consistent with a lineage resident in the flock that transferred to soil. Confirmed STEC in orchard soil was rare and transient. These results provide evidence to inform food safety guidelines on crops integrated with livestock.

title: HOG pathway modulation is a determinant of echinocandin treatment failure in Candidozyma auris
authors: Sofras, D.; Jacobs, S.; Zile, A.; Mottola, A.; Zvirgzdins, A.; Pageau, A.; Boccarella, G.; Gifford, H.; Biriukov, V.; Dube, A. K.; Walker, L.; Malavia-Jones, D.; Leaves, I.; Wang, Z.; Van den Bergh, B.; Lobo Romero, C.; van den Berg, P.; Michiels, J.; Farrer, R. A.; Berman, J.; Gow, N. A. R.; Gabaldon, T.; Lends, A.; Ralser, M.; Munro, C. A.; Landry, C. R.; Van Dijck, P.; Carolus, H.
abstract: Candidozyma auris is a rapidly emerging fungal pathogen whose drug-resistant profile poses a formidable challenge to antifungal treatment. Echinocandins are the recommended first-line therapy for invasive C. auris infections, but resistance to this drug class is on the rise. Here we show that, beyond resistance, C. auris can readily acquire genetically encoded echinocandin tolerance, a phenotype of slow but sustained growth and increased survival at concentrations above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) that reflects incomplete maximal inhibition and a reduced Hill coefficient without an increase in MIC. Tolerance was therefore undetectable by standard clinical susceptibility testing, yet it significantly reduced treatment efficacy in an immunocompromised murine model of systemic infection. Genetic dissection revealed that tolerance arises through disruption of the high-osmolarity glycerol (HOG) mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway through the loss of function of Ssk1, Ssk2, Pbs2 or Hog1, or specific substitutions in Nik1. The disruption of the HOG pathway did not confer fitness or virulence defects in C. auris, and in Candida albicans and Nakaseomyces glabratus, it did not confer tolerance, suggesting a unique non-essential rewiring of this pathway in C. auris. Proteomic and cell-wall analyses linked tolerance to altered cell-wall remodelling during echinocandin exposure. Evolutionary modelling and deep sequencing of FKS1 hotspots in experimentally evolved populations showed that tolerance increases the rate at which resistance-conferring FKS1 hotspot substitutions emerge. Putative high-impact mutations in HOG pathway effectors in clinical isolates suggest that this phenotype occurs in patients, where it might reduce treatment efficacy or facilitate resistance emergence. This work therefore identifies HOG-mediated acquired tolerance as a hidden clinically relevant direct and indirect determinant of echinocandin treatment failure.

title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
authors: Ye, R.; Li, L.; Geng, Z.; Song, S.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens complicates infectious disease management. Protein sequences encode molecular features underlying resistance functions such as antibiotic inactivation and drug efflux, providing a basis for investigating bacterial AMR. Protein language models can extract transferable representations from these sequences. However, general purpose protein language models have limited capacity to represent AMR-associated sequences, while task-specific tools often address individual prediction problems. These limitations highlight the need for protein representations that better capture resistance associated functions and can be reused across complementary tasks, supporting systematic AMR analysis from sequence variation to functional relationships among proteins. We developed BacLLM, a language-guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder, enabling sequence only inference after training. Compared with baseline models, BacLLM provided more informative representations of resistance associated sequences, achieving a mean F1 score of 0.956 across six AMR benchmarks with logistic regression, 2.7 percentage points above the strongest baseline. It also captured resistance associated mutational signals at single residue resolution and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending the same representation framework to an intervention oriented application, BacLLM also improved strain level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a reusable protein representation framework for analyzing resistance associated sequence variation and functional organization, with applications in AMR surveillance and phage candidate prioritization.

title: Unravelling bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis in the uncultured Roseilinea
authors: Rudling, N. M.; Namoon, D.; Thiel, V.; Canniffe, D. P.
abstract: Filamentous anoxygenic phototrophs (FAPs) of the Chloroflexota phylum are abundant members of microbial mat communities. All isolated and culturable FAPs are found in a single class within this phylum, but metagenomic studies of hot spring communities from around the world have indicated that phototrophic members of an additional class may exist, which have so far eluded cultivation for study in the laboratory. Metagenome-assemble genomes (MAGs) of these "Candidatus Roseilinea" species all lack genes encoding the central enzymes of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis common to all FAPs and to the seven other diverse phyla of anoxygenic phototrophs, which could indicate that these organisms are no longer phototrophic or that they employ a novel set of enzymes to generate chlorophyllide from magnesium protoporphyrin IX. Here we demonstrate that the five terminal enzymes of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis encoded in the MAG of Japanese hot spring-dwelling "Ca. Roseilinea sp. NK_OTU-006" are active and restore pigment production and phototrophic growth in a set of mutants of the model purple phototrophic bacterium Rhodobacter sphaeroides. While many organisms are known to require exogenous supply of metabolically costly modified tetrapyrroles such as vitamin B12 for growth, the retained function of the tested Roseilinea enzymes and the restriction of these species to dense microbial mats leads us to hypothesise that these organisms may be the first examples of bacteriochlorophyll auxotrophs. We suggest that Roseilinea scavenge pigment precursors and/or breakdown products excreted by other members of the mat to generate the mature bacteriochlorophyll they require to perform phototrophy, an exchange that we demonstrate can occur between Rhodobacter sphaeroides mutants. We further suggest that future attempts to isolate Roseilinea species should employ the exogenous supplementation of (bacterio)chlorophyllide into culture medium.

title: ModkitOpt: Accurate RNA modification site calling from nanopore sequencing
authors: Sneddon, A.; Prodic, S.; Eyras, E.
abstract: ModkitOpt is a pipeline for the systematic optimisation of modkit filtering thresholds and stoichiometry cutoffs using orthogonally validated modification sites. It substantially improves site-calling accuracy across modification types, even when the nanopore sample and validation sites are from different biological contexts. We report optimal site-calling parameters for m6A and pseU and provide practical recommendations for applying ModkitOpt.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Performance, Interpretability, and Cross-Database Redundancy
authors: Ruthbah, C. A.; Sadi, T. H.; Jahan, N. E. S.; Tanzim Adib, A. N. M.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) classifiers are typically developed and evaluated within a single curated database, leaving open how much two independently curated databases agree and what that implies for apparent cross-database generalization. We trained an XGBoost classifier on amino acid trigram frequencies and physicochemical descriptors using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), the field's largest curated ARG resource. The model separated resistance genes from non-resistance proteins with near-ceiling accuracy (AUROC = 0.982, MCC = 0.886); a label-shuffling null baseline collapsed to chance (AUROC = 0.508) and bootstrap confidence intervals were narrow, confirming genuine signal rather than data leakage or overfitting. SHAP analysis attributed this performance to biologically interpretable features, notably the trigram KTG, isoelectric point, and aromaticity, each consistent with known catalytic motifs in resistance enzymes. Before testing the classifier against ResFinder, one of CARD's most widely used counterparts, we assessed database independence by clustering sequences with CD-HIT, finding that 96.8-98.7% of ResFinder sequences shared substantial protein identity with CARD even at a permissive 50% identity threshold, indicating the two databases largely represent the same sequence population, with direct implications for how cross-database generalization should be measured. On the small subset of ResFinder sequences genuinely non-redundant with CARD (40-100 sequences, depending on threshold), the classifier failed completely, never classifying any as resistance genes; SHAP traced this failure to sequence length, as non-redundant sequences are nearly three times longer than training proteins, and length is among the model's most influential features. The same pattern emerged by resistance mechanism: the model achieved perfect accuracy on beta-lactamases, compact single-domain enzymes well represented in training (100%, n = 351), but correctly identified only 38.5% of efflux pump components (n = 13), a mechanism built from large, multi-domain transporters rather than compact catalytic enzymes. Together, these results describe a capable, interpretable ARG classifier alongside a quantified methodological caution: cross-database redundancy must be measured rather than assumed, and when a sequence-composition classifier fails, the failure is often explained by protein architecture rather than database origin.

title: Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG) for Antiviral and Antibacterial Drug Discovery.
authors: Martin, H.-J.; Beasley, J.-M.; Kaneva, V.; Tieghi, R.; Causey, K.; Tropsha, A.; Muratov, E.
abstract: Infectious diseases remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, while therapeutic discovery is hindered by fragmented biomedical data and antimicrobial resistance. To address this challenge, we developed the Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG), a queryable platform that integrates curated chemical, biological, pharmacological, and clinical information relevant to infectious-disease drug discovery. Using a customized ORION pipeline, we integrated 20 data sources, including DrugCentral, SMACC, Heli-SMACC, NPASS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and host-virus interaction databases, into a Neo4j graph containing more than 4.6 million nodes and 26 million edges. IDKG supports graph-based reasoning through Clinical Outcome Pathways (COPs) and incorporates curation workflows for small molecules, biologics, and complex mixtures. Illustrative applications include reconstruction of a literature-supported remdesivir pathway for COVID-19 and graph-based mechanistic interpretation of experimentally observed quorum-sensing inhibitor-antibiotic synergies in multidrug-resistant bacteria. The platform provides an interoperable framework for drug repurposing, target prioritization, and mechanism-based hypothesis generation. IDKG is freely available at https://idkg.mml.unc.edu.

title: Capsular surveillance-guided phage cocktails against carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
authors: WANG, C.; Nie, J.; Wei, M.; Tian, X.; Sun, Y.; Zeng, Y.; Wei, D.; Song, Y.; Zhang, G.; Chu, X.; Yang, Q.; Zhou, Z.; Wu, L.; Feng, J.
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is among the most urgent antimicrobial-resistance threats, yet its extraordinary capsular diversity has kept phage therapy locked in per-isolate matching-a process too slow and labor-intensive for routine use. Here we convert this specificity problem into a look-up problem. Interrogating 26,138 CRKP genomes from 96 countries, we show that capsular diversity collapses onto a tractable target list: 14 capsular locus (KL) types dominate contemporary circulation and jointly account for 67-77% of the CRKP burden in every WHO region, stably from 2010 to 2024 and after removal of sampling bias. We assembled a repository of 48 strictly lytic phages spanning all 14 types and organized it into capsule-defined modules: for eight KL types a single capsule-targeting phage sufficed to prevent resistant regrowth over 24 h, and for the remaining six a two-phage module pairs a capsule-targeting phage with a capsule-independent phage that recognizes the second receptor layer exposed upon capsule loss. We treated 28 clinical isolates, covering two distinct STs for each of the 14 KL types. Modules were assigned from the KL call alone, without isolate-level matching data. Growth was suppressed in every strain, and ST background had no significant effect in 12 of 14 types. These results establish capsule type, not lineage, as the operative unit of CRKP phage preparedness: a single rapid KL-typing step converts a diagnostic result into a therapeutic decision, providing a practical, lineage-agnostic route from surveillance to treatment.

title: Genomic blueprints of a dynamic deep sea: contrasting adaptive strategies potentially drive seasonal microbial succession
authors: Zhao, B.; Barcon, A. S.; Zhong, S.; He, Y.; Wang, Y.
abstract: Genetic variation within marine microbial populations can help reveal how deep-sea communities respond to environmental change. However, population-level genomic variation in deep pelagic waters remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic datasets from ~1,080 m depth in the South China Sea to compare genomic variation between summer and winter microbial assemblages. Among 11 persistent metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) detected in both summer and winter samples, we observed differences in abundance, nucleotide diversity ({pi}), pN/pS ratios, and gene-level differentiation. Two enriched populations showed contrasting patterns, with Sphingobium yanoikuyae enriched in winter samples and Methyloversatilis universalis enriched in summer samples. The winter-enriched S. yanoikuyae population carried winter-associated accessory genes related to restriction-modification and toxin-antitoxin systems, consistent with a defense-oriented persistence profile. In contrast, the summer-enriched M. universalis population showed higher nucleotide diversity in summer samples and divergence in genes related to motility, transport, and cobalamin acquisition. Across persistent MAGs, low pN/pS ratios indicated predominantly purifying selection, whereas gene-specific divergence and flexible accessory gene content suggested population-level adaptive potential under contrasting winter and summer conditions. These results reveal population-genomic differences associated with winter-summer microbial shifts in the deep sea.

title: Identification and characterization of a Streptococcus strain isolated from the esophagus of an adult male heterozygous for the CF allele
authors: Abrahamson, E. A.; Surve, S. V.; OToole, G.
abstract: The genus Streptococcus consists of diverse bacteria that are integral components of the human microbiome, acting as both important commensals and opportunistic pathogens. In this study, one strain of an -hemolytic species of the genus Streptococcus, GP0011T, isolated from an esophageal aspirate collected during an endoscopy, was characterised phenotypically to establish its taxonomic status. The strain was isolated from an adult male heterozygous for a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) mutation. The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the strain is a novel species within the mitis group, with Streptococcus oralis ATCC 35037T being the closest relative with 94.84% average nucleotide identity (ANI) and 58.3% digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH). Phenotypic characterization and API20 Strep strips distinguished GP0011T from S. oralis by the absence of alkaline phosphatase activity, trehalose fermentation, and starch fermentation, and by superior growth on D-mannitol and D-sorbitol, consistent with genomic data. The strain is Gram-positive, catalase-negative, and the cells are ovoid with a mean cell diameter of 1.3 {micro}m. Growth occurred at 25-43 C, with an optimum at 30 C, with an optimum at pH 8.0. Antibiotic resistance genes msrD and mefA, conferring resistance to azithromycin and erythromycin, as well as pathways for mannitol and sorbitol metabolism, were found and phenotypically confirmed in the GP0011T genome but were absent from S. oralis. These findings indicate that GP0011T represents a novel species within the genus Streptococcus with the proposed name of Streptococcus ruoffae sp. nov. The type strain is GP0011T (ATCC TSD-627 and NCTC 15312).

title: An iron acquisition system promotes Bifidobacterium longum fitness in competitive early life gut communities
authors: Acton, L.; Soe, C. Z.; Kujawska, M.; Augustine, J.; Senoo, D. K. J.; Trivett, H.; Caim, S.; Shimpo, A.; Clark, C.; Friess, L.; van Sinderen, D.; Chivers, P. T.; Hall, L. J.
abstract: Iron availability influences the composition of the gut microbiota, yet the mechanisms that enable beneficial bacteria to acquire iron and compete within iron-variable communities remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Fei (Fe import), an iron-responsive acquisition system that promotes the fitness of Bifidobacterium longum subsp. longum, a prevalent member of the early-life gut microbiota. Comparative profiling of 20 bifidobacterial strains revealed substantial inter- and intraspecies variation in growth under iron limitation, with multiple B. longum subsp. longum strains maintaining comparatively robust growth. Transcriptomic analysis identified a four-gene locus, feiMQOX, that was strongly induced during iron depletion and returned towards control expression following iron supplementation. The complete locus was highly conserved within B. longum subsp. longum but unevenly distributed across the wider genus. Disruption of individual Fei components impaired growth and reduced cell-associated iron under iron-restricted conditions, while metal-binding studies of purified FeiX demonstrated a physiological preference for Fe(II). FeiX also provided a pronounced fitness advantage during competition with an infant-derived Enterococcus faecalis isolate, particularly under iron limitation. Finally, analysis of longitudinal metagenomic data from Bangladeshi infants demonstrated that Fei is present within infant gut communities and that its abundance changes following iron supplementation. Together, these findings identify a lineage-associated iron-acquisition system that connects micronutrient availability with bifidobacterial physiology and competitive fitness. More broadly, our findings establish strain-level micronutrient acquisition as a potentially important determinant of beneficial bacterial fitness within the developing gut microbiota.

title: A full-length isoform atlas of the non-failing and failing human heart
authors: Ye, B.; Noureen, M.; He, F.; Lingamgunta, L.; Zheng, S.; Li, F.; Wang, X.
abstract: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and ischemic heart disease (IHD) are leading causes of heart failure, yet isoform-level changes in the failing heart remain poorly defined because reference annotations are derived largely from healthy tissues and short-read sequencing cannot reliably reconstruct full-length transcripts. We sequenced six human left ventricles (non-failing, DCM, and IHD; n = 2 each) with PacBio HiFi long reads and curated 48,232 isoforms across 11,760 genes, including 15,535 novel NIC and NNC isoforms. Independent evidence supported most novel structures: 81.7% of isoforms with novel splice junctions had short-read support for all novel junctions, and a cardiac CAGE atlas supported the 5' ends of 93% of NIC and 86% of NNC isoforms. Novel isoform diversification was concentrated in sarcomere genes and persisted after accounting for gene complexity, expression, sequencing depth, and transcript length. We then augmented GENCODE v43 with 18,637 non-FSM long-read isoforms and re-quantified two independent short-read cohorts (MAGNet and GSE116250). For most genes carrying a transcript that changed more than 2-fold in DCM, the gene itself changed less than 2-fold, so these changes are not apparent at the gene level. Of 626 transcripts differentially expressed in both cohorts, 98% changed in the same direction, including all 100 long-read isoforms among them. The resource is available through CardioIsoMap, an interactive isoform-centric portal (https://cardioisomap.streamlit.app/). This study provides a comprehensive isoform-resolved reference of the human heart in health and disease.

title: Air and environmental sampling expand metagenomic viral surveillance in Cambodian pig slaughterhouses
authors: Cronin, P.; Heang, V.; Siegers, J. Y.; Tok, S.; Sin, S.; Sievers, B.; Omondi, V.; Chhel, K.; Nouhin, J.; Chim, V.; Seng, B.; Hak, M.; San, S.; Tum, S.; Claes, F. F.; Firth, C.; Su, Y. C. F.; Smith, G. J. D.; Karlsson, E. A.
abstract: Surveillance of viruses in swine depends largely on the sampling of individual animals chosen at random, often limiting detection breadth. Environmental sampling has emerged as an alternative strategy, enabling faster, safer and more cost-effective pathogen monitoring at the human-animal interfaces. Across nine visits to two Cambodian slaughterhouses, we applied metagenomic sequencing to air samples (n = 25), faeces (n = 156), wastewater (n = 15), carcass wash water (n = 18), holding-pen swabs (n = 124), slaughter-box swabs (n = 73) and ropes (n = 16), comparing virus composition to pig snout swabs (n = 193). Combined environmental sampling recovered 96.6% of the viral taxa detected in snout swabs, exceeding 90.9% at every visit. Greater viral diversity was consistently captured in the environment, including swine-associated taxa absent from snout swabs and viral RNA associated with avian and human hosts. Air provided the widest coverage of any single environmental sample type and contributed the largest number of independent virus detections that were not recovered from any other environmental sample. Slaughter-box swabs recovered the fewest taxa, showing that visible contamination with swine material did not correlate with greater viral recovery. Overall, this study identifies air as a pivotal core component of any surveillance program. However, pairing air with additional environmental sample types provides the broadest virus coverage and represents the optimal surveillance strategy in swine slaughterhouses.

title: Single-cell genomics reveals genomic and functional differentiation between freshwater and saline Achromatium populations.
authors: Remy, P. H.; Ionescu, D.; Gros, O.; Heidig, S.-L.; Woyke, T.; Schiable, G.; Volland, J.-M.
abstract: Giant sulfur bacteria of the genus Achromatium reportedly contain extensive genomic diversity within individual cells. Most genomic data (35 assemblies) come from freshwater populations obtained from Lake Stechlin, Germany, alongside four single-cell genomes from a salt marsh and saline mineral springs. Here, we characterize marine Achromatium from mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe and compare them with freshwater and saline references. Microscopy, elemental mapping, and Raman spectroscopy revealed calcium-rich inclusions, and intracellular elemental sulfur as previously described for this genus. Scanning electron microscopy revealed two cell-size morphotypes. We generated eleven single-cell, four mixed-cell, and two metagenomic binned assemblies from Guadeloupe mangrove. Divergent copies of conserved marker genes revealed extensive intracellular genomic diversity in individual cells of both morphotypes. Multigene phylogenies provided separation between freshwater references and most genomes from saline environments, including the Guadeloupe population. Gene presence-absence analyses further revealed differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe and Stechlin cells across five functional annotation categories including PFAM, KEGG Orthologs, and CAZymes. Differences in genes associated with osmotic regulation, ion transport, carbohydrate degradation, and secretion systems suggest variation in functional potential related to environmental adaptation, interactions and resource utilization. No significant differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe morphotypes were found. Together, these marine genomes reveal genomic and functional differentiation from freshwater populations and suggest that intracellular diversity does not erase freshwater/saline population boundaries.

title: Three novel deep-branching orphan protist lineages from the marine rare biosphere
authors: Pohl, N.; Mendez Sandin, M.; Tuovinen Nogerius, V.; Burki, F.
abstract: Metabarcoding has transformed our view of marine protist communities, yet many sequences in environmental surveys are not assigned confident taxonomic identity. These taxonomically ambiguous sequences may include lineages that are not within any known eukaryotic supergroup, which we refer to here as orphan lineages. These orphan lineages matter beyond taxonomy-based community analyses, because they can help us understand early eukaryotic evolution. Here we used phylogenetic inferences and sequence similarity networks (SSNs) of long-read metabarcoding data of the ribosomal operon (18S-28S rDNA) to identify three novel phylum-level orphan lineages. We designate these lineages Deep Orphan Lineages 1-3 (DEEPOLs) and show that they are exclusively marine and part of the rare biosphere, yet ecologically distinct: DEEPOL1 is a cosmopolitan generalist, DEEPOL2 a conditionally rare lineage capable of local polar blooms, and DEEPOL3 a non-polar lineage with a tendency toward the dark ocean. For DEEPOL2, lineage-specific digital PCR (dPCR) combined with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) provides the first in situ visualization of these cells, revealing small, flagellated, and morphologically inconspicuous protists. Together, our results show that substantial diversity remains hidden among rare lineages, and that long-read sequencing combined with targeted molecular and microscopy approaches offers a first step toward linking orphan sequences to organisms and their evolution and ecological roles.

title: Vertical transmission and community turnover in seed-borne microbiomes: lessons from an aMAIZEing model system
authors: Henaut-Jacobs, S.; Sangi, S.; Matos, J. P.; Chaves Ribeiro, R.; Petroceli-Mota, G.; da Costa Rodrigues, B.; Jario de Lima, V.; Kamphorst, S. H.; Alves de Oliveira, U.; Nunes-da-Fonseca, R.; Lopes Olivares, F.; S. Etienne, R.; M. Venancio, T.
abstract: The seed microbiome represents a specialized ecological niche, governed by assembly processes that are only partially coupled to the surrounding soil community. While environmental recruitment and vertical transmission from the maternal plant are both recognized sources of seed-associated microorganisms, the mechanisms that determine their relative contributions and whether these contributions shift across generations remain poorly understood. Here, we used long-read metagenomic sequencing to track seed-borne bacterial community dynamics across a founding seed pool and two subsequent generations in two divergent maize (Zea mays L.) varieties exposed to contrasting organic and mineral fertilisation regimes. We recovered 112 medium- or high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes and combined MAG-level taxonomic and functional analyses with genus-level community profiling to characterize persistence and turnover dynamics within the seed microbiome. While soil taxonomic diversity was high, seed-associated communities showed a near-complete compositional disconnect from soil-dominant assemblages taxa, with a persistent Firmicutes core maintained across generations, consistent with vertical transmission. Priority effects remain a possible explanation for these patterns but were not directly tested. Genus-level source attribution suggested greater environmental recruitment under organic fertilization, with more diverse soil communities and a stronger contribution from the preceding seed generation under mineral fertilization. Seed-associated MAGs also carried genes associated with plant growth-promoting potential, although these detections could not be consistently linked to specific transmission routes. In contrast, maize genotype had no detectable effect on seed microbiome composition. Intergenerational persistence and environmental recruitment jointly shape seed-derived communities under contrasting fertilization regimes. Their relative contributions remain inferred from taxonomic overlap, and the effects of microbial source-pool diversity cannot be separated from the accompanying differences in soil chemistry in this design.

title: Evaluating local assembly strategies for human long-read structural variant calling
authors: Mirus, T.; Luepken, R.; Kehr, B.
abstract: Long-read sequencing enables detection of structural variants (SVs) with far greater accuracy and completeness than was previously possible. This advance has spurred the development of many SV callers that implement diverse algorithmic strategies. Commonly, SV calling proceeds in several processing steps. Evaluations of SV callers, however, typically focus on overall performance and conceal which steps drive observed differences. This hinders targeted, evidence-based improvements to existing SV calling approaches. Here, we implemented five consensus computation strategies similar to those employed by popular SV callers that perform a local assembly. We compare their outputs on extensive simulated and real data and reveal that some strategies are more effective for particular input data types. For example, the strategy employed by PacBio's tool Sawfish works very well on HiFi reads and recent ONT data, but fails on the older and noisier ONT reads. While the read error profiles and the read pre-processing has a substantial influence on some strategies, other strategies are more robust overall. These findings guide algorithmic decisions for the development of improved future SV callers.

title: SELECT 2.0: Refined and open access SELection Endpoints in Communities of bacTeria (SELECT) method to determine concentrations of antibiotics that may select for antimicrobial resistance in the environment
authors: Hayes, A.; Kay, S.; Lowe, C.; Gaze, W. H.; Recker, M.; Buckling, A.; Murray, A. K.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a significant threat to human and animal health, the global economy, and food security. The One Health approach to AMR recognises the role of the environment in the evolution, emergence, and dissemination of AMR. This is partly due to anthropogenic pollution that releases AMR organisms alongside cocktails of compounds that may select for AMR in situ, which then pose an exposure risk to humans and animals. This has spurred growing interest from cross-sectoral stakeholders in environmental risk assessment of antibiotics, with regards to their selective potential. Many different approaches have been used to determine the lowest concentration of an antibiotic that may select for AMR. Debates continue regarding which individual approach, if any, may be best for determining selective concentrations of antibiotics for environmental risk assessment purposes. This paper contributes to this discourse by refining a previously published method "SELECT" to generate predicted no effect concentrations for resistance (PNECRs) for 32 antibiotics, with open access code and walk-through. The PNECRs presented here is the largest number generated using a single experimental approach that will aid future efforts towards creating a standardised test.

title: EvoRx: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli Using Genomic Features
authors: Arora, A.; Natarajan, E.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterisation of Penicillium melinii, a plant growth-promoting root endophyte that remains effective under salt stress
authors: Gonzalez-Sayer, S. M.; Gutierrez-Manso, L.; Devesa-Aranguren, I.; Blasio, F.; Conchillo, L. B.; Conesa, C. M.; Ugena, L.; Nolasco, J.; Vazquez-Mora, A.; Sacristan, S.; Caro, E.; del Pozo, J. C.; Cabrera, J.
abstract: Penicillium melinii isolate 2 is a root endophyte of Arabidopsis thaliana that promotes the growth of different plant species, but the genetic basis of this activity remains unknown. Here we combined Oxford Nanopore long reads and Illumina short reads to obtain a high-quality, near-chromosome-level assembly of 29.39 Mb in six nuclear scaffolds, two of them telomere-capped at both ends (97.6% complete BUSCOs), together with, to our knowledge, the first complete mitochondrial genome reported for the species (26,730 bp). Annotation predicted 9,566 protein-coding genes. Compared with two other plant growth-promoting Penicillium species, P. bilaiae and P. citrinum, the isolate encodes fewer carbohydrate-active enzymes, biosynthetic gene clusters and candidate effectors, pointing to an overall reduction of the secreted repertoire. In vitro, the isolate grew significantly above the control on 63 of 95 carbon sources, mainly carbohydrates, and was positive for 7 of 11 plant growth-promoting traits: siderophore production, phosphate and zinc solubilisation, ammonia release, and urease, proteolytic and lipolytic activities. Radial growth was unaffected by NaCl up to 150 mM and persisted at 1 M, whereas conidiation was more salt-sensitive. On medium containing 100 mM NaCl, inoculation increased Arabidopsis shoot fresh weight and root system growth. Genome mining identified candidate genes for these traits. Together, these results provide a genomic and phenotypic basis for evaluating P. melinii isolate 2 as an inoculant for saline soils and identify candidate determinants for functional validation.

title: Tissue-specific genomic and transcriptomic dynamics of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in the Pacific oyster Magallana gigas revealed by long-read sequencing
authors: Dotto-Maurel, A.; MORGA, B.; Arzul, I.; Chevignon, G.
abstract: Ostreid herpesvirus 1 (OsHV-1) causes recurrent mass mortality of juvenile Pacific oysters (Magallana gigas) worldwide, yet its lytic cycle remains poorly characterized in vivo. In the absence of a permissive cell line, most studies have relied on intramuscular injection, which bypasses the natural route of infection, or on primary haemocyte cultures, which cannot capture tissue-level host-virus interactions. In addition, gene expression studies have relied on short-read sequencing, which fragments transcription units and cannot resolve complex transcriptional architectures. Long-read sequencing has recently revealed abundant overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts in other herpesviruses, but whether OsHV-1 shares this complexity, and how its transcriptional program varies across host tissues during natural infection, remains unknown. Here, we exposed naive oysters to OsHV-1 by bath exposure and combined long-read genomic and transcriptomic sequencing of gills, mantle, digestive gland and adductor muscle at increasing levels of infection. OsHV-1 genomes were assembled directly from infected tissues, and intra-host viral diversity was structured by host rather than tissue. We identified 410 unspliced viral transcripts, including overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts. The viral transcriptional program was largely conserved across tissues and resembled that previously described in haemocytes in vitro. In the host, infection triggered a response shared by all tissues, but earlier and stronger in the gills and mantle. Together, these results provide the first long-read view of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in its natural host.

title: Identifying disease-associated dysbiosis in image-based spatial microbiome via MiSA
authors: Liu, R.; Grodner, B.; Samorodnitsky, S.; Deng, D.; Roy, A.; Dun, Y.; Guo, B.; De Vlaminck, I.; Zhao, N.; Ling, W.
abstract: Background: Extensive studies have revealed the associations of microbiome dysbiosis with disease through compositional analysis of 16S rRNA amplicon or shotgun metagenomic sequencing data. However, dysbiosis in spatial organization of microbiome inhabiting the body sites and its implication for diseases remain understudied. Recently developed high phylogenetic resolution fluorescence in situ hybridization (HiPR-FISH) is an image-based mapping technology that provides spatial microbiome data at single-cell resolution, which allows for visualizing and quantifying spatial arrangement of microbial cells. Despite the growing availability of such data, no methods have been tailored to studying spatial dysbiosis in image-based microbiome data. Results: Here we introduce MiSA (Microbiome Spatial Aberration), the first statistical framework for identifying disease-associated spatial dysbiosis and the individual taxa that may contribute to it, based on differing degrees of clustering or regularity, i.e., microbial cells being more aggregated or more evenly spaced than expected under complete spatial randomness, between diagnostic groups. In simulations based on a real dataset, MiSA was robust across diverse and noisy spatial configurations, achieving substantially higher statistical power than a method borrowed from spatial proteomics, while controlling type I error at both the individual-taxon and community levels. When applied to an oral biofilm study, MiSA detected peri-implant mucositis-associated spatial dysbiosis at the community level and identified five taxa as potential contributors, including Actinomyces, which showed increased clustering in mucositis. Conclusions: MiSA is a powerful and robust framework for identifying spatial dysbiosis and the contributing taxa in image-based microbiome data, offering new insights into the spatial organization of microbial communities in disease.

title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
authors: Mendez, C.; Vargas-Peralta, D.; Rendon, L. A.; Castillo-Ramirez, S.
abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

title: Hidden but Expanding Sampling Bias Distorts Prokaryotic Genome Collections
authors: Götsch, H.; Baumdicker, F.
abstract: Public genome collections underpin our understanding of bacterial diversity and the distribution of traits such as antibiotic resistance, and increasingly serve as training data for genomic foundation models. Their growing size promises an increasingly complete view of microbial genetic variation. However, these collections combine studies with different sampling priorities, often overrepresenting subgroups of closely related strains of particular interest. The resulting bias reduces effective information, and its consequences for diversity estimates and the value of further sequencing remain insufficiently quantified. Here we show that accounting for this escalating sampling bias is essential for accurate gene frequency estimates and hints at greater genomic diversity than current data suggest. We propose to detect and reduce sampling bias based on phylogenetic relationships compared to expectations under random sampling, which, in contrast to dereplication and data reduction methods, preserves fine-scale diversity in large samples. Applied to 402 prokaryotic species in the NCBI genome database, our method PhyloThin indicates that the effective number of samples is 41% lower than the actual number but retains more than twice as many genomes as dereplication.
