Sampling bias varies substantially among species, showing that genome counts alone provide an incomplete measure of how well a species has already been characterized. PhyloThin thus turns biased, expanding genome collections into more representative samples for studying genome evolution and population genetic inference with implications for training genomic foundation models, pathogen surveillance, and the discovery of novel genetic functions.

title: Compound-specific DNA adduct profiling with nanopore sequencing and IonStats
authors: Koski, Y.; Patel, D.; Kakko von Koch, N.; Jouhten, P.; Aaltonen, L.; Palin, K.; Sahu, B.; Pitkanen, E.
abstract: Covalently bound DNA adducts are mutation precursors that contribute to aging and diseases such as cancer. Accurate detection of adducts in the genome will shed light on tumorigenesis. However, commonly used detection methods are unable to pinpoint the exact genomic locations of adducts. Long-read nanopore sequencing has the potential to accurately detect multiple types of DNA adducts at single-nucleotide precision. In this study, we developed a novel statistical toolkit, IonStats, to profile DNA adducts in nanopore sequencing data. With IonStats, we investigated the effects of the adduct-inducing genotoxic compounds aristolochic acid II and melphalan on nanopore sequencing and found both shared and compound-specific perturbations in base quality scores, ionic current profiles, and translocation dynamics. Notably, these treatments profoundly altered nanopore readouts and led to substantial sequence-specific read interruptions. Our study shows that nanopore sequencing can be effectively employed to detect and characterize DNA adducts, paving the way for high-resolution, high-throughput profiling of DNA damage and the exposome.

title: No detectable DNA methylation in the kelps (Laminariales): a conversion-free test of a predicted loss
authors: Sleith, R. S.; Lindell, S.; Lomas, M. W.; Molano, G.; Price, N. N.; Quigley, C. T. C.; Countway, P. D.
abstract: Kelps (Laminariales) dominate temperate and polar rocky coasts and support a fast-growing aquaculture sector. Breeding and restoration programs need to know whether a line's performance follows its genotype or its culture history. DNA methylation has been reported in kelps, with differences by life stage, thermal history and population of origin now underpinning a literature on conditioning and priming in seaweed breeding. Recent comparative genomics work predicts otherwise, because brown algae lack the canonical DNA methyltransferases and should therefore carry little or no DNA methylation. We tested the prediction with native-DNA nanopore sequencing, which requires neither bisulfite conversion nor methylation-dependent digestion, in seven kelp datasets spanning three genera, four species and four S. latissima life stages. Nuclear 5-methylcytosine stayed at the measurement background in every sequence context (CG 0.021-0.034% of sites, against 0.023% on PCR copies that carry no methyl group by construction), while the same pipeline returned 58% of CG sites methylated in a diatom and recovered the transposon-targeted distribution a functioning system predicts. In native reads, thirteen of the fourteen best-covered chloroplast positions that bisulfite sequencing placed above 2% carry at most one methylated call, and those published levels track each library's conversion efficiency rather than its tissue. Gene content and direct measurement agree, so the heritable effects reported in cultivated kelp require a carrier other than DNA methylation: chromatin modifications or non-coding RNA.

title: A metacommunity of complex microbial communities shows high spatial synchrony, ecological memory, gradual succession and invasion resistance
authors: Gao, R.; Abbaszade, G.; Li, S.; Schattenberg, F.; Suering, C.; Stueckrath, K.; Schoenfelder, E.; Grimm, V.; Mueller, S.
abstract: Complex microbial communities are increasingly applied in biotechnological and health-related environments, yet maintaining their diversity and relative community composition over extended periods remains challenging. While dispersal can counteract the divergence of spatially separated communities, it remains unclear whether controlled mass transfer can sustain compositional synchrony in highly diverse communities over extended periods, whether this synchrony persist after dispersal is interrupted, and how robust such communities are to invasion. Here, we investigate these questions using a loop-design reactor (LDR) comprising five local wastewater microbial communities connected by controlled mass transfer. The experiment covered multiple rounds of alternating mass transfer and insular phases over a time frame of 318 days, different mass transfer intensities, and the introduction of defined microbial invaders. Community dynamics were monitored at a high temporal resolution by single-cell flow cytometry and complemented by metagenomic analyses of selected samples to characterize taxonomic compositions and functional potential. A Bray-Curtis-based Synchrony Index revealed that controlled mass transfer established high compositional synchrony among five local communities, which persisted for more than 150 generations. Although the community structures underwent gradual succession, the local communities remained synchronized, demonstrating parallel rather than divergent temporal trajectories. Interruption of dispersal initially promote divergence, whereas during later insular phases high compositional similarity persisted in the absence of mass transfer, consistent with ecological memory. Introduced microbial species failed to establish within resident communities, indicating high invasion resistance. Community functional potential remained largely stable throughout the experiment, although phosphorus accumulation failed during phases of high mass transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled mass transfer can maintain long-term spatial synchrony of complex microbial communities while allowing gradual community succession. Repeated connectivity promoted compositional similarity beyond periods of active dispersal while maintaining invasion resistance and functional stability, highlighting controlled dispersal as a promising community-level strategy for managing complex microbial communities.

title: De novo Genome Assembly and Annotation of the Seep Tubeworm Lamellibrachia satsuma using Oxford Nanopore Sequencing
authors: Patra, A. K. K.; Kwon, Y. M.; Won, Y.-J.; Yang, Y.
abstract: The tubeworm Lamelllibrachia satsuma inhabits seep region by forming a mutualistic symbiotic relationship with chemosynthetic bacteria residing in its trophosome. Genomic and symbiotic studies have been extensively conducted, primarily from a bacterial perspective. But rarely vice versa. Here we present a high-quality draft genome assembly of L. satsuma and its tissue-specific transcriptome data. This genome will be valuable for further understanding the mechanisms of adaptation in cold seep environments, host-microbe interactions, as well as genome variation among tubeworms. We generated ~103 Gb of genomic sequencing data using Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms, which assembled in a 665 Mb draft genome. The assembled genome consisted of 6,320 scaffolds with 95.7% genome completeness. Among 32,394 predicted protein-coding genes, 1,063 gene families have expanded, and 1,385 gene families were contracted. Among the expanded gene families, multiple copies of leukocyte elastase inhibitor, reverse transcriptase, arylesterase, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase genes were found. Molecular clock analysis based on the phylogenomic dataset revealed that L. sastuma and L. luymesi were diverged from their common ancestor during the Early Cenozoic era, approximately 13 million years ago.

title: How good a predictor the in vitro antibiogram is, of in vivo antibiotic efficacy? An in vitro - in vivo integrated approach
authors: Vaghela, M.; Thakkar, N.; Blough, B.; Kothari, V.
abstract: Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing, particularly the disc diffusion assay (DDA), provides a convenient means of assessing bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics. However, its ability to predict antibiotic efficacy in an infected host remains uncertain. This study investigated the relationship between DDA-derived inhibition zones and host-protective antibiotic activity using Caenorhabditis elegans infection models involving three bacterial pathogens: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Clostridioides difficile. A total of 42 antibiotics were evaluated through DDA, while a separate panel of 75 antibiotics was screened using an automated C. elegans infection assay. Twenty-six antibiotics common to both panels were selected for comparative analysis. Gnotobiotic L3-L4 stage worms were challenged with individual pathogens in the presence of each antibiotic at a fixed concentration of 9.6 microgram/mL. Worm activity was quantified at 24, 48, and 72 h using an automated worm tracker system, with appropriate health, infection, vehicle, and antibiotic-toxicity controls. Overall, DDA-derived zone of inhibition (ZOI) diameters showed weak-to-moderate, pathogen- and time-dependent correlations with worm activity. At 24 h, Pearson's correlation coefficients ranged from -0.20 to 0.31 across the three pathogen-host systems, while at 48 h they ranged from -0.009 to 0.49. Notably, antibiotic rankings based on DDA and host-protective activity differed considerably. For example, against C. difficile, imipenem produced the largest inhibition zone (41 mm) but failed to protect worms at 24 and 48 h, whereas tobramycin, despite producing a smaller inhibition zone (26 mm), exhibited the highest early worm activity. Similar discrepancies were observed with the other pathogens. These findings demonstrate that DDA-derived susceptibility profiles do not consistently predict antibiotic-mediated protection in an infected host. The C. elegans model may therefore serve as a complementary whole-organism screening platform, providing additional functional information for prioritizing antimicrobial agents beyond conventional in vitro susceptibility testing.

title: A de novo reference genome of the red seaweed Furcellaria lumbricalis
authors: Noyen, L.; Van de Vloet, A.; Leliaert, F.; D'hondt, S.; Morcillo Baeza, J.; De Pooter, T.; Strazisar, M.; Knoop, J.; Audenaert, K.; De Clerck, O.
abstract: Furcellaria lumbricalis is a red seaweed that occurs across a broad salinity gradient, ranging from the saline waters of the NE Atlantic to the brackish Baltic Sea. In the Baltic Sea, natural populations of F. lumbricalis are harvested commercially, primarily for furcellaran extraction, a sulphated polysaccharide used as a stabilizing, thickening, and gelling agent. Genomic resources for this species remain absent, constraining evolutionary, ecological, and applied research. Here, we present a de novo reference genome assembly of the seaweed Furcellaria lumbricalis using PacBio Hifi and Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing. The final assembly, consisting of 149 contigs spanning 918.2 Mb, contains a high proportion of repetitive elements (90.5%), and has an N50 of 15,5 Mb. We further integrated RNA-seq data, protein homology evidence, and ab initio gene prediction to build a genome annotation comprising 6100 genes, of which 82.6% has a functional annotation. This genomic evidence contributes to a steadily growing body of genomic resources of red algae, with often expanded and highly repetitive genomes, and helps facilitate the study of genetic adaptation to their unique environments.

title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable Super Intelligence Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
authors: Mondal, K.; Padi, S.; Kaur, N.; Makambi, W.; Hoogerheide, D. P.; Heinrich, F.; Mihailescu, M.; Klauda, J. B.; Cardone, A.
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generative super intelligence (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable super intelligence (XSI). We fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. Generated candidates were screened with an AMP classifier and filtered based on predicted minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), along with human insights into AMP structure and activity in bacterial membranes. A final set of peptides was selected for synthesis and experimental testing. Biological assays confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, while fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements characterized membrane binding and peptide structure. We then applied XSI techniques to interpret the generative model and derive biological insights. Specifically, layer probing was used to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue-level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we evaluated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. We further examined associations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties in bacterial membrane mimics, relating these observations to biological activities in cell-based assays. These analyses provide insight into the model's decision-making process. This builds confidence that the learned amino acid interdependencies have physico-chemical significance, as applied to AMPs, and may facilitate the discovery of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can support rational AMP discovery.

title: ARGeement: sequence-based, versioned mapping of antimicrobial resistance gene databases
authors: Vujic, V.; Helyes, G.; Toth, A. G.; Csabai, I.; Solymosi, N.
abstract: Genomic studies of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rely on several independently curated reference databases, which describe the same genes under different names, in different structures and with different classifications. This makes results obtained with different databases difficult to compare. ARGeement maps the entries of AMRFinderPlus, the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD) and ResFinder/DisinFinder to each other by protein sequence, independently of their names. It characterises every link by its relation type, difference count and coverage, tracks the database versions, and produces a documented, immutable mapping for every release. The 17,920 entries of the release described here encode 17,959 protein sequences, corresponding to 9,337 unique proteins. For 64.4% of the cross-database entry pairs that encode the same protein, the names differ even when letter case is ignored, and 447 pairs show a genuine naming conflict. Conversely, 2.0% of the pairs with the same allele name do not encode the same protein. For synthetic variants created with known modifications, the original protein was among the best hits in 99.6% of the cases. In 100 complete RefSeq genomes annotated with AMRFinderPlus, the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI) and ResFinder, the gene names agreed at 55.3%-75.6% of the loci called by both tools of a pair, whereas after mapping the two reference proteins were identical, near-identical or length variants at 89.6%-94.2%. These results show that name-based comparison is unreliable even for identical sequences, and that a sequence-based, versioned mapping is needed.

title: ChIMe-seq enables multimodal epigenetic profiling in single molecules and single cells
authors: Verity-Legg, J.; Joly-Smith, E.; Straver, R.; Mourragui, S.; Clark, S.; Bhardwaj, V.; Blotenburg, M.; Mattiroli, F.; Torres-Garcia, S.; Reik, W.; de Ridder, J.; Zeller, P.; van Oudenaarden, A.
abstract: Recent advances in single-cell and single-molecule sequencing have enabled high-resolution characterization of epigenetic states. However, methods that jointly measure multiple layers of epigenetic regulation within the same molecules and cells remain limited. Here, we developed Chromatin Immuno-Methylation sequencing (ChIMe-seq), a multimodal approach that simultaneously profiles histone modifications, DNA methylation, and nucleosome positioning genome-wide in single molecules and single cells. In contrast to recent approaches that rely on enzymatic fragmentation, ChIMe-seq preserves long DNA molecules by using a methyltransferase to deposit exogenous methylation marks that report on proximal histone modifications. This enables integration of multiple epigenetic features within individual molecules and supports short-read, long-read, and single-cell sequencing. These multimodal measurements are integrated into a novel mathematical framework that captures the coupling between nucleosome positioning, histone modifications, and DNA methylation. Both single-molecule and single-cell analyses reveal that DNA methylation is linked to nucleosome density in a manner modulated by local histone modifications, whilst differences in nucleosome:DNA structures are observed depending on epigenetic context and cell-type. Together, these results establish ChIMe-seq as a framework to investigate multifaceted epigenetic coordination across scales, from single-nucleotide resolution to long-range chromatin organization in single molecules and single cells.

title: Target-enrichment sequencing reveals intergenotypic reassortment of infectious salmon anaemia virus in Atlantic Canada
authors: Zhao, M.; O'Brien, J.; Hawkins, L.; Da Silva Filipe, A.; Smollett, K.; Soares, S.; Ness, M.; Solheim, M. A.; Steine, N.; Karlsen, M.; Hill, S. C.
abstract: Infectious salmon anaemia virus (ISAV) causes severe disease and substantial economic losses in farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The virus has an eight-segment, negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome and is divided into European and North American genotypes. Despite their co-circulation in locations such as the Atlantic coast of Canada, reassortment between these genotypes has never been observed. However, routine diagnostic and sequence-based surveillance often target individual genome segments and may therefore fail to identify reassortant viruses or accurately resolve their genomic ancestry. In this study, we developed a probe panel targeting both genotypes and applied Oxford Nanopore sequencing to 37 ISAV-positive samples collected from 14 farm sites in the Bay of Fundy, New Brunswick, Canada. Twenty-seven samples yielded 29 consensus genomes, including separate viral consensuses recovered from two mixed infections. Segment-specific phylogenies identified 24 viruses with a previously unreported intergenotypic genomic constellation comprising a European-genotype segment 3 and North American-genotype segments 1, 2 and 4 - 8. Their consistent monophyletic clustering across segment-specific phylogenies supports a single ancestral reassortment event followed by onward circulation of the reassortant lineage. A time-scaled phylogeny of segment 3 estimated the posterior mean time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the sampled reassortant cluster as September 2016 (95% HPD: March 2013-June 2019), indicating that this segment 3 lineage pre-dated its first sampling in 2021. Five additional viruses represented several distinct EU-genotype lineages. To our knowledge, this is the first documented reassortment between the European and North American ISAV genotypes. These findings identify an intergenotypic reassortant lineage detected across multiple farms in the Bay of Fundy and demonstrate the value of whole-genome sequencing for detecting reassortment, mixed infections and epidemiologically relevant viral diversity.

title: HARICOT: De Novo Assembly of Raw Nanopore Signals using Fuzzy de Bruijn Graphs
authors: McConnell, U.; Ngo, Q.; Firtina, C.
abstract: Nanopore sequencing enables reading long nucleotide sequences by measuring characteristic changes in ionic current as molecules pass through a nanopore. These current measurements, known as raw signals, can be analyzed without translating them into bases (i.e., without basecalling), which provides fast and resource-efficient genome analysis. Prior work, Rawsamble, enables finding overlaps between raw nanopore signals, without basecalling them, and generating assemblies from these overlaps with off-the-shelf assemblers such as miniasm. Constructing assemblies directly from raw signals can substantially reduce redundancy and fragmentation in signal datasets, which is useful for many downstream tasks such as constructing non-redundant and accurate basecalled reads from assembled signals. However, existing overlap-based signal assembly strategies suffer from limited scalability and resolution mainly due to using off-the-shelf assemblers (e.g., miniasm) that are designed for basecalled sequences. While scalability and performance limitations can be addressed by existing de Bruijn graph approaches to assembly, their reliance on exact matches makes these methods too sensitive to the inherently noisy raw nanopore signals. To improve assembly of raw signals using de Bruijn graph approaches, we present HARICOT, a mechanism that constructs assemblies from raw nanopore signals by utilizing fuzzy de Bruijn graphs and Hough-transform-based overlap detection to robustly tolerate errors and noise in raw nanopore signals. Our evaluations on various genomes of different sizes show that HARICOT significantly improves assembly contiguity and quality compared to Rawsamble, helping close the gap to popular assembly tools such as Flye or wtdbg2 operating on nucleotide sequences. At the same time, performance remains comparable to these assemblers, without requiring additional basecalling. We discuss that assembling raw nanopore signals before basecalling enables future work in various ways such as building these de Bruijn graphs in a streaming way and assembly-aware basecalling techniques that can basecall assembly graphs for accurate and redundancy-resolved basecalling. HARICOT is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/HARICOT . We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page.

title: Comparative metagenomics reveals diversity and metabolic heterogeneity of sediment microbes from the Great Barrier Reef
authors: Ishida, H.; Robbins, S. J.; Bell, S. C.; Lim, J. Y.; Terzin, M.; Webster, N.; Bourne, D. G.; Laffy, P. W.; Hugenholtz, P.; Yeoh, Y. K.; Chan, C. X.
abstract: Microbial communities in coral reefs are highly connected through benthic-pelagic coupling. Pelagic and host-associated microbiomes have recently been characterised via genome-resolved metagenomics. However, similar characterisation of sediment communities has lagged behind due to their higher complexity. Here, using short- and long-read shotgun sequence data, we characterised sediment microbial communities of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. From 191 samples across 48 broadly distributed sites, we recovered 2,698 prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) representing 1,201 species-level clusters, most of which are novel. Compared against their sympatric counterparts in seawater, sediment MAGs exhibited greater phylogenetic diversity and flexibility in metabolic potential, implicating diverse respiration strategies and cycling of nitrogen, sulphur, and hydrogen. They also encode more abundant and novel biosynthetic capabilities, likely reflecting competition and adaptation to intermittent fluctuations in nutrient regimes, and between oxic and anoxic conditions. Our results provide foundational genomic resources for reef sediment microbes, uncovering biodiversity and function that together with planktonic microbes shape the ecological success and stability of coral reef ecosystems.

title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
authors: Batista, C. S. P.; Altaba, R.; Miniac, D. d.; Rodriguez, D.; Navarro Risueno, F.; Rivera, A.
abstract: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

title: PYTHOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM SATIVUM SEED EXTRACTS AGAINST SELECTED HUMAN PATHOGENS.
authors: Gambo, A.; Dawaki, S. S.
abstract: This study evaluates the antimicrobial activity of Lepidium sativum (Garden Cress) seed extracts against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Fusarium oxysporum, and Candida albicans using methanol and acetone as solvents. The antimicrobial effects were assessed through the zone of inhibition and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using serial dilution. The methanol extract exhibited the highest inhibition zones, measuring 23.6 mm for S. aureus and 21.5 mm for E. coli, while the acetone extract showed 22.9 mm and 18.3 mm, respectively. C. albicans exhibited moderate susceptibility, with inhibition zones of 16.2 mm (methanol) and 14.8 mm (acetone), whereas F. oxysporum showed weaker inhibition at 12.4 mm and 10.7 mm, respectively. MIC values ranged from 10-1 to 10-4 dilutions, with methanol extracts maintaining higher efficacy at lower concentrations. These findings validate Lepidium sativum as a potential natural antimicrobial agent, particularly against gram-positive bacteria, and suggest further exploration of its bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical applications.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
authors: Zhao, Q.; Ma, Q.; Luo, J.; Chen, C.; Ke, S.
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
authors: Singh, J.; Singh, K.
abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

title: Persistence of commensal Escherichia coli strains and plasmid transfer in a healthy adult
authors: Moran, R. A.; Hall, R. M.
abstract: Little is known about the ecological dynamics of Escherichia coli strains in the healthy human intestinal tract. Here, the composition of commensal E. coli in a healthy adult was tracked over 700 days. 100 E. coli isolates recovered directly from each of 21 faecal samples collected at monthly intervals were characterised. In total 15 strains were recovered; five were resistant to one or more antibiotics. Five "persistent" strains were found in multiple samples spanning 1- to 5-month periods. The relative abundance of persistent strains ranged from 1-100% of E. coli per sample, but they were dominant (>80%) in 14/21 samples and the only strain in 12. Complete genomes were determined for all strains, including isolates of persistent strains from their first and last appearances. Persistent strains belonged to phylogroups B2 (ST1236 and ST420), A (ST10 and ST93), or D (ST362). Single-sample strains were phylogroup A, B1, B2, D or F. Confirming extended survival in the gut, only minor changes were detected in the chromosomes of persistent strains over their residence periods. However, one lost a plasmid and two gained plasmids, providing evidence for horizontal gene transfer in the gut. A Z-type multidrug resistance plasmid moved from one persistent strain to the next and exchanged a small backbone region with a plasmid in the recipient. An M-type arsenic resistance plasmid was acquired by two different strains and transferred to laboratory E. coli with two co-resident plasmids. All persistent strains, but only 2/10 single-sample strains, carried one or more plasmid-borne bacteriocin determinants.

title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
authors: Ramireddy, V. S. R.; Srivastava, S. K.
abstract: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.

title: EFFECT OF A LACTOBACILLUS POSTBIOTIC ON DIGESTIVE HEALTH IN DOGS RAISED IN CONDITIONS AT RISK OF GIARDIA DUODENALIS INFECTION
authors: Eckhardt, E.; Andreu-Sanchez, S.; van den berg, M. A.; Boucard, A.-S.; Tamasi, B.; Klein, B.; Pagani, E.; Espuche, D.; Chevilot, A.; Kurtz, M.; Lagofun, B.; Deshuillers, P. L.; Le Roux, D.; Cochet-Faivre, N.; Polack, B.; Mammeri, M.
abstract: Giardia duodenalis infection is associated with diarrhea and dysbiosis in dogs, while metronidazole treatment can further disrupt the microbiota. We evaluated adjunctive LB fermentate HF (LBHF), a Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic, in a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study of 30 naturally infected dogs (Terriers). Animals received metronidazole (50 mg/kg/day) with LBHF (50 mg/kg/day) or microcrystalline cellulose placebo (70 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. Clinical outcomes, fecal biomarkers, canine dysbiosis index, and cyst shedding were monitored over 45 days. Fecal shotgun metagenomics was performed at baseline and day 45. After baseline covariate adjustment, LBHF was associated with significantly lower Giardia burdens during treatment, particularly at days 10 and 20, improved fecal consistency, and reduced odor. No significant effects were found for fecal calprotectin, secretory IgA, blood biomarkers of digestive function, or canine dysbiosis index. Overall microbiome turnover was similar between groups, but multivariate analyses identified distinct treatment-associated community trajectories. LBHF was associated with increased Bacteroidota representation and functional capacity for plant polysaccharide degradation, alongside depletion of gene sets involved in flagellar assembly, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and epithelial-cell signaling. Baseline microbiome composition also predicted Giardia burden, highlighting an association between parasite load and bacterial community structure. Adjunctive LBHF supplementation was associated with faster resolution of canine giardiasis, improved fecal quality, and coordinated microbiome remodeling. Further mechanistic studies are needed to establish whether the observed microbiome functional changes contribute to parasite clearance and recovery of intestinal health.

title: Multireplicon plasmids show broad host distributions, high transfer potential, and are enriched in antimicrobial resistance genes
authors: de Quinto, I.; Ramiro Martinez, P.; Silva Rosa, R.; Herencias, C.; Lanza, V. F.; Rodriguez-Beltran, J.
abstract: Plasmids are DNA molecules that replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome and are typically associated with the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence determinants, among other relevant traits. Complex genetic rearrangements (including plasmid fusion) can result in plasmids carrying two or more replication systems, known as multireplicon plasmids. Despite decades of study, we are still far from understanding how multireplicon plasmids arise, persist, and shape the evolution of AMR. Here, we analyzed 24,000 non-redundant plasmids across bacterial genera and found that more than 30% encoded multiple replicons. Compared with single-replicon plasmids, multireplicon plasmids were larger, enriched in antimicrobial, metal, and biocide resistance genes, virulence factors, and transfer-associated features, and observed across broader host taxonomic distributions. Some replicon pairs frequently co-occurred on multireplicon plasmids, whereas others were typically maintained on separate plasmids even when present within the same cell. Replicon pairs also showed non-random spatial organization, being preferentially located either in close proximity or at distant positions along the plasmid backbone. Their phylogenetic congruence varied substantially, suggesting that some replicon associations are evolutionarily transient, whereas others may be persistently co-inherited. Finally, we highlight the contribution of insertion sequences to multireplicon plasmid formation. Together, our work sheds light on the abundance, gene content, organization, and evolutionary dynamics of multireplicon plasmids and underscores their relevance to bacterial evolution and human health.

title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale
authors: Bagci, C.; Talamas-Tanner, A.; Ziemert, N.
abstract: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eightfold to more than 16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), single-amplified genomes and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.cs.uni-tuebingen.de.

title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
authors: Rodriguez-Bouza, V.; von Wachsmann, J. H.; Constantinides, B.; Andreoletti, A.; Odih, E. E.; Nesterenko, L.; Gupta, V.; Lees, J. A.
abstract: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

title: Depth-partitioned oxidation of atmospheric hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane in a glacier forefield soil
authors: Herbert, J.; Dede, B.; Koschitz, L.; Sarbach, J.; Schroth, M. H.; Schoelmerich, M. C.
abstract: Glacier forefields are model systems for pioneer ecosystem assembly under extreme oligotrophy. Their microbial communities carry widespread genomic potential to oxidize atmospheric trace gases, yet whether this potential is transcribed in situ, and by which lineages, remains largely untested. Here we combined depth-resolved profiling of hydrogen (H2), carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH4) at ten locations in the Wildstrubel glacier forefield, Swiss Alps, with mesocosm experiments, long-read metagenomics, and genome-resolved metatranscriptomics. Soils were consistent net sinks for atmospheric H2 and CH4, with fluxes ~2-fold and ~6-fold higher, respectively, in older than in younger terrain. H2 uptake was concentrated in the upper 20 cm, whereas CH4 uptake extended deeper. In the field, CO uptake was masked by apparent subsurface production, but in mesocosms lacking this source both CO and H2 were drawn below atmospheric concentrations. Although 57% of metagenome-assembled genomes encoded trace-gas oxidation enzymes, topsoil transcription was dominated by Group 1h [NiFe]-hydrogenases from a few Actinomycetota populations, in which the CO dehydrogenase coxL was transcribed 20- to 35-fold less. The second most transcribed marker was smoX, most closely related to C2-C6 alkane monooxygenases, suggesting the use of short-chain alkanes of possible subsurface origin. Mobile genetic elements were widely transcribed, matching host transcription, but a 104-kb plasmid-borne coxMSL operon was largely silent. Acetylene perturbation induced no detectable switching between trace-gas pathways. Together, these data suggest that trace-gas metabolism is partitioned across soil depth: atmospheric H2 scavenging dominates topsoil transcription, whereas methanotrophy and CO production occur deeper. Net surface fluxes, particularly for CO, therefore, underestimate gross trace-gas turnover.

title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
authors: Mendez-Hurtado, A.; Coleto-Checa, D.; Alvarez, A.; Marcos-Pasero, H.; Calderon, A.; Maestri, A.; Perez-Cuervo, A.; Blanco-Rivero, A.; Lacruz-Pleguezuelos, B.; Cardenas-Roig, N.; Carrasco-Guijarro, L.; Martin-Segura, A.; Aguilar-Aguilar, E.; Marcos-Zambrano, L. J.
abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

title: Cell-type-resolved methylation analysis using bulk long-read sequencing across human tissues
authors: Chen, H.; Mead, E. A.; Zhang, Y.; Karvelas, N.; Chen, Z.; Thorn, E. L.; Fan, Y.; Ni, M.; Bethancourt, C.-N.; Cohen, D. A.; Fan-Huang, G.; Yan, Z.; Bouhassira, E.; Soualhi, S.; Kozlenkov, A.; Abdul-Ghafar, J.; Mzoughi, S.; Guccione, E.; Dracheva, S.; Cohen, L. J.; Brody, R.; Charney, A. W.; Wu, H.; Kohli, R. M.; Farrell, K. W.; Vijg, J.; Gabre, J. T.; Cohen, D. J.; Elahi, F. M.; Crary, J. F.; Fang, G.
abstract: DNA methylation shapes cellular identity and changes with aging and disease, but most human methylomes come from bulk tissue, which mixes signal across many cell types. A methylation change at the bulk tissue level can reflect a change in cellular composition or an intrinsic shift within a cell type, and the two cannot be separated from bulk data. Single-cell and sorted-cell methods resolve cell types directly, but their cost and workflow complexity pose challenges to large studies. Long-read sequencing of single DNA molecules can directly detect DNA methylation on each read. We built COMET (Cell-of-Origin from METhylation), a framework that uses cell-type-specific methylation to assign individual long reads to cell types from standard bulk long-read sequencing. COMET detects changes in cell-type composition robustly even from shallow bulk long-read data, quantifies methylation level of repetitive DNA within each cell type, and, with deeper sequencing, resolves methylation differences between health and disease in individual cell types. We applied COMET to 140 human blood samples, 104 human brain samples and 59 human colon samples. In blood, we found epigenetic aging clock is primarily driven by shifts in cell-type composition, and that APOE4 carriers have myeloid-specific methylation changes. In brain, we found sex-biased change in cell-type composition with age, resolved methylation and hydroxymethylation separately within each cell type. In colon, we found a consistent expansion of fibroblasts in tumors relative to matched normal tissue, localized methylation loss at LINE-1 in fibroblast cells, and identified tumor- and cell-type-specific hypermethylation in epithelial cells at the promoters of known colorectal cancer genes. By resolving cell-type-specific methylation directly from bulk long-read data, this approach opens broad study of cell-type epigenetics across human tissues in aging and disease.

title: Pili-like proteins are essential for conjugation also in Gram-positive bacteria
authors: ter Beek, J.; Svedberg, D.; Deane-Alder, K.; Ibrahim, M. I. A.; Mateus, A.; Berntsson, R. P.-A.
abstract: Type IV secretion systems (T4SS) enable the spread of antibiotic resistance and other virulence factors. In Gram-positive bacteria, T4SSs have long been thought to lack VirB2-like proteins that form conjugative pili and instead rely on adhesins for cell-cell contacts. Yet, it has remained unclear how subsequent DNA transfer (conjugation) is mediated. Here we identify a VirB2-like protein, PrgFB2, from the clinically isolated plasmid pCF10 in Enterococcus faecalis and show that it is essential for conjugation. Structural modelling confidently predicts a pilus-like assembly for PrgFB2. This is in line with recently proposed models for conjugative pili in Gram-negative T4SSs. We validate the PrgFB2 pili prediction through mutagenesis, conjugation assays, and targeted chemical labelling. By combining various machine learning bioinformatic techniques, we analysed >1000 Gram-positive conjugative plasmids from diverse species, including major pathogens, and identified probable pili-forming VirB2-like proteins in a large majority. Our findings challenge the prevailing view that Gram-positive T4SSs lack pili and highlight critical targets for combating antimicrobial resistance and virulence in Gram-positive bacteria.

title: HIV-1 Mutational Bias Shapes the Supply of Drug Resistance Mutations
authors: Nitido, A. D.; Ömür, N.; Balazs, A. B.
abstract: The development of durable HIV-1 therapeutics requires understanding not only which mutations confer resistance, but also how readily those mutations arise. Prior work has characterized the effects of individual mutations on viral fitness and drug or immune escape; however, the contribution of mutational bias to HIV-1 evolutionary pathways remains largely unquantified. Here, we report and provide an interactive HIV-1 Mutation Rate Atlas (MRA), built on a dataset of empirical measurements of single-cycle HIV-1 mutation accumulation in the absence of selection pressure, using error-corrected long-read sequencing. The MRA estimates the mutation rate at every genomic position to each possible nucleotide, enabling evaluation of amino acid mutability across the genome. Using the MRA, we show that mutation rate biases predict HIV-1 drug resistance variant frequencies across patients. These results demonstrate that mutational biases shape HIV-1 evolutionary outcomes, providing a framework for predicting HIV-1 evolution and drug resistance.

title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia
authors: Pellegrino, M. R.; McLean, J. L.; Kottom, T.; Limper, A.
abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.

title: Linking Early Bacterial Responses to Growth Inhibition via Glucose-Turbidity Dynamics for Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
authors: Deng, Y.; Xu, S.; Hu, H.; Yang, H.; Jiang, W.; Zhu, T.; Li, Q.; Lin, J.
abstract: Earlier susceptibility information can guide timely antibiotic selection, while metabolic measurements can broaden the characterization of bacterial drug responses. We developed glucose-turbidity antimicrobial susceptibility testing (GT-AST) to pair residual-glucose assay signals with turbidity and relate early responses to growth inhibition. Among 43 cultured isolates, some antibiotic-exposed cultures showed glucose-associated changes despite attenuated turbidity responses. These observations provide physiological clues for studying metabolic activity when growth is limited, including future investigations of viable but non-culturable states or persister cells. Conventional broth microdilution relies on overnight growth readings; GT-AST used trajectories collected during approximately 2 h of antibiotic exposure to predict subsequent growth and estimate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Across 100 repeats of isolate-grouped cross-validation, essential agreement between predicted MICs and independently measured reference MICs averaged 87.1%. Eight bronchoalveolar lavage fluid specimens were tested directly without prior bacterial isolation. Levofloxacin susceptibility classifications based on observed growth agreed with hospital results in all four culture-positive specimens. Exact and essential agreement between predicted and hospital MICs each averaged 99.0%. Together, these findings support developing GT-AST to provide earlier susceptibility information for effective, appropriately targeted treatment of patients. Keywords: antimicrobial susceptibility testing; glucose metabolism; turbidity; machine learning; minimum inhibitory concentration

title: Beyond the tripartite genome: a widespread, mobile and gene-rich accessory plasmidome expands the genomic landscape of the model symbiont Sinorhizobium meliloti
authors: Picon-Cossio, J. J.; Crossman, S. G.; Price, A. J.; McGrath, S.; Gupta, T.; Geddes, B.; Gil-Polo, M. A.; Clouse, K.; Guha, S.; Burghardt, L.; Sankari, S.
abstract: Sinorhizobium meliloti is one of the best-studied nitrogen-fixing symbionts, yet research has focused almost entirely on its chromosome and two megaplasmids, pSymA and pSymB. Many strains carry additional accessory plasmids, but these large, pSymA-like elements are rarely recovered from short-read assemblies, leaving a hidden part of the genome unexplored. By sequencing 346 strains with long reads, we recovered 386 accessory plasmids from 76% of strains, with 318 absent from public databases, showing that accessory plasmids are the rule and not the exception. These plasmids were large (34-749 kb), including the largest accessory plasmid reported in S. meliloti, and most were mobilizable or conjugative (relaxases in 85% and mating-pair formation systems in 75% of plasmid clusters), equipping them to move between strains. RepA typing defined 13 replicon groups unique to Sinorhizobium, which could serve as a framework for tracking these plasmids in natural populations. We also found evidence of plasmid expansion by fusion, and one ~315 kb plasmid was a cointegrate of two smaller plasmids from our collection. About two-thirds of plasmid gene families were absent from the main replicons, including defense systems, the anti-restriction protein ArdC, and biosynthetic gene clusters, 53% of which had never been observed before. Overturning the view that S. meliloti lacks restriction-modification systems, we found them in 153 genomes, including on 32 accessory plasmids. Most inferred gene transfers stayed within the family Rhizobiaceae. Accessory plasmids thus form a large, mobile and largely unexplored gene pool that may shape how this model symbiont competes and adapts.

title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
authors: Bueno de Mesquita, C. P.; Woodcroft, B. J.; Fierer, N.
abstract: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

title: WITHDRAWN: Metagenomics reveals a phylogenetically informed microbial signature associated with Morgellons disease
authors: Lambert, A. N.; Kindschuh, W. F.
abstract: The authors have withdrawn this preprint because the human-participant samples underlying the study were collected without Institutional Review Board (IRB) review. In light of unresolved questions concerning research oversight, the authors recognize that public dissemination of these findings was premature. Therefore, the authors request that this preprint not be cited as these matters are addressed.

title: Detection of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and discrimination of vanA and vanB genotypes by VITEK MS Prime MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry and machine learning
authors: Sanchez-Cueto, M.; Gutierrez-Pareja, M.; Cercenado, E.; Munoz, P.; Marin, M.; Rodriguez-Sanchez, B.; Rodriguez-Temporal, D.
abstract: Rapid identification of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and discrimination of resistance mechanisms (VanA and VanB) are critical for appropriate antimicrobial therapy and infection control, particularly during outbreaks. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), combined with machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool for this purpose. We evaluated whether MALDI-TOF mass spectra acquired on VITEK MS PRIME, combined with machine learning, could provide this information. Spectra from 388 from clinical and rectal surveillance samples (135 vancomycin-susceptible (VSEfm), 138 vanA and 115 vanB VREfm) were processed with Clover MSDAS, and four algorithms (partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), linear and polynomial support vector machines (SVM-L and SVM-P) and random forest (RF)) were trained to discriminate VSEfm from VREfm and VanA from VanB isolates. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation and using independent set of characterized E. faecium isolates from routine practice. Pairwise and triplet ensembles of these algorithms were also assessed. In the test set, PLS-DA was the best individual classifier for VSEfm versus VREfm (balanced accuracy, 78.9%), and the ensemble of PLS-DA and linear SVM reached 80.7%. Validation within routine isolates confirmed the models robustness, achieving 100% correct classification. Discrimination of VanA from VanB was more accurate: 93.2% with RF and up to 97.1% with ensembles. Identical sequence types were found among susceptible, VanA and VanB isolates, indicating that classification was not driven by clonal lineage. MALDI-TOF MS combined with machine learning is a promising, low-cost tool for VREfm screening and vanA/vanB differentiation.

title: A small molecule inhibits Neisseria gonorrhoeae pilus formation
authors: Nicholson, K. R.; Yin, S.; Hayes, K. A.; Ahmad, S. S.; Jutras, B. L.; Edwards, J. L.; Luan, C.-H.; Seifert, H. S.
abstract: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is becoming increasingly antimicrobial-resistant. N. gonorrhoeae requires the Type IV pilus (T4p) for pathogenesis, wherein the T4p promotes colonization through adherence to host cells and resistance to neutrophil killing. The pilus also is required for natural transformation and twitching motility. Collectively, these critical functions make the T4p an attractive drug target. Previously, we developed a high-throughput screen to identify compounds with activity against the zinc metalloprotease Mpg, which is involved in T4p biogenesis. Here, we identified a lead compound, SC144, that inhibits Mpg peptidoglycan-hydrolyzing activity in both N. gonorrhoeae and other bacteria encoding Mpg-like M23B metallopeptidase orthologs. Interestingly, SC144 targets Mpgs carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities. Importantly, SC144 inhibited N. gonorrhoeae colonization and prevented its survival in two primary human cell culture models of infection without toxic effects on these host cells. This work provides strong evidence that SC144 is a promising lead compound with anti-virulence activity against N. gonorrhoeae.

title: Evaluating cell-free RNA extraction platforms for RNA liquid biopsy via nanopore sequencing
authors: Mattingly, C. S.; Hill, A. D.; Kim, D. H.
abstract: RNA liquid biopsies provide systemic insights into health and disease by profiling cell-free RNAs (cfRNAs) secreted into the circulation. While cfRNAs are thought to be short or fragmented, recent efforts using long-read nanopore sequencing have found that thousands of longer, full-length cfRNAs are highly abundant in plasma. However, cfRNA extraction methods have not been rigorously evaluated to assess reproducibility, cfRNA length, and transcriptome complexity. Here we show that extraction workflow is a major source of variation by comparing identical plasma samples across three different cfRNA extraction platforms. While these platforms recover comparable quantities of cfRNA, we perform nanopore sequencing to show that they differ in their cfRNA composition based on read-length distribution and biotype representation. Principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering of variable protein-coding and repeat-derived cfRNAs show that samples tend to cluster based on extraction platform. Robust detection of specific biotypes is contingent on extraction platform, as evidenced by significant enrichment of Alu element- and long noncoding RNA (lncRNA)-derived cfRNAs in some but not all methodologies. Our results reveal that cfRNA extraction platforms influence the composition and complexity of downstream libraries, highlighting the importance of selecting the right platform for profiling disease-relevant biomarkers in RNA liquid biopsy studies.

title: Genomic Characterization of a Typical Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli Isolate from an Egyptian Fruit Bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus from Coastal Kenya
authors: Kamau, J.; Kimemia, B. B.; Abuom, D.; Agwanda, B.; Musila, L.; Odoyo, E.; Kivata, M. W.; Mbae, C.; Onguso, J.; Haynes, R.; Kellar, G.; Lutomiah, J.; Eads, J.; Eyase, F.
abstract: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality cases among young children under the age of five, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

title: Environmental heterogeneity and microbial community architecture shape N2O fluxes in intertidal coastal sediments
authors: Dolivet-Marechal, M.; Palacin-Lizarbe, C.; Schwob, G.; Siljanen, H. M. P.; paul, D.; Delort, A.; Gervaix, J.; Creuze des Chatelliers, C.; Schmidt, S.; Cognat, M.; Sebag, D.; Taugourdeau, O.; Schubert, C.; Labourdette, N.; Bertrand, I.; Rossi, L. M. W.; Le Roux, X.; Richaume, A.; Florio, A.
abstract: Seagrass meadows are key ''blue carbon ecosystems'', yet their contribution to nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions remains poorly constrained. We investigated environmental and microbial descriptors of N2O fluxes in intertidal sediments of Arcachon Bay, home to Europe's largest Zostera noltii meadow. At six sites, we measured in situ N2O fluxes in adjacent bare and vegetated sediments and characterized sediment properties, N2O-cycling genes using qPCR and targeted metagenomics, and microbial co-occurrence networks. Fluxes ranged from -3.7 to 8.4 mol N2O m-2 d-1. Spatial location was the strongest descriptor of flux variation, with inner-bay sites showing higher emissions associated with environmental conditions, carbon accumulation, pH, and microbial community characteristics. Vegetation effects were comparatively small and site-dependent. Metagenomic descriptors of N2O-cycling genes were more informative than qPCR-based descriptors. Taxa associated with nirS (Thiohalophilus), nirK (Planktotalea) and nosZ1 (Roseobacter) were identified as potential contributors to N2O production or reduction, respectively. These findings indicate that spatially structured environmental conditions and microbial community characteristics better describe N2O flux variation than seagrass presence alone. Measurements across tidal and seasonal cycles are needed to establish the temporal consistency of these patterns.

title: Emergence of mobile fosA3-blaCTX-M-65 with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) on conjugative plasmids in avian pathogenic Escherichia coli from industrial poultry in Pakistan
authors: Umair, M.; Fatima, F.; Mathias, J.; Iannetelli, T.; Mohsin, M.; Farlow, A.; Walsh, T. R.
abstract: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.

title: RAD: A Read-structure Agnostic Demultiplexer for Single-Cell Long-Read Sequencing and Analysis
authors: Vaidya, C. M.; Carpenter, M. C.; Abdullah, L.; Kolling, F. W.; Huang, Y. H.; Song, L.; Ackerman, M. E.
abstract: Single-cell long-read sequencing (LRS) techniques enable the analysis of full transcript sequences within a cell. However, LRS introduces computational challenges for parsing information, often necessitating the development of custom workflows to handle complex read layouts, such as split combinatorial barcodes. To address these challenges, we introduce an error-robust, read-structure agnostic demultiplexer (RAD). In RAD, users can easily specify read structure, such as adapter sequence and relative barcode position, and can rapidly extract these elements for each read. RAD implements highly accurate barcode whitelist generation from long-read data alone, without the benefit of short-read support or priors while uniquely avoiding common but previously uncharacterized errors during demultiplexing. RAD's comprehensive barcode error correction protocols allow for more sensitive and precise barcode-read assignments. In synthetic and real-world benchmarks against gold-standard demultiplexers, RAD is faster and achieves better biological discovery capability in downstream gene expression analysis than existing pipelines. We show RAD can be applied to datasets ranging from high-definition long-read spatial transcriptomics to targeted long-read single-cell immune receptor sequencing, making it a powerful and scalable tool for both standard and custom long-read sequencing experiments.

title: MicroBioAgent: an AI agent for automated microbiome analysis
authors: Li, Z.; WANG, J.; Wang, C.; Ding, Y.; Zhang, L.
abstract: Microbiome data analysis demands customized workflows tailored to specific biological questions, sequencing modalities, and data properties. However, constructing and executing these workflows requires navigating heterogeneous software dependencies, reference databases, and multi-step parameter tuning. Here, we present MicroBioAgent, an autonomous, domain-specific agent framework that translates high-level biological queries into executable, study-specific pipelines across 16S rRNA amplicon, reference-based shotgun, and de novo assembly-based metagenomics. Rather than relying on static pipeline templates, MicroBioAgent employs a closed-loop execution architecture: it dynamically selects and runs bioinformatics tools within user-controlled environments while iteratively inspecting intermediate outputs to adapt downstream analytical decisions. Furthermore, to address the long-running nature of metagenomic computation, we introduce an asynchronous background task-management mechanism that reduces LLM token consumption by over 50% while enabling real-time plan adjustment and automated workflow resumption. We systematically evaluated MicroBioAgent across three benchmarks of increasing complexity: (1) paired amplicon and shotgun profiling of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes, (2) taxonomic and functional profiling coupled with machine-learning classification in a colorectal cancer cohort, and (3) de novo metagenomic assembly, metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) binning, and metabolic pathway reconstruction in a polyethylene degradation study. Across all benchmarks, MicroBioAgent faithfully recapitulated the primary biological findings of the original studies, exhibiting high analytical concordance despite expected tool- and database-dependent variations. In systematic robustness evaluations across 27 independent runs spanning three backbone large language models and three prompt-complexity tiers, MicroBioAgent achieved a 98.8% task completion rate and yielded highly reproducible diversity and differential-abundance estimates. MicroBioAgent establishes a scalable, adaptive paradigm for end-to-end computational microbiome research.

title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research
authors: Christensen, R. N.; Gilliland, M.; Young, J.; Manning-Neal, R.; Fan, H.; Lu, S.; Payne, S.; Johnson, W. E.
abstract: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.

title: Remarkable Biosynthetic Diversity in the Bionectriaceae: Uncovering the genomic basis of antipathogen bioactivity of cacao fungal endophytes Clonostachys rosea and Waltergamsia zeylanica.
authors: Atencio, L. A.; Castillo, H. E.; Barrios-Jaen, M.; Quintero, I.; Martinez, A.; Rodriguez, C.; Gutierrez, M.; Mejia, L. C.
abstract: Cacao (Theobroma cacao) production in tropical countries is threatened by fungal diseases caused by Moniliophthora roreri and M. perniciosa. Two cacao pod endophytes from Bionectriaceae, Clonostachys rosea TCF417 and Waltergamsia zeylanica TCF400, exhibit growth antagonism towards M. roreri; however, the genetic basis underlying the bioactivity of these strains has not been addressed. Here, we aimed to identify biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) potentially associated with the antifungal bioactivity of these two strains and performed a comparative analysis with 30 publicly available Bionectriaceae genomes using BiG-SCAPE. Whole-genome sequencing using Oxford Nanopore and Illumina technologies, resulted in assemblies of 52.9 Mb (C. rosea TCF417) and 31 Mb (W. zeylanica TCF400). Genome annotation was conducted using Funannotate, and secondary metabolite BGCs were predicted using antiSMASH. The two cacao endophytes harbored 92 BGCs (C. rosea: 67; W. zeylanica: 25), indicating remarkable biosynthetic diversity. Across all 32 genomes, 1,523 BGC-containing regions were identified, most belonging to T1PKS clusters. Network-based clustering revealed 209 gene cluster families (GCFs), of which 52 corresponded to previously characterized BGCs. Conserved BGCs for antifungal compounds, including sorbicillinoids and verticillins, were identified in cacao endophytes and across Bionectriaceae. Additionally, an antifungal assay conducted here demonstrated that verticillin D from C. rosea TCF417 exhibited growth inhibition of plant pathogens Moniliophthora roreri and Mycena citricolor. With about 75% of unassigned GCFs, our results reveal a largely untapped biosynthetic repertoire in the Bionectriaceae and identify verticillin D as a candidate contributor to the antagonism of C. rosea against plant pathogens.

title: NanoHIV-DR: a Nextflow workflow for consensus and read level HIV-1 drug resistance profiling from Oxford Nanopore sequencing
authors: Lule, D.; Ssemwanga, D.; Kaleebu, P.; Tully, D. C.
abstract: Oxford Nanopore sequencing offers a rapid and portable approach for HIV-1 drug resistance (HIVDR) genotyping, but analysis of the resulting long-read data requires multiple bioinformatics steps and currently available nanopore workflows are limited.
