We developed NanoHIV-DR, a Nextflow-based workflow that streamlines the analysis of Oxford Nanopore sequencing data and generation of HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR processes raw POD5 files through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, quality filtering, read alignment and consensus generation, before identifying resistance-associated mutations and interpreting predicted drug susceptibility. The workflow provides two complementary approaches to HIVDR analysis: consensus-based resistance interpretation using Sierra and read-level detection of resistance-associated variants, enabling mutations below the consensus level to be identified and quantified. Outputs are integrated with clinical metadata to generate human-readable HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR provides a reproducible and accessible workflow for Nanopore-based HIVDR analysis with reduced bioinformatics expertise and manual processing for translating long-read sequencing data into interpretable resistance profiles.

title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory metagenomes
authors: Sy, M. A.; Prosperi, M.; Benos, P. V.; Marini, S.
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Metagenomics; Long-Read Microbiology; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific {chi}2-ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Performance for P. aeruginosa was more heterogeneous: long-read models performed well for amikacin, reaching 0.89 with PacBio and 0.88 with Nanopore, whereas Illumina performed substantially better for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, and levofloxacin, reaching accuracies of approximately 0.87, 0.77, and 0.70, respectively. Across most organism-antibiotic combinations, RF accuracy was numerically higher than the classification accuracies obtained with KARGA and ResFinder, which generally remained near 0.50. Increasing pathogen abundance from 5% to 10% and increasing the number of selected features from 2,500 to 5,000 generally produced modest improvements in classification accuracy, although the magnitude of improvement varied across organism-antibiotic combinations and sequencing platforms. Conclusions: Genome-wide k-mer machine learning can recover phenotype-associated antimicrobial resistance signals from simulated respiratory metagenomes, although performance depends strongly on the organism, antibiotic, and sequencing platform. These results represent a simulation-based proof of concept.

title: Cross-species dissemination of diverse plasmid lineages and mobile resistance modules shapes carbapenemase co-production in Chilean Enterobacterales
authors: Guerra-Leal, N.; Pilquinao, N.; Berrios-Pasten, C.; Arros, P.; Galvez-Silva, M.; Acosta, J.; Ascencio, A.; Valdivia, E.; Lagos, R.; Chavez, F. P.; Araya, I.; Iglesias, R.; Araya, P.; Hormazabal, J. C.; Villamil, A.; Marcoleta, A. E.
abstract: Carbapenemase co-production among Enterobacterales is an emerging clinical challenge, yet the relative contributions of clonal expansion, cross-species plasmid dissemination, and movement of resistance modules remain unclear. We integrated national surveillance data with plasmid-resolved hybrid genomes to investigate these processes in Chile. Among 414 isolates carrying at least two carbapenemase families referred during 2018-2024, annual numbers increased markedly alongside broader taxonomic and geographic representation. Thirty isolates were selected to span variation in year, species, region, and carbapenemase profile. These represented 11 species from six genera and contained 149 complete plasmids, 57 of which carried carbapenemase genes. Of 63 carbapenemase gene copies, 62 were plasmid-borne, and 55 of the 57 carbapenemase-carrying plasmids were predicted to be conjugative or mobilizable. Complementary plasmid typing, whole-sequence clustering, structural comparisons, and pan-plasmidome analysis identified three recurrent lineages: IncX3/blaNDM-7, IncN/blaKPC-2, and IncHI2A/blaVIM-1. Their occurrence across multiple species and sequence types supported cross-species dissemination, while numerous minor groups and singletons revealed a broader repertoire of plasmid architectures and accessory genes. Related backbones carried variable resistance regions, and equivalent class 1 integrons and transposon-associated platforms occurred in otherwise unrelated plasmids, indicating modular redistribution of carbapenemase genes. In selected isolates, co-resident plasmids created resistance redundancy, brought recurrent carbapenemase plasmid lineages together, or coupled resistance and virulence within the same cell. Thus, co-production did not arise through a single route: bacterial clones, plasmids shared across species, and mobile resistance modules each contributed to its emergence. Complete plasmid resolution is essential to distinguish these processes and track their dissemination.

title: Transposon-driven pervasive genome restructuring and regulatory evolution in early-diverging Holomycota
authors: Lax, C.; Tahiri, G.; Croll, D.
abstract: Early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi showcase major evolutionary transitions in the fungal kingdom, share features with other eukaryotic clades and bacteria, and include pathogens of significant concern. These lineages contain some of the most reduced and expanded genome architectures of the fungal kingdom and have adopted unique DNA methylation systems. Yet, the evolutionary trajectory of early-diverging non-Dikarya fungi remains poorly understood. A key driver is thought to be transposable elements, which shape genomic plasticity, organization and regulation. Here, we perform a comprehensive comparative analysis across the Holomycota to chart drivers of early fungal evolution. We demonstrate that contrasting transposon dynamics directly shape genomic diversity across these lineages, fueling extensive protein domain expansions through widespread co-option. This heterogeneous landscape is regulated by a multi-layered epigenetic network impacting chromatin configuration, and we reveal a distinct transcriptional activation role for adenine methylation over specific transposons. Beyond driving functional innovation, mobile elements serve as a source of regulatory diversification, providing transcription factor binding sites at key chromosomal features. Furthermore, synteny tracking uncovers multiple whole-genome duplication events across Mucoromycotina, where DNA transposons preferentially accumulate at duplication breakpoints and undergo rapid inactivation. Strikingly, we also show that horizontal transposon transfers frequently cross deep evolutionary boundaries, including cross-kingdom exchanges with protists. Together, our findings illuminate key drivers of genome architecture in non-Dikarya fungi and reshape our understanding of genome dynamics across the fungal kingdom.

title: Cortical neurons accumulate point mutations at similar rates in mice and humans
authors: Saeidi, M.; Yoo, J.; Stolyarova, A.; Polleux, F.; Przeworski, M.; Spisak, N.
abstract: Across vertebrate species, it has long been known that germline mutation rates per year are inversely proportional to reproductive ages. A similar pattern was recently reported in mammals for mutations in colonic epithelium, leading to speculation that this inter-species scaling may apply to many cell types. We tested whether a similar relationship holds in postmitotic cells, by estimating point mutation rates in mouse cortical neurons from PacBio HiFi circular consensus sequencing data. Our analysis revealed a significant effect of age on the number of point mutations, of 25.9 mutations per diploid genome per year (95% CI: [17.7, 34.1]). This rate is comparable to the one reported for human neurons, indicating that somatic rates need not scale with lifespan. Our findings further demonstrate that a readily available sequencing method can be used to reliably identify somatic mutations at single-cell resolution.

title: Identification of eukaryotes as a bycatch in global microbiome data
authors: Maistrenko, O. M.; Kim, C. Y.; Nishijima, S.; Fullam, A.; Ferretti, P.; Schudoma, C.; Keller, M. I.; Robbani, S. M.; Kartal, E.; Akanni, W.; Alves, R.; Van Rossum, T.; Khedkar, S.; Podlesny, D.; Kojima, Y.; Hamabata, T.; Uemura, N.; Nagata, N.; Spang, A.; Heintz-Buschart, A.; Schmidt, T. S.; Kuhn, M.; Bork, P.
abstract: Eukaryotes shape microbiomes as macroscopic hosts, microscopic community members, and food sources, yet the diversity and ecological significance of microbial eukaryotes remain poorly resolved. Here, we present metaEukaryome, an organelle genome-centered framework for detection of eukaryotes in metagenomic data that leverages mitochondrial and plastid sequences as robust signatures of presence. Applying metaEukaryome to 75,727 metagenomic samples collected across the globe reveals strong environment-specific patterns in the prevalence of detected eukaryotes. Integrating eukaryotic and prokaryotic profiles further reveals recurrent cross-domain co-occurrence and symbiosis in the human gut. In particular, Blastocystis is associated with metabolically reduced, uncultured bacterial clades, including Candidatus Borkfalkia and CAG-345, whose DNA and RNA are detected in a Blastocystis culture previously reported as axenic. Their complementary metabolic repertoires further support a candidate symbiotic relationship. These findings imply that more novel (endo-)symbionts of gut protists can be discovered by reanalysing existing data.

title: Oral microbiome and DNA virome profiling in pigs reveals age-associated dynamics and extracellular recovery of Streptococcus suis-associated phage lineages
authors: Osei, E. K.; Ornelas, M. A. S.; Garcia Manzanilla, E.; Mahony, J.; Kenny, J. G.
abstract: The pig oral cavity is a critical interface for microbial transmission and herd health monitoring, yet its microbiome and virome remains poorly characterised. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing of oral fluids from pigs across 15 commercial farms in Ireland, using paired bulk and virus-like particles (VLP) enrichment to capture comprehensive microbial and DNA virome diversity. Microbial communities shifted progressively with age, with early post-weaning animals enriched in environmental genera such as Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus and later stages dominated by lactic acid bacteria and anaerobes. Only 20.6% of vOTUs could be assigned to a known genus, with the most abundant being Astrithrvirus, which increased with age. Both microbiome and DNA virome exhibited predictable, coordinated age-associated succession with strong cross-domain coupling supported by virus-host networks. Functional profiling of the microbiome revealed that predicted carbohydrate substrates tracked the dietary transitions, while accessory viral functions partitioned by lifestyle and host. The early post-weaning stage was characterised by high abundance of viral integration and excision functions, as well as elevated resistome diversity that was almost exclusively of prokaryotic origin rather than viral. Importantly, 26 of the 25,223 vOTUs identified were predicted to target Streptococcus suis, providing the first metagenomic catalogue of such phages from pig oral environments. These findings expand our understanding of oral microbiome-virome dynamics and establish a framework for integrated microbiome and viromics approaches that could enable therapeutic phage discovery and inform microbiome-targeted interventions in pig production systems.

title: The Barcode Inference Pipeline (BIP): From Sequencer Output to DNA Barcodes
authors: Prosser, S. W.; Thompson, K. A.; Bard, N. W.; Floyd, R. A.; Ozsahin, E.; Hebert, P. D. N.
abstract: DNA barcoding involves the recovery of a DNA sequence for a target gene region from its source specimen. This process becomes complex when multiple sequences are recovered from a specimen. This diversity can reflect methodological artifacts (e.g., chimeras, PCR errors, sequencing errors, tag jumps) and real template diversity in the DNA extract (e.g., contamination, endosymbionts, nuclear-mitochondrial pseudogenes (NUMTs), parasites). To support the analysis of sequence data from millions of specimens annually, the Centre for Biodiversity Genomics (CBG) has developed BIP, the Barcode Inference Pipeline. Compatible with all major sequencing platforms, BIP processes fastq files and returns both target DNA barcodes and non-target sequences (NTS). BIP implements filtration, demultiplexing, primer trimming, read denoising, chimera scanning, sequence error correction, operational taxonomic unit (OTU) delineation, OTU taxonomy assignment, and selection of the target barcode. When analysis examines the cytochrome c oxidase 1 (COI) barcode region, BIP assigns each OTU to a Barcode Index Number (BIN) when there is a match. BIP also returns summary files, including a taxonomic assignment for each OTU based on a DNA barcode reference library. We describe BIP's flexibility and structure before demonstrating its functionality by analyzing COI sequence data generated from both nanopore and Illumina platforms, as well as rbcLa and ITS2 data generated from plants, and 18S data generated from arthropods. Because it disambiguates target and non-target sequences, BIP outperforms an alternative pipeline package, ONTbarcoder. To ease access, installation, and functionality, BIP is provided as a Docker container and is also available in the Galaxy toolshed.

title: A rapid and sensitive Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) assay for detection of mecA antibiotic resistance gene in clinical and food bacterial isolates
authors: Baldenweck, L.; Djisalov, M.; Pinamonti, D.; manzano, M.; Gadjanski, I.; Vidic, J.
abstract: An advanced LAMP assay targeting the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was developed and validated using clinical and foodborne S. aureus isolates. Reference strains, including both methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant S. aureus, were used to evaluate and optimize assay performance. With the newly designed ID16 LAMP primer set, the detection limit for mecA was 15 fg/{micro}L of total genomic DNA, equivalent to 5 copies/{micro}L, and the assay turnaround time was only 25 min. All mecA-positive isolates identified by conventional qPCR were successfully detected by the LAMP assay. Overall, the developed LAMP method provides a rapid, highly specific, and sensitive alternative for mecA detection.

title: Genome-resolved metagenomics reveals population-dependent gut microbiome responses to albendazole-ivermectin treatment
authors: Gandasegui, J.; Fleitas, P.; Messa, A.; Gelaye, W.; Shao, Y.; Degarege, D.; Bedane, D.; Novela, V.; de Jesus, A.; Dias, J.; Ambridge, K.; Sevilleno, N.; Bewsher, A.; K. Judah, T.; Mandomando, I.; Enbiale, W.; Lawley, T.; Krolewiecki, A.; Munoz, J.; Doyle, S. R.
abstract: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. We characterised the microbiome, resistome, and functional profiles of 858 paired stool metagenomes from 429 children treated with albendazole or a fixed-dose albendazole-ivermectin co-formulation in the ALIVE clinical trial in Ethiopia and Mozambique. Baseline microbiome composition differed more by country than infection status and was not associated with albendazole efficacy or adverse events. Co-formulation treatment, particularly three consecutive daily doses, was associated with depletion of Enterobacteriaceae, predominantly Escherichia coli, in Ethiopia, with reductions in E. coli-associated resistance genes and metabolic pathways. Genome-resolved analyses of over 22,000 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes confirmed this depletion across multiple E. coli strain-level populations, linking taxonomic, resistome, and functional signals to one ecological event. These findings reveal an off-target effect of combination anthelmintic treatment relevant to large-scale deworming programmes and expand genomic resources for African gut microbiota.

title: Antibiotic prescribing and resistance beyond hospital surveillance networks in India
authors: Kaur, J.; Madaan, V.; Sharma, R.; Agarwal, Z.; Gudi, N.; Bisen, T.; Gupte, S.; Mutreja, A.; Doegar, N.; Singh, H.; Agarwal, G.; Sethi, T.
abstract: Hospital-based networks provide much of Indias antimicrobial resistance surveillance evidence, but community-facing data on both prescribing and resistance remain limited. We analysed 2.78 million prescription-validated antibiotic records and 155,764 microbiology samples from Tata 1mg, a digital healthcare platform, during 2023-2025. We assessed prescribing composition and resistance trends, and explored ecological prescribing-resistance associations using merged monthly series. Access antibiotics accounted for 28.7% of records, compared with 47.0% for Watch and 11.9% for Not Recommended antibiotics. Across 25 eligible states and union territories, Access shares ranged from 16.1% to 38.0%. Urine comprised 93.9% of samples. Among urinary Escherichia coli isolates, resistance was 4.9% to nitrofurantoin and amikacin, compared with 53.6% to ceftriaxone and 57.0% to ciprofloxacin. Exploratory prescribing-resistance associations varied by organism and antibiotic. These findings identify stewardship priorities within a digitally mediated care pathway and illustrate the complementary value of routinely collected pharmacy and laboratory data for surveillance beyond hospital-centred networks.

title: Long-term transmission chains fueling the drug-resistant tuberculosis burden in Southern Brazil
authors: Soares, T. d. S.; Pivato, A. F.; Frosi, F.; Pavanelo, D. B.; Godinho, F.; Minghelli, S.; de David, S.; Bello, G. L.; Walter, K.; Perdigao, J.; Ramis, I.; da Silva, P. E. A.; Salvato, R. S.
abstract:
BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious cause of death, with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) challenging disease control. Brazil has a high TB burden, and Rio Grande do Sul state reports persistently high incidence and drug-resistance rates. The drivers shaping the regional DR-TB burden remain poorly characterised.

MethodsWe conducted genomic surveillance of confirmed DR-TB cases in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, from January 2023 to September 2024. Clinical isolates underwent genotypic (gDST) and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We analyzed 33 newly sequenced genomes and 267 historical Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes collected in 2011-2019 to characterize resistance, transmission, and spatiotemporal patterns and estimate the contributions of transmitted and acquired rifampicin resistance.

FindingsMolecular testing detected rifampicin resistance missed by pDST, including borderline rpoB mutations in 18.2% and emerging resistance-associated variants in 3% of the 33 analyzed isolates. Conversely, pDST detected baseline bedaquiline resistance missed by WGS in one newly diagnosed case. Among 300 genomes, 181 (60.3%) clustered into 32 genomic clusters at a 5-SNP threshold, including 12 with long-term circulation and several spanning prisons and communities. Sublineage frequencies remained stable over time, whereas we observed marked geographic structuring and localized clonal expansion. Among 178 rifampicin-resistant isolates, transmission accounted for an estimated 79.2-88.2% of resistance, corresponding to 11.8-20.8% of cases arising through de novo acquisition during treatment.

InterpretationOur findings identify active transmission as the main driver of rifampicin-resistant TB in Rio Grande do Sul, with long-term transmission chains extending across both incarcerated and community settings. These results underscore the urgent need to strengthen timely TB case detection and resistance testing, enhance contact investigations, and implement targeted interventions aiming to interrupt persistent transmission chains.
